title: Sovereign Credit Ratings
text:
How risky is it to lend to a euro-area government? In this course, you rate the credit risk of euro-area sovereigns with the minimal rating process (MRP), a transparent, model-based rating process. The MRP asks how large a drop in global risk appetite a country could withstand before it loses access to markets, and how much fiscal effort would take it out of danger.
The rating itself is mechanical: parameters in, rating out. Your job is the judgment around it. In the discretionary adjustments process (DAP), you work in a country team, check whether the parameters for your country are the best defensible ones, and say clearly when they are in doubt.

  
    Rating App
    Set the model parameters for a country and see its rating, its position relative to the fragile region, and how sensitive the result is to each input.
    Open the app →
  
  
    Wiki
    Find the evidence to challenge, corroborate, or fill in the parameters for your country.
    Open the wiki →

text:
Use in the Rating Process
The document type feeds the minimal rating process and discretionary adjustments process for the following tasks:

Growth (C1*): It provides growth forecasts and assessments of potential growth.
Inflation Differential (C2*): It supplies inflation projections and analysis of price competitiveness.
Fiscal Capacity (C3*): It offers fiscal projections and assessments of debt sustainability.
Outlook Factors (R7*): It provides context on structural challenges, demographic pressures, and political risks.

title: Country-Specific Recommendations
text:
Use in the Rating Process
This document type provides bright-line inputs for the minimal rating process (MRP) and the discretionary adjustments process (DAP).

It feeds backstop eligibility (R6*) by stating whether a country is subject to an excessive deficit procedure and the status of that procedure (e.g., whether it is held in abeyance or abrogated).
It feeds the fiscal plan (C3-T*) by assessing compliance with the recommended net expenditure path, including the application of national escape clauses for defence spending or other flexibility measures.

title: Country-Specific Recommendations
text:
Methods

The documents assess compliance with the net expenditure path and the status of the excessive deficit procedure. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses effective action under the excessive deficit procedure, which can lead to the procedure being held in abeyance. ⓘ
Deviations from recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure are calculated, accounting for flexibilities such as the national escape clause for defence spending. ⓘ
The Council of the EU endorses national medium-term fiscal-structural plans and sets maximum growth rates for net expenditure. ⓘ
The European Commission proposes opening an excessive deficit procedure if the deficit is projected to exceed the 3% of GDP reference value. ⓘ
The European Commission adopts a report under Article 126(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to assess compliance with the deficit criterion, but does not propose opening an excessive deficit procedure if the deviation is fully explained by the activated national escape clause for defence spending. ⓘ
The European Commission uses the concept of “net expenditure” and its growth rate to monitor compliance with the EU fiscal framework. The “fiscal stance” is defined as the annual change in the underlying budgetary position, measured as the difference between medium-term potential growth and the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
The document references the “excessive deficit procedure” under Article 126(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union as a bright-line indicator of fiscal compliance. ⓘ
The document uses HICP inflation projections from the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to assess price stability and differentials implicitly through the context of euro-area policy coordination. ⓘ
The document assesses fiscal capacity through the lens of the EU fiscal framework, using net expenditure growth rates, structural plans, and the definition of fiscal stance as the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
Debt sustainability is monitored via general government debt-to-GDP ratios, budget surpluses, and the external position, noting that debt and external debt ratios are expected to fall further. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to project general government balance and debt, based on policy measures known at the cut-off date. ⓘ
Growth projections are derived from the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast, accounting for strong real growth and subsequent adjustments. ⓘ
The document assesses fiscal sustainability risks and the alignment of the budget with the corrective path under the excessive deficit procedure, focusing on net expenditure growth rates and the primary balance implied by the deficit and interest costs. ⓘ
The document references the status of the excessive deficit procedure and the assessment of effective action, which are bright-line inputs for backstop eligibility under the EU fiscal framework. ⓘ
The document identifies macroeconomic imbalances and high government debt as drivers for in-depth reviews under the Alert Mechanism Report. ⓘ
The document assesses compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact and the European Semester, reporting on net expenditure deviations and the activation of national escape clauses for defence spending. ⓘ
The document concludes whether the deficit criterion is fulfilled despite projected deficits exceeding 3% of GDP, due to the activation of the national escape clause, and does not propose an excessive deficit procedure. ⓘ
The document reports on the abrogation of excessive deficit decisions following timely and durable correction, indicating formal closure of the procedure. ⓘ
The document assesses material deviations in net expenditure growth against Council-endorsed ceilings, including cumulative deviations over multi-year periods. ⓘ
The document assesses the fiscal stance and net expenditure growth against recommended maximum rates under the EU fiscal framework (Regulation (EU) 2024/1263). Deviations from these rates are calculated in percentage points of GDP. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to project deficit and debt developments, incorporating policy measures known at the cut-off date. ⓘ
Net expenditure growth is assessed against recommended maximum growth rates established by the Council, accounting for flexibility under the national escape clause for defence spending. ⓘ
Debt sustainability is assessed through the projected debt-to-GDP ratio, noting the impact of the interest-growth differential and stock-flow adjustments. ⓘ
The assessment of excessive deficit procedure eligibility follows the EU fiscal framework (Regulation (EU) 2024/1263), considering the activation of the national escape clause and the Article 126(3) TFEU report. ⓘ

title: Austria
text: This dossier synthesises findings from the OECD Economic Survey (published 2026-03-19), the European Commission Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations (published 2026-06-03), the European Commission Debt Sustainability Monitor (published 2026-02-12), and the European Commission Economic Forecast (published 2026-05-21). The evidence highlights that Austria is emerging from a prolonged 2022–2024 recession with modest growth, though structural headwinds remain, including low productivity, high unit labour costs, and an aging population. The country is under an excessive deficit procedure, which is currently held in abeyance. A national escape clause active from 2026 to 2028 permits increased defence spending. Additional challenges include housing affordability pressures, energy import dependence, and risks in commercial real estate lending. The Debt Sustainability Monitor projects debt to exceed 100% of GDP by 2036 under a no-policy-change baseline, citing medium-term risks driven by a persistent structural primary deficit and ageing costs.

title: Austria
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

[C1-T, structural break in trend]: The OECD notes that potential GDP per capita growth has weakened since the pandemic, driven by a shrinking working-age population, low productivity growth, and high energy costs. Trend labour productivity growth is low, held back by low capital intensity and rising part-time employment. The medium-term growth forecast (1.1% in 2026) deviates significantly from the pre-crisis trend, reflecting permanent output loss from the 2022–2024 recession. ⓘ
[C1-T, Structural break in trend]: The European Commission notes that potential GDP growth is estimated at 0.5% in 2025 and is expected to recover to only about 1% by 2028. This weak outlook is hampered by demographic challenges (population ageing) and sluggish productivity growth, with total factor productivity lagging behind the euro-area average. Real GDP declined by around 1.4% cumulatively in 2023 and 2024, whereas EU GDP grew by 1.5%. ⓘ
[C1-T, structural break]: GDP is expected to grow by 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027. The energy price shock disrupts recovery momentum, weighing on consumption and investment. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

[C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed or serially independent]: The economy experienced a prolonged recession (2023–2024), its longest since 1945, triggered by energy price shocks. Growth shortfalls came in runs, with real GDP declining by 2.8% between Q4 2022 and Q3 2024. The OECD highlights exposure to rare disasters, including energy dependence on imported fossil fuels and geopolitical risks affecting trade value chains. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

[C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap]: Unit labour costs rose by 24% since 2021, among the largest increases in the EU. Industrial competitiveness has been eroded by high energy prices and rapid wage growth following inflation. Electricity prices for non-household consumers were 60% higher in 2025 than in late 2021. ⓘ
[C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap]: Unit labour costs increased by 21% between 2022 and 2025, which is 6 percentage points above the EU average. This has further eroded Austria’s competitiveness, particularly hitting energy-intensive industries hard as industrial electricity prices almost doubled between 2021 and 2023. Manufacturing gross value added decreased by almost 9% between 2022 and 2024. ⓘ



Other growth context

[C1*, context]: The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth of 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, following 0.6% growth in 2025. ⓘ




C2* Inflation differential (Inflation Differential)

C2-E Projections unavailable or implausible
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-T Projections stale

[C2-T, projections stale]: Inflation projections account for mechanical price effects from expiring energy support measures. Energy inflation surged from -7.8% in December 2024 to +5.2% in January 2025 due to the end of the electricity price brake and reinstatement of levies. ⓘ



C2-A Imperfect indexation

[C2-A, imperfect indexation]: Austria has widespread indexation mechanisms linking prices, wages, and benefits to past inflation. About 13% of household spending is directly indexed. A simulation suggests second-round effects from indexation add 0.4 percentage points to inflation in the first year after a 1% shock. ⓘ
[C2-A, Imperfect indexation]: Inflation has persistently exceeded euro-area levels. Cumulative inflation from 2022 to 2025 amounted to around 25%, 5.2 percentage points higher than in the euro area. In 2025, inflation ticked up again after the phasing out of energy relief measures, causing household electricity prices to increase by roughly 36%. In January 2026, inflation fell to 2%, but a new energy shock from the Middle East conflict is expected to raise inflation to 3% in 2026. ⓘ



C2-M Labour-cost versus consumer-price differential
No evidence in the sources yet.


Other inflation context

[C2*, context]: HICP inflation was 3.6% in 2025, projected to stand at 3.0% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. ⓘ

title: Austria
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode

[C3-E, estimator fails or rests on one episode]: The structural primary balance was substantial and negative at -2.5% of potential GDP in 2024. The OECD notes that long-term fiscal pressures from ageing and climate transition will require steady structural adjustments in tax and spending policies. The current tax and spending structure places the debt-to-GDP ratio on an upward trajectory over the long term. ⓘ



C3-T History lags policy

[C3-T, history lags policy]: Austria entered an excessive deficit procedure in July 2025. The European Commission recommended limiting net expenditure growth to 2.6% in 2025, 2.2% in 2026–2027, and 2.0% in 2028. The government aims for spending and revenue measures amounting to 1.3% of GDP in 2025 and 1.6% in 2026 to narrow the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2028. ⓘ
[C3-T, History lags policy]: Austria adopted a medium-term fiscal-structural plan (MTP) for 2025–2029, committing to limit net expenditure growth and reduce the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2028. The trajectory implies an improvement of the structural primary balance of 2.1 percentage points of GDP between 2025 and 2029. An excessive deficit procedure was opened in 2025. ⓘ
[C3-T, context]: Austria has activated a national escape clause from February 2026 to 2028, allowing deviation from recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure to support higher defence spending. ⓘ
[C3-T, history lags policy]: The general government deficit is projected to remain broadly unchanged at 4.1% in 2026 and 2027. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered
No evidence in the sources yet.


Other fiscal context

[C3*, context]: Public debt is expected to increase from around 81.5% of GDP in 2025 to 84.9% in 2027, mostly due to persistent fiscal deficits and subdued GDP growth. Austria faces one of the highest age-related spending pressures in the EU. Total ageing-related spending is projected to rise by about 1 percentage point of GDP between now and 2040. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: Austria’s total tax revenues were 44.0% of GDP in 2025, significantly above the EU average of 39.9%. The tax mix relies heavily on labour taxation (56.1% of total tax revenue in 2024, vs 51.5% EU average). Recurrent property taxes are comparatively low (0.2% of GDP in 2024, vs 0.9% EU average). ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The general government deficit decreased from 4.6% of GDP in 2024 to 4.2% in 2025, reflecting a consolidation package. It is projected to be 4.1% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The fiscal stance was contractionary by 1.1% of GDP in 2025 and is projected to be contractionary by 0.4% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: Net expenditure grew by 2.0% in 2025, which is below the recommended maximum growth rate. It is projected to grow by 2.1% in 2026, also below the recommended maximum. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: Public pension expenditure was 14.5% of GDP in 2025. The document highlights demographic ageing and low effective retirement ages as challenges to fiscal sustainability. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: Healthcare and long-term care expenditure levels are elevated due to fragmentation and cost-inefficiencies. Reforms, including a healthcare reform fund established in 2026, aim to improve efficiency but are constrained by regulatory support and coordination issues. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The tax mix relies heavily on labour income and consumption. Personal income tax brackets have been indexed to inflation since 2023 to prevent bracket creep. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 1.6% of GDP as of 2026, assuming no fiscal policy change from 2027. This level is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The S2 debt-stabilisation indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 4.2 percentage point improvement in the structural primary balance by 2027 to stabilize debt. This is driven by the initial budgetary position (2.3 pps) and ageing costs (1.8 pps). ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The S1 debt-reduction indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.7 percentage point effort to reduce debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ

title: Austria
text:
Debt

R1* Refinancing need (Refinancing Need)

R1-E Components missing or distorted

[R1-E, components missing or distorted]: Gross public debt rose to 80.0% of GDP in 2024. The OECD notes that stock-flow adjustments and interest payments are key drivers. Interest payments increased to 1.5% of GDP in 2024. Non-performing loans in the banking sector rose to 3.0% of total loans in 2024, driven by commercial real estate exposures. ⓘ
[R1-E, components missing]: The debt-to-GDP ratio is forecast to increase to 84.9% by 2027. ⓘ



R1-T Financing behavior shifts

R6-A Bright lines versus real eligibility

[R6-A, bright lines versus real eligibility]: Austria is under an excessive deficit procedure. The OECD emphasizes the need to implement the multi-year fiscal adjustment plan to restore compliance with EU fiscal rules. Effective action is established through the consolidation plan agreed with the European Union. ⓘ




Bank–sovereign nexus and captive creditors

[Bank-Sovereign Nexus]: The document highlights that Austria’s venture and growth capital markets are underdeveloped. Venture capital investment declined to 0.03% of GDP in 2022–2024, well below the EU average of 0.06%. Pension fund assets amounted to only 7.2% of GDP in 2024 (vs 32.3% in the EU), limiting long-term capital availability. ⓘ
[Business Environment]: A lack of risk financing hampers innovative firms. Start-up funding dropped by 56% in 2025. Administrative and regulatory burdens weigh on the business environment. ⓘ

title: Austria
text:
Outlook Material

[Geopolitical risks]: Intensification of geopolitical tensions in Europe could disrupt value chains and raise energy prices. Austria is highly integrated into German and Central European value chains. ⓘ
[Demographic pressures]: Population ageing is projected to reduce the working-age population and increase old-age dependency ratio to 52% by 2050. This will drive up spending on pensions, health, and long-term care. ⓘ
[Energy and Geopolitical Shocks]: The conflict in the Middle East in early 2026 and the ensuing energy shock threaten to derail the modest economic recovery. Austria eliminated direct imports of Russian pipeline gas after Gazprom stopped delivery in November 2024. Dependence on fossil fuel imports exposed the economy to volatile prices. ⓘ
[Labour Market]: Labour shortages persist, with regional mismatches and skills shortages hampering recruitment. Around 24,500 aspiring apprentices were unable to find placements in 2025. ⓘ
[Energy]: Fossil fuels accounted for more than half of the energy mix in 2024. Renewable energy accounted for 83.9% of electricity generation in 2025. The document calls for accelerated roll-out of renewable energy, particularly wind. ⓘ
[Social Situation]: The share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion rose in 2025, disproportionately affecting children. ⓘ

title: Portugal
text: This dossier draws on the European Commission’s Country Report for Portugal (2026-06-03), the Post-Programme Surveillance Report (2026-06-03), and the Country-Specific Recommendations (2026-06-03). It incorporates evidence from the European Commission’s Debt Sustainability Monitor (2026-02-12), the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast (2026-05-21), and the OECD’s Economic Survey (2026-01-06). The evidence highlights solid economic growth outpacing the euro-area average, supported by domestic consumption and investment. Public debt declined to 89.7% of GDP in 2025, with a projected shift to a small deficit in 2026–2027. Key challenges include structural productivity gaps, rising pension costs, housing affordability pressures, and external shocks. Banking stability remains strong. The European Commission notes that net expenditure growth exceeded recommended rates, partly due to the activation of the national escape clause for defense spending.

title: Portugal
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break: Medium-term potential growth reached 2.3% in 2025, but long-term outlook is constrained by an aging population. Structural challenges include a reliance on low-value-added services (80% of economy) and weak innovation output despite high business R&D intensity. ⓘ
C1-T, context: Real GDP growth moderated to 1.9% in 2025. Growth is projected at 1.7% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027. Risks are tilted to the downside due to global geopolitical uncertainty and adverse shocks from storms and energy prices. ⓘ
C1*, context: The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth of 1.7% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, following actual growth of 1.9% in 2025. ⓘ
C1-T, Structural break in trend: The OECD projects GDP growth to stabilize at 1.8% in 2027, down from 2.2% in 2026, driven by a slowdown in global and European growth and rising trade barriers, including an assumed 15% US tariff on Portuguese goods. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: GDP growth is forecast to drop marginally to 1.7% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027. Adverse shocks include severe storms and energy price surges. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, growth volatility: The economy is exposed to external risks, with exports accounting for 44% of GDP. Energy trade deficit is 1.7% of GDP. Climate risks (wildfires, drought) pose significant economic damage potential. ⓘ
C1-A1, Fat tails/Rare disasters: Trade tensions and geopolitical fragmentation pose significant downside risks. A 25 percentage point increase in US tariffs on the European Union, combined with retaliation, could reduce Portugal’s GDP by 0.7% to 1.1% after three years. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, competitiveness gap: Portugal’s labor productivity remains well below the European Commission’s euro-area average, at 68.2% in 2024. High-tech exports account for only 5% of total exports (EU average: 17%), limiting productivity gains. ⓘ
C1-A2, Competitiveness gap: Unit labour costs have increased rapidly, outpacing productivity growth, which remains 17% below the OECD average. This pressures competitiveness, particularly in labour-intensive services. ⓘ



Other growth context

C1*, context: Portugal has made progress in educational attainment, with upper secondary and tertiary completion rates approaching OECD averages. However, skill mismatches remain high, and temporary employment is widespread among youth. Vocational education and training (VET) quality is uneven, and work-based learning opportunities are often short. Investments of EUR 710 million are upgrading facilities across secondary schools and training centres. ⓘ
C1*, context: Employment rates drop sharply after age 55 due to low opportunities, poor health, and lack of flexible work conditions. Chronic health conditions affect 42% of people aged 16 and over in 2024, above the EU average. Occupational risks are high, particularly in micro and small firms. ⓘ
C1*, context: Immigration is a key driver of labour supply, with the foreign-born share rising to 16% in 2024. However, migrant skills are often underutilised, with high rates of overqualification, especially for tertiary-educated migrants. Administrative bottlenecks in visa issuance and qualification recognition persist. ⓘ
C1*, context: Gender gaps in employment and wages are moderate compared to OECD standards. Closing remaining gaps could raise GDP per capita by approximately 5% by 2060. Access to early childhood care for 0-2-year-olds remains low, at close to 50%, with a large gap between income tertiles. ⓘ
C1*, context: The gender wage gap stood at around 10% in 2023. Women are overrepresented in lower-paying firms and occupations. Mandatory gender-disaggregated pay reporting and equal pay audits have improved transparency, but enforcement resources may be limited. ⓘ

title: Portugal
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, policy lag: Portugal has committed to fiscal discipline under its medium-term fiscal-structural plan for 2025–2028, aiming for linear consolidation of 0.1 percentage points of GDP per year excluding European Commission’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) loan impacts. However, permanent measures such as public wage increases and tax cuts risk weakening the budget balance. ⓘ
C3-T, pension sustainability: Public pension expenditure is projected to rise from 12.8% of GDP in 2025 to 15.1% by 2045, peaking in 2046. This poses a medium-term fiscal sustainability challenge. Preparatory steps for pension reform are underway, with a report due in June 2026. ⓘ
C3-T, tax expenditures: Tax expenditures resulted in foregone revenue of 7.2% of GDP in 2024. This includes reduced VAT rates and exemptions. The Commission recommends phasing out fossil fuel subsidies and reforming inefficient tax incentives. ⓘ
C3-T, context: Starting from a surplus of 0.7% of GDP in 2025, the budget balance is forecast at -0.1% of GDP in 2026 and -0.4% in 2027. The 2026 deficit is adversely impacted by support measures for storm damages and higher interest expenditure. ⓘ
C3*, context: Portugal recorded a general government surplus of 0.7% of GDP in 2025, an increase from 0.6% in 2024. The European Commission projects a deficit of 0.1% of GDP in 2026 and 0.4% of GDP in 2027. The deterioration in 2026 is attributed to government support measures for storms and balance-deteriorating fiscal policy measures. The 2027 deterioration is linked to additional measures, including a new housing package and a reduction in corporate income tax. ⓘ
C3*, context: Net expenditure grew by 5.5% in 2025 and is projected to grow by 5.6% in 2026. Both figures exceed the recommended maximum growth rates set by the Council of the EU. The cumulative deviation of net expenditure is 0.4% of GDP for 2024–2025 and projected at 0.6% of GDP for 2024–2026. These deviations are considered in light of the flexibility provided by the national escape clause for higher defense spending. ⓘ
C3*, context: The fiscal stance was broadly neutral in 2025, projected to be expansionary by 1.6% of GDP in 2026, and contractionary by 1.3% of GDP in 2027. This stance includes both nationally and European Union financed expenditure. ⓘ
C3*, context: The European Commission highlights sustainability pressures on the pay-as-you-go pension system due to population ageing. Public pension expenditure is projected to rise from 12.8% of GDP in 2025 to 15.1% in 2045. Concrete policy proposals to alleviate this pressure have not yet been presented by the working group established for this purpose. ⓘ
C3*, context: Tax expenditures are widespread, with value-added tax (VAT) expenditure alone representing 4.3% of GDP in 2024. The European Commission notes that effective action to streamline tax expenditures remains limited despite the creation of a new permanent tax policy unit (U-TAX). ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance (SPB) is assumed to be a surplus of 1.8% of GDP as of 2026, excluding changes in the cost of ageing. This level is described as rather ambitious compared with past fiscal performance. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The S2 debt-stabilisation indicator points to low risk, signaling that Portugal could relax its structural primary balance by 1.4 percentage points and still ensure debt stabilizes over the long term. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The S1 debt-reduction indicator points to low risk, showing that Portugal could relax its fiscal position by 0.8 percentage points and still ensure debt reaches 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
C3*, context: The structural primary balance is projected at 1.8% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 100% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government surplus is forecast to turn into a small deficit of 0.1% in 2026 and 0.4% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, History lags policy: The fiscal stance is accommodative in 2025-2026, with the headline balance projected to deteriorate from 0.1% of GDP in 2025 to -0.6% of GDP in 2026. This reflects higher public investment from the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP), pension increases, and tax cuts. ⓘ
C3*, context: Ageing-related expenditures are projected to rise by 3.8 percentage points of GDP between 2025 and 2045, reaching 27.3% of GDP. Without reforms, public debt could rise above 100% of GDP by 2060. ⓘ
C3*, context: Public spending on social housing was only about 0.1% of GDP in 2022, among the lowest in the OECD. The Recovery and Resilience Plan funding of over EUR 1.2 billion is expected to provide housing for around 26,000 households by 2026. ⓘ
C3*, context: Housing allowances are poorly targeted, with a larger share of upper-income households receiving support compared to low-income households in 2022. Most programmes are available for households with gross annual incomes above EUR 40,000, despite 80% of tax households earning below EUR 28,650. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

C3-A, context: Fiscal outlook is subject to risks relating to state-owned enterprises and liabilities arising from public-private partnerships. ⓘ
C3-A, Default risk/Political feasibility: The OECD warns that further expansionary measures, such as corporate and personal income tax cuts, risk fueling inflation and lowering fiscal buffers. ⓘ



Other fiscal context

C3-E, historical capacity: The general government recorded a surplus of 0.7% of GDP in 2025. Public debt fell to 89.7% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ

title: Portugal
text:
Debt

R1* Refinancing need (Refinancing Need)

R1-E Components missing or distorted

R1-E, contingent liabilities: Risk-increasing factors include vulnerabilities in some public corporations and ongoing requests for financial rebalancing of public-private partnerships (PPPs). ⓘ
R1-E, components missing: Public debt is set to decline to 86.7% in 2026 and 86.0% in 2027. ⓘ
R1-E, components missing: Data not explicitly detailed in country summary, but included in aggregate tables. ⓘ



R1-T Financing behavior shifts

R1-T, context: Gross financing needs for 2026 are estimated at EUR 28.4 billion. The Treasury’s cash buffer is projected to increase to EUR 5.0 billion in 2026. ⓘ
R1-T, bill share: Risk-increasing factors are related to large short-term debt, although it mainly consists of saving certificates held by Portuguese households as long-term savings. ⓘ



R1-A Part of the debt not exposed to the market

R1-A, official loans: Portugal utilizes EU funding significantly. The RRF provides EUR 21.9 billion (EUR 16.4 billion in grants and EUR 5.6 billion in loans). Cohesion policy funds provide EUR 22.6 billion for 2021-2027. These funds are partially off-market or captive in nature, supporting public investment. ⓘ
R1-A, context: As of April 2026, outstanding debt to the European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism was EUR 19.8 billion and to the European Financial Stability Facility was EUR 23.0 billion. Repayments totalling EUR 4.2 billion are due to the EFSM in the second half of 2026. ⓘ
R1-A, captive/official: Mitigating factors include a comfortable cash buffer, a maturity structure with mostly fixed rates, and a large share of debt denominated in euro. ⓘ
R1-A, Off-market/Contingent liabilities: Government guarantees declined to 3.7% of GDP in 2023. Contingent liabilities of State-Owned Enterprises involved in financial activities reached 28.4% of GDP. ⓘ



Other refinancing context

R1*, context: Public investment is expected to reach 4.3% of GDP in 2026, driven by RRF execution, but is set to decline as the RRF ends in 2027. ⓘ
R1*, context: General government debt decreased from 93.5% of GDP in 2024 to 89.7% of GDP in 2025. The European Commission projects a further decrease to 87.6% in 2026 and 86.0% in 2027. This decline is attributed to persistent primary surpluses and a favorable interest-growth differential. ⓘ
**R1*, context**: Government gross financing needs are expected to average around 10% of GDP over 2026-2027 and reach 11% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
R1*, context: Gross financing needs were 9.7% of GDP in 2025. Debt is projected to decline to 83.1% of GDP by 2036. ⓘ
R1*, context: High reliance on passenger cars and an old fleet (average age 14 years) contribute to transport emissions. Charging infrastructure remains limited, with 1.6 charging points per 1,000 registered passenger cars in 2024. ⓘ

text:
Institutions

R6* Backstop eligibility (Backstop Eligibility)

Bright-line inputs

R6-A, bright lines: The Council of the EU activated the “national escape clause” for Portugal in July 2025 to facilitate higher defense spending without immediate compensatory measures. Portugal requested EUR 5.8 billion in EU loans under SAFE (Security Action for Europe) for defense procurement. ⓘ



R6-A Bright lines versus real eligibility

R6*, context: Portugal adhered to the maximum growth rates of net expenditure recommended by the Council of the EU, with a budget surplus in 2025 and a projected near-balance in 2026. ⓘ
R6*, context: The Council of the EU endorsed Portugal’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan on 21 January 2025. The plan covers 2025–2028 and sets maximum growth rates for net expenditure. On 8 July 2025, the Council of the EU allowed Portugal to deviate from these rates under the national escape clause for 2025–2028 to support higher defense spending. ⓘ
R6*, context: The European Commission assessed Portugal’s draft updated National Energy and Climate Plan. It also urges Portugal to fully transpose EU rules accelerating permitting procedures for renewable energy projects. ⓘ
R6*, context: The European Commission reported implementation delays in public transport projects funded by the Recovery and Resilience Plan. ⓘ
R6*, context: The European Commission estimated investment needs to fully transform Portugal’s building stock at EUR 4.95 billion per year. Current funding, including EUR 300 million from the Recovery and Resilience Plan, falls short of these needs. ⓘ
R6*, context: Sovereign bond spreads have fallen to historically low levels relative to Germany, reflecting improved fiscal credibility. ⓘ




Bank–sovereign nexus and captive creditors

Banking stability: Banks’ common equity tier 1 capital ratio was 17.9% at end-2025. Non-performing loans declined to 2.1% in the last quarter of 2025. ⓘ

title: Portugal
text:
Market Signals

Factor decoupling: No specific evidence of persistent spread decoupling from global risk appetite or redenomination premium is provided in the text. Bond spreads are not explicitly detailed in terms of basis points relative to AAA. ⓘ
Factor decoupling, context: The 10-year Portuguese government bond yield stood at 3.4% as of end-April 2026, with the spread over 10-year German Bunds at around 40 basis points. ⓘ
Context: Financial markets’ perceptions of sovereign risk are investment grade, with a 10-year sovereign yield spread of 33 basis points versus the German Bund as of December 31, 2025. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: House prices have outpaced incomes since 2013. Many low-income households are overburdened by housing costs. Variable interest rate mortgages account for 62% of the mortgage stock, passing monetary tightening quickly to holders. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: Housing demand from foreigners accounted for about 10% of the value of all housing transactions between 2019 and 2024, focused on more expensive properties. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: Portugal’s export performance has been strong since 2007, with exports growing faster than export markets. However, indirect effects of trade tensions may weigh on exports via European partners. ⓘ

title: Portugal
text:
Outlook Material

Topic: Housing Affordability: A housing affordability crisis persists, with house prices rising nearly 124% cumulatively from 2015 to 2024. High vacancy rates (30% of dwellings not primary residences) coexist with supply shortages in high-demand areas like Lisbon and Porto. Homelessness reached a record high in 2024. ⓘ
Topic: Healthcare Access: Significant shortages of healthcare workers exist. The National Health Service faces challenges in recruiting and retaining staff, with long waiting times for surgeries and specialist visits. Approximately 15% of the population did not have an assigned general practitioner in early 2025. ⓘ
Topic: Energy Transition: Permits for renewable energy projects are delayed due to complex regulatory frameworks. Wind deployment stagnated, and solar is the main growth driver. Energy storage capacity is below targets. Fossil fuel subsidies remain a barrier to decarbonization. ⓘ
Geopolitical shocks: Portugal faced significant adverse shocks from storms and a steep rise in energy prices due to the conflict in the Middle East. ⓘ
Housing Affordability: Structural challenges in the housing market, including regulatory barriers to investment and weak rental markets, have undermined affordability. Young people are disproportionately affected. Reforms are needed to remove investment obstacles, use existing housing more effectively, and improve rental markets. ⓘ
Climate Adaptation: Portugal is highly exposed to climate risks, including wildfires, heatwaves, and coastal erosion. Lack of stable funding and weak coordination at the local level hold back adaptation progress. Strengthening private insurance coverage is recommended to reduce contingent liabilities. ⓘ
Labour Market Potential: Mobilising untapped labour market potential requires improving school-to-work transitions, creating enabling environments for older workers, maximising the contribution of foreign workers, and strengthening women’s participation. ⓘ
Trade policy: The OECD assumes a 15% US tariff on most European exports, including cars and pharmaceuticals, in its baseline projection. This is expected to weigh on Portugal’s exports and private investment. ⓘ
Defense spending: Portugal has committed to increasing defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, up from 1.5% in 2023, posing additional fiscal pressure. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, Housing vulnerability: Household debt remains a vulnerability. Gross household debt fell to 76% of gross disposable income in 2024, but housing prices have increased significantly, outpacing income growth. A sectoral systemic risk buffer of 4% was implemented in 2024 for residential real estate. ⓘ

title: Luxembourg
text: This dossier synthesizes information from the OECD Economic Survey (2025-04-28), the European Commission Debt Sustainability Monitor (2026-02-12), the European Commission Economic Forecast (2026-05-21), and the European Commission Country Report (2026-06-03). The evidence highlights a slowdown in economic growth driven by structural productivity stagnation and external shocks, alongside a shift from fiscal surplus to deficit. Structural challenges include housing affordability, pension sustainability risks due to demographic aging, and low long-term growth potential. The European Commission classifies medium-term debt sustainability risks as low to medium, though long-term fiscal gaps are significant.

Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample

C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break in trend: Real GDP growth slowed to 1.1% in 2020–2025, significantly below the historical mean of 4.5% in 2000–2007 and 2.5% in 2010–2019. Medium-term forecasts project growth of 1.6% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027, remaining below historical trends. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: Real GDP growth is expected to accelerate to 1.6% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027, supported by services exports. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Labor productivity has stagnated since the early 2010s, with labor productivity decreasing by 1.6% and total factor productivity falling by 1.8% on average per year between 2021 and 2025. The financial sector, accounting for around 25% of value added, shows negative productivity growth, pointing to diminishing efficiency gains. ⓘ
[C1-A2, competitiveness gap]: Unit labor costs increased by about 15% since the end of 2021, leading to an appreciation in the unit labor cost-based real effective exchange rate, although this has partially reversed as nominal wages in neighboring countries caught up ⓘ.
[C1*, context]: Measured labor productivity in Luxembourg is among the highest in the OECD, but growth has stagnated since 2010, driven by declining multi-factor productivity and slowing capital deepening ⓘ.



Other growth context

C3-T, history lags policy: Luxembourg was found not compliant with its medium-term fiscal-structural plan commitments in 2025. The annual deviation from the recommended net expenditure path was 1.3% of GDP, and the cumulative deviation was 0.6% of GDP. The general government balance turned to a deficit of 2.0% of GDP in 2025, after a surplus of 0.9% in 2024, driven by higher spending on defense, housing, and climate measures. ⓘ
[C3-T, history lags policy]: Under unchanged tax and spending policies, gross public debt would remain stable until the late 2040s but would rise rapidly thereafter due to aging-related expenditure, particularly pensions ⓘ.
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government balance is forecast to remain in deficit, improving to -1.2% in 2026 and widening slightly to -1.5% in 2027. ⓘ

C3*, context: Public debt is projected to increase from 26.5% of GDP in 2025 to 30.2% in 2027, mostly due to budget deficits and stock-flow adjustments. Risks to the fiscal plan include lower than projected economic growth and increasing spending pressures from aging and defense commitments. ⓘ
C3*, context: The European Commission projects a structural primary surplus of 1.4% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ

text:
Market Signals

Rollover pessimism: The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 29 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ

title: Luxembourg
text:
Outlook Material

Housing and Labor Market: High house prices and limited supply pose systemic risks. House prices in 2025 were 60% higher than a decade ago. The unemployment rate rose above the EU average for the first time since 2009, reaching 6.5% in 2025. Skills mismatches are significant, with macroeconomic skills mismatches rising to 34.4% in 2025, far above the EU average of 19.2%. ⓘ
Pension Sustainability: The pension system is projected to start running a deficit as of 2029 due to unfavorable demographic dynamics. The pay-as-you-go Pillar I reserve is projected to be entirely depleted by 2048. A 2025 pension reform increased contribution rates by 1.5 percentage points to 25.5% but is deemed insufficient to fully address structural sustainability issues or significantly increase the low participation rate of workers aged 55–64 (51.9% in 2025). ⓘ
Tax Planning: Aggressive tax planning remains unaddressed. Luxembourg introduced a non-deductibility rule for interest and royalty payments, but its scope is limited. The country is identified as a conduit for capital flows, with net inward FDI stock 31 times larger than GDP. ⓘ
[Pension Sustainability]: The OECD identifies the pension system’s sustainability as a major long-term risk, projecting pension expenditure to rise from 9.4% of GDP in 2024 to 17.5% in 2070 without reform ⓘ.
[Climate Transition]: The transition to green growth will have a net negative impact on the budget balance, estimated at around 2% of GDP by 2050, primarily due to lower fuel revenues ⓘ.
[Housing]: Housing affordability remains low, with real house prices falling by about 20% since late 2022, but affordability deteriorating further due to higher interest rates ⓘ.

title: Bulgaria
text: This dossier draws on the 2026 Country Report and the 2026 Recommendation for a Council Recommendation, both issued by the European Commission on 2026-06-03, and the 2026 Economic Survey issued by the OECD on 2026-02-05. New evidence incorporates the European Commission’s Debt Sustainability Monitor from 2026-02-12 and the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast from 2026-05-21. The reports highlight that Bulgaria joined the euro area in January 2026 and faces rising fiscal deficits and public debt. Key themes include an expansionary fiscal stance driven by defense expenditure under the national escape clause and social spending, leading to a proposed excessive deficit procedure. Structural challenges persist in tax collection, public administration, and the independence of the Supreme Judicial Council. The OECD and European Commission assessments note that while public debt remains low, long-term pressures from an ageing population and near-term deficits require consolidation. The Spring 2026 forecast projects growth deceleration due to a global energy shock.

Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, Structural break in trend: Real GDP growth reached 3.1% in 2025, driven by strong domestic demand including private consumption, investment, and public consumption. Private consumption was driven by rising real wages. Investment grew by 11.4%, supported by high credit volumes and increased absorption of Recovery and Resilience Facility funds. ⓘ
C1*, context: Real GDP growth in 2025 was 3.1%. The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP to grow by 2.5% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027 ⓘ.
C1*, context: Real GDP growth returned to its pre-pandemic average rate of 3% in recent years, driven by strong consumption growth supported by robust wage increases and credit growth. Growth is projected to moderate to 2.6% in 2026 as the economy rebalances toward investment. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break in trend: The OECD notes that even at current growth rates, it would take 28 years for Bulgaria to converge to average OECD income levels. Structural reforms (investment, skills, productivity) are estimated to raise per capita GDP by 2.3% in the next ten years and 9% by 2060. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: Real GDP growth is forecast to decelerate to 2.5% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027. Domestic demand growth slows. ⓘ
**C1*, context**: Real GDP growth is projected at 3.0% in 2025, 2.7% in 2026, and averaging 2.3% from 2028 to 2036. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap: Nominal unit labour costs rose by 9.4% in 2025, mostly driven by increases in real wages. Wage growth stood at 10.4% in 2025, following increases of more than 13% between 2022 and 2024. This growth is well above the European Commission average and outpaces labour productivity growth. Unit labour costs remain among the lowest in the EU, but the rapid growth raises competitiveness concerns. ⓘ
C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Unit labour costs (ULC) have tripled since EU accession, surpassing cost growth in other EU competitor countries. This has eroded the country’s cost advantage, as manufacturing is positioned at low value-added segments of global value chains. ⓘ



Other growth context

C1*, context: The labour market remains tight with an unemployment rate of 3.5% in 2025. Labour market tightness, measured by the ratio of vacancies to unemployed workers, is at historically high levels. Labour shortages are acute in healthcare, industry, and construction. ⓘ
C1*, context: R&D expenditure remains low. Public R&D spending was 0.27% of GDP in 2024, well below the EU average of 0.72%. Business R&D expenditure was 0.50% of GDP in 2024, stagnant and below the EU average of 1.49%. ⓘ
C1*, context: Labour productivity growth slowed since the pandemic. The manufacturing sector, which accounts for around 15% of the economy, has seen negative average quarterly growth since 2023 due to higher energy prices and unit labour costs. ⓘ
C1*, context: Bulgaria joined the euro area in January 2026, replacing the longstanding currency board. This should reduce costs and strengthen integration, but a temporary increase in inflation from price resets is a risk. ⓘ

text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode

C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to low risk, requiring only a 1.4% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator also points to low risk, requiring 0.7% of GDP effort to keep debt below 60% by 2070. ⓘ



C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, History lags policy: The general government deficit is projected to increase from 3.5% of GDP in 2025 to 4.1% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. This increase is driven by social spending, increases in public sector salaries, and planned defence expenditure under the national escape clause. Large and permanent increases in expenditure without compensatory structural financing measures have contributed to continued deficits. ⓘ
C3*, context: The general government deficit increased from 3% of GDP in 2024 to 3.5% of GDP in 2025. The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects a deficit of 4.1% of GDP in 2026 and 4.3% of GDP in 2027 ⓘ.
C3*, context: The fiscal stance was expansionary by 2.3% of GDP in 2025. It is projected to be expansionary by 1.0% of GDP in 2026, and contractionary by 1.6% of GDP in 2027 ⓘ.
C3*, context: Net expenditure in Bulgaria grew by 12.3% in 2025, which is above the recommended maximum growth rate. Net expenditure is projected to grow by 5.5% in 2026, and 18.5% cumulatively over 2025 and 2026 ⓘ.
C3*, context: A fiscal deficit emerged following recent crises and unfunded spending increases. The general government balance reached -3.0% of GDP in 2024, down from a surplus in 2019. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The government’s medium-term budget plan relies heavily on higher tax collection to fund increases in pensions, public salaries, and investment, aiming to maintain the deficit around 3%. The OECD recommends front-loaded consolidation to narrow the deficit and maintain the current debt ratio. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The government deficit is set to exceed 4% of GDP, reaching 4.1% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The SPB before cost of ageing is assumed at -1.7% of GDP from 2026 onwards. This is low compared with past performance. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered
No evidence in the sources yet.


Other fiscal context

C3*, context: Bulgaria committed to a structural primary deficit target of 1.8% of GDP by 2028. The fiscal strategy aims to deliver commitments on net expenditure mainly through discretionary revenue-increasing measures with short-term impacts. ⓘ
C3*, context: Total tax revenues amounted to 30.5% of GDP in 2024, well below the EU average of 39.4%. The tax system relies heavily on consumption taxes. The flat-rate personal income tax system limits redistributive capacity. ⓘ
C3*, context: Outstanding tax arrears increased from 2019 to approximately 60% of total revenue collected at the end of 2023, more than double the EU average of 31%. The shadow economy accounts for almost 35% of GDP. ⓘ
C3*, context: Bulgaria faces challenges in tax collection, with high levels of tax arrears and a large estimated shadow economy, which undermines tax compliance and limits revenue capacity ⓘ.
C3*, context: Long-term fiscal pressures stem from an ageing population, with the old-age dependency ratio projected to increase from 38% in 2024 to around 60% by 2070. The pension system deficit reached 5.4% of GDP in 2024. ⓘ
C3*, context: Defence spending stood at 1.3% of GDP in 2024 and is projected to rise to around 2.5% over the next three years, with a commitment to reach 5% of GDP by 2035. ⓘ
C3*, context: Widespread labour informality results in significant fiscal losses. The National Revenue Agency estimated an average annual revenue loss of BGN 420 million in 2023 from underreported wages alone. Broader estimates suggest total revenue losses of 2.2% of GDP from 2017 to 2021. ⓘ

R1*, context: General government debt increased from 23.8% of GDP at the end of 2024 to 29.9% of GDP at the end of 2025. The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects the debt-to-GDP ratio to increase to 32.3% by the end of 2026 and to 35.5% by the end of 2027 ⓘ.

title: Bulgaria
text:
Institutions

R6* Backstop eligibility (Backstop Eligibility)

Bright-line inputs

R6*, context: Bulgaria adopted the euro in January 2026. The European Commission assesses that Bulgaria may face challenges meeting its commitments under the medium-term fiscal-structural plan in the absence of robust consolidation efforts. ⓘ
R6*, context: The European Commission has proposed to open an excessive deficit procedure for Bulgaria, recommending the Council adopt a Decision establishing the existence of an excessive deficit due to non-compliance with the deficit criterion in 2026 ⓘ.
R6*, context: Bulgaria has activated the national escape clause for defense expenditure (2025-2028), allowing deviation from recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure ⓘ.
R6*, context: Bulgaria joined the euro area on 1 January 2026, following positive assessments from the European Commission and the European Central Bank, and decisions by ECOFIN and the EU Parliament. ⓘ
Backstop Eligibility: With euro adoption, Bulgaria is now part of the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), providing additional financial protection. It is also fully integrated into the European banking framework subject to supervisory standards. ⓘ
**R6*, context**: The document notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Bulgaria. ⓘ



R6-A Bright lines versus real eligibility

R6-A, Bright lines versus real eligibility: Concerns about the independence of regulatory bodies and the Supreme Judicial Council persist. The Supreme Judicial Council has operated with an expired mandate since 2022. Anti-corruption measures, particularly in high-level cases, have not improved sufficiently. ⓘ
R6-A, bright lines versus real eligibility: The OECD notes that managing economies without independent monetary policy is challenging. While Bulgaria has been in a similar position under its currency board, the transition requires prudent management of public finances to control domestic demand. ⓘ




Bank–sovereign nexus and captive creditors

Banking Sector: Non-performing loans in the banking sector are cited as a risk-increasing factor. ⓘ



Willingness to pay and political stability

Political stability and rule of law: Strengthening the prosecution of corruption remains key. Bulgaria has not yet set a robust track-record in investigating and prosecuting high-level corruption cases. The independence and effective functioning of the Supreme Judicial Council are essential, as it has operated with an expired mandate since 2022 ⓘ.
Outlook Factors, political stability: A period of political instability with seven early elections in four years ended with a government forming in January 2025, which resigned in December 2025. This instability has delayed reforms and disbursement of EU funds. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, rule of law: Corruption remains a critical issue. The OECD estimates that reducing corruption to Visegrad-4 levels would raise per capita GDP by 2.1% in the long run. Public procurement is identified as a high-risk area for state capture. ⓘ



National institutions
No evidence in the sources yet.

title: Bulgaria
text:
Market Signals

Outlook Factors: The introduction of the euro in January 2026 is expected to lower reserve requirements for commercial banks, potentially fueling credit growth. However, euro area membership will also broaden Bulgarian banks’ access to EU-wide capital markets, which could divert funds away from domestic lending. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: Due to the currency board arrangement and low government debt, long-term government interest rates have largely tracked those in the euro area. Spreads to Germany have risen recently from near-zero levels, reflecting perceived political risk. ⓘ
Rollover pessimism: Mortgage and deposit rates in Bulgaria have diverged from the euro area during the tightening cycle, remaining lower due to high liquidity in the domestic banking system. This has contributed to negative real rates and a housing boom. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 112 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ

title: Bulgaria
text:
Outlook Material

Structural Challenges: Significant regional disparities persist. Economic activity and employment are heavily concentrated in urban areas, particularly the capital, which generates about half of national GDP. The north of the country remains structurally weak. ⓘ
Energy: Wholesale electricity prices were among the highest in the EU in 2025, reflecting reliance on fossil fuels. Renewables surpassed coal in the electricity mix for the first time in 2025. Energy poverty remains widespread. ⓘ
Public Administration: The public administration faces operational and capacity challenges, particularly at regional and municipal levels. The workforce is ageing, and municipalities struggle to attract and retain talent. ⓘ
Justice: The justice system performs efficiently overall, but digitalisation gaps remain. Political independence of regulatory bodies is limited, and the Parliament plays a direct role in appointing regulators. ⓘ
Energy security: Bulgaria adopted fiscal policy measures to mitigate the impact of high energy prices on households and firms, with a projected fiscal cost of 0.1% of GDP in 2026 if measures remain in force until end-2026 ⓘ.
Topic: Climate risks: Bulgaria is vulnerable to extreme weather events such as floods and droughts. Insurance coverage against catastrophic risks remains extremely limited, with only 2% of all insurance contracts covering climate-related risks. ⓘ
Topic: Demographics: The working-age population is shrinking rapidly. Net migration has turned positive since 2020, but emigration of skilled labour remains a serious issue. ⓘ
Fiscal Capacity: The OECD projects that without policy adjustments, the government debt ratio (Maastricht definition) would rise to 160% by 2060 due to current budget deficits and ageing pressures. A consolidation scenario assumes an improvement in the primary fiscal balance by 0.5% of GDP per year over 2027-2033. ⓘ
Climate Risk: Debt deviations under climate scenarios are generally small (below 1.5 pps. of GDP). ⓘ

title: Croatia
text: This dossier draws on the European Commission Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations published on 2026-06-03, the OECD Economic Survey published on 2026-01-30, the European Commission Debt Sustainability Monitor published on 2026-02-12, and the European Commission Economic Forecast published on 2026-05-21. The documents assess Croatia’s economic performance, noting strong but moderating real GDP growth driven by domestic demand, while inflation remains above the euro-area average. Key fiscal issues include a general government deficit exceeding the 3% of GDP threshold in 2025 due to rising expenditures on investments, wages, and pensions, alongside the activation of the National Escape Clause for defence spending. Structural challenges persist, including high unit labour costs, labor shortages, an inefficient housing market, and significant demographic headwinds from a shrinking and aging population.

title: Croatia
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, Structural break in trend: The OECD notes that economic growth is set to moderate but remain robust in 2026 and 2027. Real GDP growth is projected to decline from 3.8% in 2024 to 2.4% in 2027. This moderation reflects slower real disposable income growth moderating private consumption and the end of the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility funding, which will ease investment growth in 2027. ⓘ
C1-T, Structural break in trend: The European Commission notes that wages grew faster than labour productivity in 2025, leading to a further appreciation of the real effective exchange rate and suggesting a loss of competitiveness. Unit labour costs increased significantly, growing by 11.3% in 2023 and 10.8% in 2024, with forecasts of an 8.9% increase in 2025. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: GDP growth is expected to moderate to 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. Domestic demand supports growth, but net exports weigh negatively. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, context: Structural challenges weigh on growth potential, including labor and skills shortages, regulatory complexity, and administrative inefficiencies. Permitting processes are burdensome, and business-to-business payment periods are the longest in the EU. ⓘ
C1-A1, context: The fragmented public research and innovation sector dilutes resources and hinders collaboration, resulting in lower research outputs and reduced scope for technology transfer. Public R&D expenditure as a share of GDP remains below the EU average and has been stagnating. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Wage growth has exceeded productivity growth in recent years, raising concerns about cost-competitiveness. Unit labour costs have risen rapidly, partly mitigated by reduced profit margins, but service price inflation remains high and sticky due to strong wage growth and tourism demand. ⓘ
C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap: Wage growth has outpaced productivity, contributing to higher unit labour costs. The European Commission warns that this persistent gap could weigh on future competitiveness, despite solid goods export growth. ⓘ



Other growth context

C1*, context: The direct impact of recent trade tensions on the Croatian economy is limited, but the country could be indirectly affected by weakening demand from European trading partners, to which it directs about 65% of goods exports. ⓘ
C1*, context: The European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth of 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, following actual growth of 3.4% in 2025. ⓘ
C1-E, Context: Real GDP growth slowed to 3.4% in 2025 from 3.8% in 2024, but remains strong. Growth is projected to continue at decreasing rates. Domestic demand remains the primary driver, supported by rising incomes and employment. ⓘ

C2-E Projections unavailable or implausible

C2-T Projections stale

C2-T, Projections stale: Administered price effects, such as the phase-out of energy support and the reintroduction of fuel price caps in March 2026 due to geopolitical tensions, create mechanical price impacts. The European Commission notes that food price caps have had limited long-term effectiveness in curbing inflation. ⓘ



C2-A Imperfect indexation

Other inflation context

title: Croatia
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, history lags policy: The fiscal stance has been expansionary despite a positive output gap and elevated inflation. The general government deficit target for 2025 was revised up to 2.9% of GDP from 1.9% in 2024, driven by hikes in public sector compensations, social benefits, and cost-of-living support measures. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: A tighter fiscal policy stance is warranted. The medium-term fiscal-structural plan aims to reach a primary structural deficit of 0.4% of GDP by 2028, implying a consolidation need of around 1.8% of GDP between 2025-2028. Further measures to reach these targets have not been specified. ⓘ
C3-T, History lags policy: Croatia has activated the National Escape Clause under the EU fiscal framework to facilitate higher defence spending. Defence expenditure is projected to rise from 1.5% of GDP in 2024/2025 to 1.6% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, context: Net expenditure grew by 10.9% in 2025, exceeding the recommended maximum growth rate. The cumulative deviation for 2024-2025 was 1.4% of GDP, or 0.9% of GDP when accounting for defense spending flexibility under the national escape clause. Projected net expenditure growth for 2026 is 5.7%, leading to a cumulative deviation of 1.6% of GDP (1.0% with flexibility) for 2024-2026. ⓘ
C3-T, context: The Council of the EU allowed Croatia to activate the national escape clause for defense spending in 2025-2028, permitting deviations from net expenditure ceilings to support higher defense expenditure. ⓘ
C3-T, context: The fiscal stance was expansionary by 1.6% of GDP in 2025. It is projected to be contractionary by 0.3% of GDP in 2026 and 0.9% of GDP in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, context: Croatia adopted temporary fiscal measures to mitigate the impact of high energy prices following the war in the Middle East in February 2026, including excise duty reductions and targeted support. The projected fiscal cost is 0.1% of GDP in 2026, or 0.2% if measures remain in force until year-end. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government deficit is projected to narrow from 3.0% in 2025 to 2.9% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered
No evidence in the sources yet.


Other fiscal context

C3*, context: Long-term spending pressures from aging, the green transition, and defense are significant. Without further measures, public debt would rise to about 90% of GDP by 2040. A recent pension reform aims to increase pension adequacy but is estimated to increase pension expenditure by about 1 percentage point of GDP by 2040. ⓘ
C3*, context: Tax revenues stood at 38.4% of GDP in 2024. Tax expenditures accounted for around 4.2% of GDP in 2022. The OECD recommends broadening the VAT base and phasing out inefficient tax expenditures. ⓘ
C3*, context: The general government deficit increased from 2.3% of GDP in 2024 to 3.0% in 2025, driven by nationally financed investments, public wages, and social assistance. The European Commission projects the deficit to decrease to 2.9% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ
C3*, Context: The general government deficit widened to narrowly exceed the 3% of GDP reference value in 2025. This was driven by increased expenditure on public investments, wages, pensions, and social benefits. The European Commission projects a decrease to 2.9% of GDP in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ

title: Croatia
text:
Outlook Material

Demographics: Croatia’s population is shrinking and aging rapidly. The working-age population is projected to decline by about 25% between 2024 and 2050. The old-age dependency ratio is projected to increase from around 40% in 2024 to 59% in 2050. ⓘ
Housing: High vacancy rates (around 15%) and short-term holiday rentals (around 10%) limit the housing stock for residential purposes. Real house prices and rents have increased rapidly in the past decade. ⓘ
Climate: Croatia has significantly reduced greenhouse gas emissions since 2007 but needs additional measures to reach net-zero by 2050. Investment needs for the energy sector are estimated at EUR 45.5 billion (58% of 2023 GDP) to meet 2030 targets. ⓘ
Geopolitical shocks: The conflict in the Middle East is expected to weigh on the macroeconomic outlook, dampening domestic demand. Croatia reintroduced fuel price caps in March 2026 in response to soaring oil prices. ⓘ
Economic security: Croatia faces challenges related to economic security, including dependency on fossil-fuel imports and material import dependency above the EU average. ⓘ
Regional disparities: Significant disparities persist in income, productivity, and public service provision between the capital region and less developed areas like Panonska Hrvatska. ⓘ
Structural reforms: The document recommends consolidating public research institutes, simplifying regulation, merging local administration functions, and accelerating broadband deployment in rural areas. ⓘ
Energy transition: Recommendations include accelerating renewable energy deployment, upgrading electricity grids, phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, and improving energy efficiency in buildings and transport. ⓘ
Social challenges: The document highlights high poverty and income inequality, particularly among older people and those with disabilities, and calls for better targeting of social benefits and improved access to long-term care and healthcare. ⓘ
Labor market: Persistent labor and skills shortages are addressed through recommendations to remove participation obstacles, strengthen education, and upskill workers. ⓘ
Climate resilience: With low insurance coverage against climate risks, the document recommends creating incentives for climate risk insurance and investing in climate-proof infrastructure. ⓘ

title: Ireland
text: The dossier draws on an Economic Survey issued by the OECD on 2025-02-12, a Country Report issued by the European Commission on 2026-06-03, a Post-Programme Surveillance Report issued by the European Commission on 2026-06-02, a Debt Sustainability Monitor issued by the European Commission on 2026-02-12, and a Economic Forecast issued by the European Commission on 2026-05-21. The evidence highlights Ireland’s economic resilience but emphasizes structural exposure to external shocks and high concentration risks in corporate tax revenues. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth surged in 2025, driven by pharmaceutical exports, while domestic indicators suggest a moderation in growth for 2026. Public finances remain strong with a general government surplus, though this is partly inflated by windfall corporate taxes. The reports identify significant vulnerabilities, including reliance on multinational corporations, high energy import dependency, severe housing shortages, and insufficient progress toward climate targets. Fiscal sustainability is challenged by projected increases in age-related spending, large planned public investments, and repeated breaches of domestic spending rules.

title: Ireland
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample

C1-E, broken or dominated sample: Assessing Irish GDP performance is complicated by multinational firms whose large transactions heavily impact national accounts, such as the sharp contraction in real GDP in 2023 due to reduced contract manufacturing, contrasting with a 5% increase in Modified Gross National Income (GNI*). ⓘ



C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break in trend: The OECD projects robust real GDP growth of 3.7% in 2025 and 3.5% in 2026, driven by subsiding volatility from the multinational sector, improving financial conditions, and recovering exports. Modified domestic demand, which excludes volatile multinational transactions, is projected to stabilize around 3.0% in 2025-26, below its long-term average of roughly 3.5%. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break in trend: The European Commission projects real GDP growth to decline by 1.2% in 2026 due to base effects from the front-loading of pharmaceutical exports in 2025, before stabilizing at 3.4% in 2027. This deviation from the historical high growth rate indicates a structural normalization rather than a permanent break in trend, although the domestic economy (modified domestic demand) grew by 4.9% in 2025. ⓘ
**C1*, context**: Real GDP growth is projected at 10.7% in 2025, 0.2% in 2026, and averaging 3.2% from 2028 to 2036. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: GDP is forecast to decline by 1.2% in 2026 due to base effects from pharmaceutical export frontloading, before growing 3.4% in 2027. Domestic activity remains resilient. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed: Downside risks to growth have risen, including geopolitical fragmentation, weaker global demand, tighter capacity constraints, and renewed pressures on energy and food prices. Potential shocks to systemically important large firms could adversely impact the domestic economy and tax revenues. ⓘ
C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed: The economy is highly concentrated in multinational corporations, particularly in pharmaceuticals and ICT. This creates exposure to firm-specific disruptions and external geopolitical tensions, such as US tariff policy changes. The European Commission notes that 84% of business research and development expenditure is performed by large, foreign-owned firms, making the innovation system vulnerable to global headwinds. ⓘ
C1-A1, context: Growth is exposed to risks arising from high concentration of activity within a few sectors dominated by multinational companies, leaving the economy vulnerable to firm- and sector-specific shocks. A persistent energy shock could exert additional downward pressure. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Labour productivity is high at 221.6% of the EU average in 2025, but there is a persistent gap between domestic small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and large multinationals. High costs, including energy and housing, constrain domestic firms. Unit labour cost growth has fluctuated, reflecting volatile GDP trends. ⓘ



Other growth context

C1-A2, context: Real GDP increased exceptionally by 12.3% in 2025, largely driven by strong pharmaceutical exports, reflecting front-loading in anticipation of US tariffs and strong global demand. ⓘ

title: Ireland
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, history lags policy: The domestic spending rule, limiting permanent spending increases to 5% per annum net of tax policy changes, has been systematically breached since its introduction. Budget 2025 implies a net spending increase of 9.2% in 2024 and 5.8% in 2025. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: Public debt is low at 43.2% of GDP in 2023 but stands at 76% of GNI*. Population ageing and digital/green transitions will increase future costs, requiring fiscal reforms to ensure long-run debt sustainability. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: Repeated, sizeable spending overruns, especially in the health sector, undermine fiscal credibility. EUR 3.7 billion of the increase in spending in Budget 2025 was due to overruns compared to Budget 2024. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The Council of the European Commission adopted a recommendation endorsing Ireland’s revised medium-term fiscal-structural plan for 2026-2030 on 10 March 2026. This plan includes a fiscal adjustment over four years and addresses spending pressures. However, the European Commission notes limited progress in broadening the tax base to reduce reliance on corporate taxes, despite country-specific recommendations. ⓘ
C3-T, context: Sustained spending pressures fuel strong current expenditure growth, leading to repeated mid-year revisions of Exchequer expenditure ceilings. The government adopted temporary measures in March and April 2026 to mitigate high energy prices. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance is projected at 1.4% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 50% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The SPB before cost of ageing is assumed at 1.4% of GDP from 2026 onwards. This is in line with past fiscal performance. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government surplus is forecast to decline to 1.4% of GDP in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered: The tax base is narrow and highly reliant on corporate and personal income taxes from multinationals, creating vulnerability to economic shocks. Around one-third of income earners do not pay personal income tax or the universal social charge. ⓘ
C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered: While not indicating default risk, the European Commission highlights that mainstream political platforms and budget decisions rely heavily on transient corporate tax revenues. The government’s medium-term fiscal and structural plan acknowledges that half of current corporate tax receipts are “windfall profits” not linked to domestic activity. A scenario where corporate taxes decline to 2020 levels would turn surpluses into deficits. ⓘ
C3-A, context: Fiscal risks stem from significant concentration of corporate tax revenue in a small number of large companies in pharmaceutical and ICT sectors. A substantial portion of this revenue is estimated to be ‘windfalls’, exposing public finances to profitability and decisions of individual companies and changes in US trade and tax policies. ⓘ



Other fiscal context

**C3*, context**: Public expenditure on health is projected to increase significantly, rising by 0.6 percentage points of GDP by 2040 and a further 0.9 percentage points by 2070 due to an ageing population. The old-age dependency ratio is set to more than double between 2022 and 2070. ⓘ
C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.3% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt, driven by ageing costs. The S1 indicator points to low risk, requiring a 1.0% of GDP effort to reduce debt to 60% by 2070. ⓘ

R6* Backstop eligibility (Backstop Eligibility)

Bright-line inputs

**R6*, context**: Ireland is compliant with the EU fiscal framework. The Council of the European Commission endorsed its revised medium-term fiscal-structural plan in March 2026. There is no excessive deficit procedure open. The European Commission assesses debt sustainability as manageable given the current surplus, though vulnerable to revenue shocks. ⓘ

R6-A, bright lines versus real eligibility: The European Commission’s debt-sustainability risk classification and compliance record are relevant for backstop eligibility, though specific status details are not explicitly detailed in this survey beyond general references to EU rules. ⓘ
R6-A, bright lines versus real eligibility: The new EU fiscal rules are not currently a binding constraint for Ireland, highlighting the need for a more binding and credible domestic framework with stronger political anchoring. ⓘ

Banking stability: Irish retail banks recorded a return on equity of 11.2% in 2025. The fully loaded common equity tier 1 ratio was 15.9% by end-2025. Non-performing loan ratios improved to lowest levels in over a decade. ⓘ
