General government debt (Maastricht) 2023: 20.2; 2024: 23.5; 2025: 24.1; 2026: 27.6; 2027: 31.3% of GDP. Defence expenditure 2025: 3.4; 2026: >5.0% of GDP.
R1-A: Part of debt not exposed to the market. Council agreed to make available a loan of up to EUR 2.3 billion under the Security Action for Europe instrument. Debt increases reflect high deficits and positive stock-flow adjustments. R1-T: Fiscal policy turned countercyclical in 2026, with the budget deficit widening to 4.3% of GDP in 2026 and 4.7% in 2027.
ⓘ ⓘ ⓘ


Cyprus
General government debt 2025: 55.0%; 2027: 45.5% of GDP
R1-A: Part of debt not exposed to the market. Applied for specialized loans under the EU SAFE instrument for defense spending (up to EUR 1.2 billion). Gross financing needs 2026: 1.6 billion EUR.
ⓘ ⓘ


Austria
General government gross debt 2024: 80.0%; 2027f: 85.7% of GDP. Interest payments 2024: 1.5% of GDP
R1-E: Components missing or distorted. Stock-flow adjustments and interest payments are key drivers. Non-performing loans in the banking sector rose to 3.0% of total loans in 2024, driven by commercial real estate exposures. R1-T: Financing behavior shifts. Around one-third of new corporate loans in 2024 went to construction and real estate.
ⓘ


Belgium
General government debt 2025: 107.9%; 2027f: 112.8% of GDP
R1*: Context. Debt increasing driven by high primary deficit and stock-flow adjustments. Defence expenditure 2025: 1.4%; 2026f: 1.6% of GDP. National escape clause activated.
ⓘ


Finland
General government gross debt 2021: 81.4; 2022: 85.6; 2023: 90.4; 2024: 93.7; 2025: 96.3% of GDP. Maastricht debt 2021: 74.0; 2022: 77.5; 2023: 82.1; 2024: 85.4; 2025: 88.0% of GDP.
R1-A: Part of debt not exposed to the market. The Council of the EU has made financial assistance of up to EUR 1 billion available through the Security Action for Europe instrument. Public investment is expected to increase significantly in 2026–2027 due to defence equipment purchases. R1-T: Defense spending has risen rapidly from close to 1.5% to around 2.4% of gross domestic product in 2024 and is targeted to increase to 3% of gross domestic product by 2029.
ⓘ ⓘ


France
General government gross debt 2022: 109.4; 2023: 112.6; 2024: 115.5; 2025: 118.8; 2026: 120.9% of GDP. Net interest payments 2022: 1.7; 2023: 1.9; 2024: 2.1; 2025: 2.3; 2026: 2.6% of GDP.
R1-A: Part of debt not exposed to the market. Eurosystem holdings of government debt are relevant for backstop eligibility. Non-resident share and domestic bank holdings are key for haircut assessment.
ⓘ ⓘ


Germany
General government gross debt (Maastricht) 2023: 62.4; 2024: 63.4; 2025e: 64.6; 2026f: 65.5% of GDP. Net debt 2023: 25.8; 2024: 27.8; 2025e: 30.2% of GDP. Interest expenditure 2024: 1.1% of GDP.
R1-E: Components missing or distorted. Interest payments rose to 1.1% of GDP in 2024 and are projected to further rise. Repayment of pandemic- and energy-crisis-related debt will start in 2028. R1-T: Financing behavior shifts. The fiscal framework changed significantly in 2025 with the reform of the national debt brake, creating fiscal space for a Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality worth EUR 500 billion.
ⓘ ⓘ


Greece
General government gross debt (Maastricht) 2021: 177.0; 2022: 163.9; 2023: 157.3; 2024f: 152.2; 2025f: 148.1% of GDP. Ten-year bond yield 2024f: 3.1%; 2025f: 3.2%. Weighted average maturity 2024: ~19 years.
R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. The structure of public debt is dominated by loans from official institutions. The government repaid all borrowings from the International Monetary Fund in April 2022. R1*: Refinancing risks are limited in the medium term due to fixed interest rates and euro denomination.
ⓘ


Italy
Public debt (Maastricht) 2025 (p): 137.1; 2026 (f): 137.5; 2027 (f): 137.4% of GDP. General government gross debt 2026: 150.9% of GDP.
R1-E: Components missing or distorted. Gross refinancing needs are currently near 25% of GDP. The term structure of outstanding debt is near the euro-area average at close to 8 years. R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. Domestic banks hold a relatively large share of government bonds (approx. 25% of bank assets).
ⓘ


Latvia
General government gross debt (Maastricht) 2024: 46.2; 2025: 46.9; 2026: 48.1; 2027: 50.3% of GDP. General government gross debt 2026: 58.7; 2027: 61.0% of GDP. Defence spending 2026: 4.7% of GDP.
R1-A: Contingent fiscal risks exist related to cost increases in the Rail Baltica project and the financial situation of some state-owned enterprises. R1*: Debt sustainability is sensitive to interest rate movements and growth trajectories.
ⓘ


Ireland
General government debt, Maastricht definition 2023: 43.2; 2024: 38.4; 2025: 35.6; 2026: 33.0% of GDP.
R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. The government established the Future Ireland Fund and the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund in July 2024 to save part of estimated windfall corporate tax revenues. R1-E: Components missing or distorted. Risks from high share of non-bank lending to small and medium-sized enterprises and commercial real estate sector leverage.
ⓘ


Lithuania
Government debt 2024: 38.0%; 2027f: 48.4 % of GDP
R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. Lithuanian firms rely heavily on internal funding (51% of SMEs in 2025 vs 28% EU average) and private equity due to underdeveloped capital markets. Bank loans to GDP are among the lowest in the euro area at 36.1% (end-2024) or 37.8% (Q3 2025).
ⓘ


Luxembourg
Gross general government debt 2025: 26.5%; 2027f: 30.2% of GDP
R1*: Context. Public debt is projected to increase mostly due to budget deficits and stock-flow adjustments. Public investment remained high at 5.0% of GDP in 2025.
ⓘ


Netherlands
General government debt 2025: 44.4; 2027f: 47.0 % of GDP
R1-T: Financing behavior shifts. Government debt rose mainly reflecting loans to TenneT, the electricity transmission system operator, and EBN, the state energy company.
ⓘ


Malta
General government gross debt 2023: 49.6; 2027f: 46.2 % of GDP
R1*: Context. General government gross debt stood at 46.4% of GDP at the end of 2025.
ⓘ


Portugal
Gross general government debt 2025: 89.7; 2027f: 86.0 % of GDP
R1-A: Part of debt not exposed to the market. Outstanding debt to European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism: EUR 19.8 billion; European Financial Stability Facility: EUR 23.0 billion as of April 2026. R1-T: Gross financing needs 2026: EUR 28.4 billion. Treasury cash buffer End-2025: EUR 4.3 billion.
ⓘ ⓘ


Slovenia
General government gross debt (Maastricht) 2023: 68.3; 2024: 66.4; 2025: 65.7; 2026e: 65.6; 2027e: 67.1% of GDP. Net financial debt 2023: 22.2; 2024: 18.9; 2025: 16.4; 2026e: 19.7; 2027e: 21.3% of GDP. Ten-year government bond yield, average 2023: 3.1; 2024: 3.1; 2025: 3.4; 2026e: 3.4; 2027e: 3.4%.
R1-E: Components missing or distorted. General government gross debt remained elevated at 65.7% of GDP in 2025, above the 60% Maastricht threshold. Net financial debt was 16.4% of GDP in 2025. R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. The banking sector is well-capitalised and profitable, with non-performing loans stable at 1.6% in late 2025. Household indebtedness is low at 28% of GDP in early 2025, well below the euro area average of 58.5%.
ⓘ


Slovakia
General government debt, Maastricht definition 2023: 59.7; 2024: 61.4; 2025: 62.6; 2026: 64.6% of GDP. General government net debt 2023: 41.8; 2024: 44.3; 2025: 45.5; 2026: 47.6% of GDP. Ten-year government bond yield, average 2023: 3.5; 2024: 3.4; 2025: 3.6; 2026: 3.6; 2027: 3.6%.
R1*: Context. Public debt (Maastricht definition) rose to 61.4% of GDP in 2024. Without further adjustment, debt-to-GDP could exceed 100% over the next 15 years due to ageing pressures. R1-E: Components missing or distorted. The introduction of a financial transactions tax (FTT) in April 2025 is highlighted as a risk. The FTT imposes a 0.4% tax on corporate bank transactions and 0.8% on cash withdrawals. The OECD argues this is highly distortionary, reduces economic activity, and may increase informality, warranting its abolition.
ⓘ


Spain
General government gross debt (Maastricht) 2024: 101.6; 2025: 99.4; 2026: 97.9; 2027: 97.0% of GDP. Gross financial debt (OECD: 2023): 108.9% of GDP. Net financial debt (OECD: 2023): 77.9% of GDP.
R1-E: Components missing or distorted. Gross general government debt (Maastricht) was 101.6% of GDP in 2024, declining to a projected 97.0% in 2027. OECD data shows gross financial debt at 108.9% of GDP (2023) and net financial debt at 77.9% of GDP (2023). The debt-to-GDP ratio would significantly increase in the 2040s under current policies due to aging costs. R1-A: Part of the debt not exposed to the market. The housing market shows structural challenges with persistent supply bottlenecks. Mortgage lending remains cautious, with a high share of variable-rate mortgages (about 70% of the stock), exposing households to interest rate volatility.
ⓘ

title: European Central Bank
text: The European Central Bank publishes the euro-area AAA yield curve that determines the Safe Rate (C4). It provides inflation projections used for the Inflation Differential (C2). The bank reports government bond yields and spreads, which feed into the Haircut calculation (R4). Together with the European Stability Mechanism, the European Central Bank acts as a backstop provider (R6). Holdings of government bonds by the Eurosystem are a key factor in determining the market-held portion of the debt, affecting the Refinancing Need assessment (R1-A*).

title: Eurostat
text: Eurostat is the statistical office of the European Union. It supplies essential data for the Minimal Rating Process (MRP) and the Discretionary Adjustments Process (DAP). Eurostat publishes the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) used for the Inflation Differential (C2). It provides government debt and deficit statistics, including notifications for excessive deficit procedures, which feed into Fiscal Capacity (C3) and Refinancing Need (R1), specifically the DAP task R1-E. Eurostat also publishes unit-labour-cost-based real effective exchange rates, supporting assessments of competitiveness gaps under Growth (C1-A2) and Inflation Differential (C2-M*).

Eurostat provided data on general government surplus, debt, and defense expenditure cited in the document. ⓘ
The OECD uses Eurostat data for Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) inflation, labour force statistics, and contingent liabilities metrics. ⓘ
Eurostat provided data on population, labour market statistics, accidents at work, social protection statistics, and housing indicators. ⓘ



Slovakia

Data on GDP, unemployment, inflation, and other macroeconomic indicators are sourced from Eurostat. ⓘ
Eurostat provided data on government deficit, debt, and defense expenditure used in the assessment. ⓘ
Eurostat data are used to track AI adoption among enterprises, showing that 18% of Slovak enterprises used AI in 2025. Eurostat also provides data on energy prices and electricity trading. ⓘ



Slovenia

Eurostat provided data on labor market, inflation, and structural indicators. ⓘ
Eurostat provided data on Slovenia’s general government deficit, debt, and defence expenditure. ⓘ



Spain

Eurostat provides statistical data on GDP, inflation, unemployment, debt, and regional indicators used throughout the report. ⓘ
Eurostat provided data on general government deficit and debt for 2024 and 2025. ⓘ



Euro area

The European Commission’s Economic Forecast uses budgetary data validated by Eurostat up to 2025. ⓘ

title: European Commission
text: The European Commission provides bright-line inputs to the Backstop Eligibility parameter (R6) through its debt-sustainability analysis and risk classification. It supplies the gross financing need cross-check for Refinancing Need (R1) via its Debt Sustainability Monitor. The institution runs fiscal surveillance, including assessments under the excessive deficit procedure, which informs Fiscal Capacity (C3-T) and Backstop Eligibility (R6). It publishes the AMECO database, which serves as a source for unit-labour-cost and real-exchange-rate data relevant to Growth (C1-A2) and Inflation Differential (C2-M*).

title: European Commission
text:
Evidence by Country

Euro Area

The European Commission assesses countries under the EU fiscal framework, monitoring compliance with net expenditure growth rates and the implementation of national medium-term fiscal-structural plans. ⓘ
The institution evaluates the activation of the “national escape clause” for defense spending across several member states, permitting deviations from fiscal rules provided fiscal sustainability is not endangered in the medium term. ⓘ
The European Commission published the Debt Sustainability Monitor 2025, classifying medium-term fiscal sustainability risks for 12 Member States as high, 10 as medium, and 5 as low, based on a no-fiscal-policy-change baseline. ⓘ
The European Commission assessed the fiscal sustainability condition for activating the national escape clause for 16 Member States. ⓘ
The European Commission forecasts that EU GDP growth will slow to 1.1% in 2026 and the Euro area to 0.9%, due to an energy price shock from the Middle East conflict. Growth is projected to recover to 1.4% (EU) and 1.2% (Euro area) in 2027. ⓘ
The aggregate EU general government deficit is projected to widen from 3.1% of GDP in 2025 to 3.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission notes that fiscal space is narrower than in 2022, with many Member States burdened by legacy costs and rising defense expenditure. ⓘ
The European Commission issued the Spring 2026 European Economic Forecast and provided a toolbox to address the energy crisis, emphasizing targeted and temporary fiscal measures. ⓘ



Austria

The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 1.6% of GDP as of 2026, assuming no fiscal policy change from 2027. This level is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
The S2 debt-stabilisation indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 4.2 percentage point improvement in the structural primary balance by 2027 to stabilize debt. This is driven by the initial budgetary position (2.3 pps) and ageing costs (1.8 pps). ⓘ
The S1 debt-reduction indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.7 percentage point effort to reduce debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to remain large, reaching around 21% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
A large share of debt is held by non-residents. Contingent liability risks stem from the private sector and state guarantees. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 28 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Belgium

The structural primary balance is projected at -2.3% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 19.7% of GDP in 2025 and are projected to remain elevated. ⓘ
The European Commission notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Belgium. ⓘ
The S2 debt-stabilisation indicator signals high risk, requiring a 7.0% of GDP improvement in the structural primary balance in 2027 to stabilize debt long-term. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 51 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 3 percentage points of GDP higher in 2050 compared to the baseline. ⓘ
GDP growth is expected to decelerate to 0.7% in 2026 and rebound to 0.9% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is projected to stabilize at 5.2% in 2026 and rise to 5.4% in 2027. ⓘ
The debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to increase to 112.8% by 2027. ⓘ



Bulgaria

The structural primary balance is projected at -1.7% of GDP from 2026 onwards. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to low risk, requiring only a 1.4% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. ⓘ
The European Commission notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Bulgaria. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 112 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP growth is forecast to decelerate to 2.5% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027. ⓘ
The government deficit is set to exceed 4% of GDP, reaching 4.1% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. ⓘ



Croatia

The European Commission provided “technical information” at the country’s request, aligning with the medium-term fiscal-structural plan. ⓘ
The European Commission reported that Croatia’s economy grew by 3.4% in 2025, with inflation at 4.4%, significantly above the euro-area average. ⓘ
The Commission noted that the general government deficit widened to narrowly exceed the 3% of GDP threshold in 2025. ⓘ
The Commission assessed Croatia’s implementation of Country-Specific Recommendations and activated the National Escape Clause for defence spending in coordination with the Council. ⓘ
The Commission highlighted challenges in fiscal consolidation, high unit labour costs, and structural issues such as fragmented public administration. ⓘ
The European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projected real GDP growth of 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, following actual growth of 3.4% in 2025. ⓘ
The general government deficit increased from 2.3% of GDP in 2024 to 3.0% in 2025. The European Commission projected the deficit to decrease to 2.9% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ
Net expenditure grew by 10.9% in 2025, exceeding the recommended maximum growth rate. ⓘ
The Council of the EU allowed Croatia to activate the national escape clause for defense spending in 2025-2028. ⓘ
The fiscal stance was expansionary by 1.6% of GDP in 2025. It is projected to be contractionary by 0.3% of GDP in 2026 and 0.9% of GDP in 2027. ⓘ
Croatia adopted temporary fiscal measures to mitigate the impact of high energy prices following the war in the Middle East in February 2026. The projected fiscal cost is 0.1% of GDP in 2026. ⓘ
General government debt decreased from 57.4% of GDP at the end of 2024 to 56.3% at the end of 2025. The European Commission projected a further decline to 55.9% in 2026 and 55.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The Council of the EU endorsed Croatia’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan for 2025-2028. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -1.7% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 12.6% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
GDP growth is expected to moderate to 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 1.7% of GDP as of 2026. This is in line with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to decrease slightly. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to low risk, requiring a 1.5 percentage point improvement in the structural primary balance by 2027. The S1 indicator also points to low risk, requiring a 1.3 percentage point effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to amount to just above 12% of GDP over 2026-2027, reaching 14% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
The net international investment position (NIIP) adjusted for non-defaultable instruments reached +23.8% of GDP in Q3 2024. Financing sources are broadly stable. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 33 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Cyprus

The structural primary balance is projected at 3.3% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 1.4% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP is projected to grow by 2.3% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government surplus is projected to ease to 2.1% of GDP in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary surplus of 3.3% of GDP as of 2026. This is ambitious compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase significantly. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to low risk, requiring a 0.1 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to low risk, with no fiscal effort required to keep debt below 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to decrease, dwindling to 0.4% of GDP by 2036. ⓘ
Substantial cash reserves exist. The share of short-term public debt is low. Financing sources are stable with a diversified investor base. Debt is exclusively denominated in euro. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 19 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Estonia

The structural primary balance is projected at -3.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 2.7% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Estonia. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 57 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP is projected to grow by 1.6% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is set to widen to 4.5% of GDP in 2026 and 4.8% in 2027. ⓘ



Finland

The European Commission stated that Finland’s economy is emerging from stagnation and is expected to transit to broad-based growth in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reported that an excessive deficit procedure was opened in January 2026, although it is held in abeyance due to the activation of a national escape clause for increased defence spending. ⓘ
The Commission projected the general government deficit to rise to 4.5% in 2026 and 4.6% in 2027, with public debt increasing to 93.1% by 2027. ⓘ
The Commission assessed the implementation of Country-Specific Recommendations and the degree of compliance with the EU fiscal framework. ⓘ
The document referenced European Commission data and policies, such as the European Union fiscal framework and the European Union’s Restoration Regulation. ⓘ
The European Commission’s assessment and the OECD’s projections highlighted the need for continued fiscal consolidation to ensure debt sustainability. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -0.9% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 20.1% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Long-term fiscal sustainability risks are medium. The S2 indicator signals that Finland would need to improve its structural primary balance by 4.1 percentage points to ensure debt stabilizes over the long term. ⓘ
The S1 indicator shows that a fiscal effort of 3.1 percentage points would be needed to reduce debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
Financial markets’ perceptions of sovereign risk have remained broadly stable, except for a downgrade by Fitch in July 2025 to the third highest rating, ‘AA’. ⓘ
Real GDP growth is projected to accelerate to 0.8% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is forecast to widen from 3.4% of GDP in 2025 to 4.5% in 2026 and 4.6% in 2027. ⓘ



France

The European Commission projected real GDP growth to remain subdued at 0.8% in both 2025 and 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reported that the general government deficit is projected to remain at 5.1% of GDP in 2026, with debt-to-GDP rising to a projected 118.1% in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission assessed France’s status under the Excessive Deficit Procedure, which is currently held in abeyance. ⓘ
The Commission assessed the implementation of Country-Specific Recommendations and the progress of the Recovery and Resilience Plan. ⓘ
Simulations by the European Commission suggested that linking retirement age to life expectancy could reduce public pension expenditure by 1.0 percentage point of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
European Commission projections were used to estimate the evolution of ageing-related costs in debt sustainability scenarios. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -2.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 21.6% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.1% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 75 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 6 percentage points of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ
Economic activity is forecast to grow at 0.8% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is forecast to remain at 5.1% in 2026 and rise to 5.7% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit before cost of ageing of -3.0% of GDP in 2026, stabilizing at -2.1% from 2027 onwards. ⓘ
The S2 indicator requires a 3.1% of GDP effort to stabilize debt, driven by the initial budgetary position (3.0%) and ageing costs (0.1%). The S1 indicator requires a 3.9% of GDP effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are projected at 21.1% of GDP in 2026, rising to 27.8% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ



Germany

The European Commission highlights prolonged economic stagnation, with real GDP growth remaining near zero since 2019, and projects modest recovery of 0.6% in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reports that the general government deficit is projected to rise from 2.7% of GDP in 2025 to 4.1% in 2027, driven by defense spending and infrastructure funds. ⓘ
The Commission notes that the Council activated the National Escape Clause for Germany to facilitate its transition to higher levels of defense spending. ⓘ
The Commission assesses the implementation of 2025 Country-Specific Recommendations. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -2.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 14.3% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission assessed the fiscal sustainability condition for activating the NEC. It concluded that sustainability is preserved over the medium term. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 4.1% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. ⓘ
Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 3 percentage points of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ
Real GDP growth is forecast at 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is projected to increase to 3.7% of GDP in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027. ⓘ



Greece

The European Commission conducted post-programme surveillance missions in March and April 2026. ⓘ
The Commission assesses that Greece retains the capacity to service its debt. ⓘ
The Commission assesses Greece’s economy as having grown solidly, with real GDP projected to remain robust at 1.8% in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reports that Greece recorded a general government budget surplus in 2024 and 2025, projected to narrow to 0.8% in 2026. Public debt is projected to decrease from 146.1% in 2025 to 134.4% by 2027. ⓘ
The Commission noted that the Council activated the National Escape Clause for Greece to facilitate the transition to higher levels of defense spending. ⓘ
The Commission conducted an in-depth review of Greece under the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure in 2026. ⓘ
The OECD cited the European Commission’s Ageing Report, which projects a decline in ageing-related expenditures in Greece compared to the European average. ⓘ
The OECD referenced the European Commission’s Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI), noting Greece’s rapid progress in digitalising public services. ⓘ
The outlook remains positive for 2024–2026, supported by rising disbursements from the European Commission’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (“Greece 2.0”). ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at 1.8% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 8.2% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Greece. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to low risk, as no improvement relative to the baseline is needed to stabilize debt. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 63 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 6 percentage points of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ
GDP growth is forecast to decelerate to 1.8% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government surplus is set to moderate to 0.8% of GDP in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. ⓘ



Hungary

The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 0.9% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to high risk, requiring a 6.7 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to high risk, requiring a 5.3 percentage point effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to increase, reaching around 21% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
Significant proportion of foreign currency debt exposes the government to exchange rate risk. High exposure of domestic banks to government debt. Sizable amount of redeemable retail government bonds (approx. 20% of central government debt in 2024) poses refinancing risk. High level of contingent liabilities from state guarantees. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 408 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Ireland

The European Commission conducted post-programme surveillance missions in March and April 2026. ⓘ
The Commission assesses that Ireland retains the capacity to service its debt. ⓘ
The Commission projects real GDP growth to decline by 1.2% in 2026 due to base effects from the front-loading of pharmaceutical exports in 2025, before stabilizing at 3.4% in 2027. ⓘ
The Commission highlights that Ireland’s economy is highly concentrated in multinational corporations, particularly in pharmaceuticals and ICT, creating exposure to firm-specific disruptions. ⓘ
The Commission notes that mainstream political platforms rely heavily on transient corporate tax revenues. ⓘ
The Commission assesses that Ireland is compliant with the EU fiscal framework and that the Council endorsed its revised medium-term fiscal-structural plan in March 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reports that gross government debt decreased to 32.9% of GDP in 2025 and is projected to fall to 31.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The OECD references the European Commission’s Ageing Report for economic and budgetary projections for EU Member States from 2022 to 2070. ⓘ
The OECD cites the European Commission’s assessment of the draft Updated National Energy and Climate Plan of Ireland. ⓘ
The OECD notes that the European Commission’s debt-sustainability risk classification and compliance record are relevant for backstop eligibility. ⓘ
The OECD notes that the new EU fiscal rules are not currently a binding constraint for Ireland. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at 1.4% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 2.1% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Ireland submitted a revised medium-term plan following elections, which was still being assessed at the cut-off date. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.3% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund was 20 bps at the end of 2025. ⓘ
GDP is forecast to decline by 1.2% in 2026 due to base effects from pharmaceutical export frontloading, before growing 3.4% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government surplus is forecast to decline to 1.4% of GDP in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027. ⓘ



Italy

The European Commission reports that real GDP growth decelerated to 0.5% in 2025 due to geopolitical uncertainty and trade barriers. ⓘ
The Commission notes that labor productivity stagnation persists, with Italy’s GDP growth lagging behind employment growth. ⓘ
The Commission reports that the general government deficit fell to 3.1% of GDP in 2025 but remains above the EU reference value. ⓘ
The Commission projects the debt-to-GDP ratio to rise from 137.1% in 2025 to 139.2% in 2027. ⓘ
The Commission undertook an in-depth review of the Italian economy under the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission reports that Italy is subject to an excessive deficit procedure, which is held in abeyance. ⓘ
The OECD notes that Italy’s Medium-Term Fiscal-Structural Plan aligns with commitments under the revised EU fiscal rules approved by the European Commission. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at 1.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 23.3% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP is expected to grow by 0.5% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The government deficit is projected to fall to 2.9% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary surplus of 1.1% of GDP as of 2026. This is broadly in line with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to low risk, as no improvement is needed to stabilize debt due to projected decreases in ageing costs. The S1 indicator points to low risk, requiring a 1.6% of GDP effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to remain large, reaching around 27% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
Risk-increasing factors relate to the share of short-term government debt. Risk-mitigating factors include the major share of debt held by domestic lenders and euro denomination. The favourable net international investment position mitigates fiscal risks. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 74 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Latvia

The European Commission reported that Latvia’s economy recovered with real GDP growth of 2.1% in 2025, driven by private consumption and investment. ⓘ
The Commission noted that labor productivity reached 62.2% of the EU average in 2025, lagging behind wage growth. ⓘ
The Commission projected the general government deficit to widen to 4.3% of GDP in 2027, driven by increased defense spending and labor tax reforms. ⓘ
The Commission reported that the Council of the EU activated the national escape clause for Latvia in July 2025 to facilitate the transition to higher levels of defense spending. ⓘ
The Commission noted that the general government debt-to-GDP ratio reached 46.9% in 2025. ⓘ
The document referenced the European Commission’s assessment of Latvia’s National Energy and Climate Plan and its data on cohesion policy funding absorption. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -2.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 8.7% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
GDP growth is forecast to slow to 1.4% in 2026 and pick up to 1.6% in 2027 due to the Middle East conflict. ⓘ
The general government deficit is forecast to increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 2.1% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to remain stable. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.2 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.4 percentage point effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected at around 10% of GDP on average over 2026-2027, rising to around 11% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
A relatively large share of public debt is held by non-residents. The net international investment position is negative. Risk-mitigating factors include the low share of short-term debt and euro denomination. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 85 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Lithuania

The European Commission reports that Lithuania’s real GDP growth reached 2.9% in 2025 and is projected at 3.0% in 2026. ⓘ
The Commission notes that unit labour costs per hour rose sharply in 2022 and 2023, implying risks to cost competitiveness. ⓘ
The Commission projects the general government deficit to rise to 2.7% of GDP in 2027, with public debt increasing to 48.4% of GDP. ⓘ
The Commission reports that the Council of the EU activated the national escape clause for defense spending. ⓘ
The Commission highlights that the 2026 pension reform allowing opt-outs is expected to reduce pension fund assets under management by approximately 41%. ⓘ
The OECD cites the European Commission’s 2024 Ageing Report for projections of ageing-related expenditure. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at -1.3% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 7.3% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP is projected to grow by 3.0% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government deficit is projected to increase to 2.2% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 1.3% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 5.1 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 4.0 percentage point effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to remain low, at around 10% of GDP over 2026-2027, reaching around 11% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
A relatively large share of public debt is held by non-residents. Risk-mitigating factors include the low share of short-term debt and full euro denomination. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 7 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Luxembourg

The European Commission reports that real GDP growth slowed to 1.1% in the 2020–2025 period, driven by stagnating labor productivity. ⓘ
The Commission notes that labor productivity decreased by 1.6% per year on average between 2021 and 2025. ⓘ
The Commission reports that Luxembourg was found not compliant with its medium-term fiscal-structural plan commitments in 2025, with a general government deficit of 2.0% of GDP. ⓘ
The Commission projects gross general government debt to increase from 26.5% of GDP in 2025 to 30.2% in 2027. ⓘ
The Commission notes that the pension system is projected to start running a deficit as of 2029 due to unfavorable demographic dynamics. ⓘ
The structural primary balance is projected at 1.4% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. ⓘ
Gross financing needs were 3.6% of GDP in 2025. ⓘ
Real GDP growth is expected to accelerate to 1.6% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027. ⓘ
The general government balance is forecast to remain in deficit, improving to -1.2% in 2026 and widening slightly to -1.5% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission projects a structural primary surplus of 1.4% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
The S2 indicator points to high risk, requiring a 7.1 percentage point improvement, driven by ageing costs (7.8 pps). The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.0 percentage point effort. ⓘ

Malta

Real GDP is expected to grow by 3.7% in 2026 and 3.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The government deficit is forecast to remain stable at 2.2% in 2026 and fall to 2.1% in 2027. ⓘ

The S2 indicator points to high risk, requiring an 8.1 percentage point improvement, driven by ageing costs (6.5 pps). The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.1 percentage point effort. ⓘ
Gross financing needs are expected to amount to 7.5% of GDP over 2026-2027, decreasing to 6.5% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
Risk-mitigating factors include a high share of domestically-held debt and a positive international investment position. ⓘ
The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 91 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Netherlands

The European Commission reports that the Dutch economy grew by 1.8% in 2025, supported by strong domestic demand. ⓘ
The Commission projects public finances to remain sound, with the government deficit projected to rise to 2.5% of GDP in 2026 before declining. ⓘ
The Commission highlights significant challenges in housing supply, labour market segmentation, and the transition to sustainable energy. ⓘ
The Commission conducted an in-depth review of the Dutch economy under the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure. ⓘ

The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.9 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.5 percentage point effort. ⓘ

The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 16 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ



Portugal

The European Commission conducted post-programme surveillance missions in March and April 2026. ⓘ
The Commission assesses that Portugal retains the capacity to service its debt. ⓘ
The Commission highlights solid economic growth outpacing the euro-area average, driven by domestic consumption and investment. ⓘ
The Commission reports that public debt declined to 89.7% of GDP in 2025, with a general government surplus of 0.7% of GDP. ⓘ
The Commission projects a shift to a small deficit in 2026–2027. ⓘ

Slovakia

Slovenia

Spain

The European Commission notes that Spain’s GDP growth expanded by 2.8% in 2025 and is projected to remain robust in the near term (2.4% in 2026) before moderating to 1.9% in 2027. ⓘ

Spain adhered to the maximum growth rates of net expenditure recommended by the Council in 2025. ⓘ
Following the outbreak of war in the Middle East in February 2026, Spain adopted fiscal policy measures to mitigate high energy prices. ⓘ

The Council endorsed Spain’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan covering 2025–2028. ⓘ

title: Council of the EU
text: The Council of the EU is a key decision-maker in the fiscal surveillance framework. It formally opens and closes excessive deficit procedures and decides on effective action. These decisions serve as bright-line inputs for assessing Backstop Eligibility (R6). The Council also endorses national fiscal plans under the EU fiscal framework, which relates to the assessment of Fiscal Capacity and history-lags-policy risks (C3-T*).

title: European Fiscal Board
text: The European Fiscal Board is an independent advisory body. It evaluates how the European Union fiscal framework is implemented. This evaluation feeds into the assessment of backstop eligibility under task R6-A. It also informs the assessment of fiscal capacity under task C3. The Board provides independent checks on fiscal policy compliance and sustainability. These inputs help rating teams judge whether fiscal institutions are credible and effective.

title: International Monetary Fund
text: The International Monetary Fund supplies core macroeconomic and fiscal data for the minimal rating process. Its World Economic Outlook is the primary data source for Growth (C1), Inflation Differential (C2), Fiscal Capacity (C3), and Refinancing Need (R1) parameters. The Fiscal Monitor provides additional coverage of primary balances (C3). Article IV reports offer a cross-check for gross financing needs (R1). Additionally, loans issued under IMF programs count as off-market financing (R1-A*), reducing the market-exposed portion of sovereign debt.

title: Inflation Differential
text: Δπ is the projected five-year average HICP (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices) inflation of the country minus that of the euro area, using projections from the International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook or the European Central Bank. Common euro-area inflation cancels out of the model, so only the differential matters. The MRP uses min{0, Δπ}: a negative differential is debited in full (about 6.3 percentage points of GDP of borrowing capacity per 100 basis points at the reference calibration); a positive differential is not credited, because differentials in a currency union tend to reverse through competitiveness.

title: Inflation Differential
text:
In the DAP
C2-E covers projections that are unavailable or implausible, with a fallback Δπ = 0. C2-T covers stale projections, with red flags such as legislated wage rounds, administered-price resets, or tax changes with mechanical price effects. C2-A covers imperfect indexation, with red flags such as bracket creep or a high share of expenditure indexed by law; these effects go to fiscal capacity, not Δπ. C2-M covers the labour-cost versus consumer-price differential, with a red flag being a unit-labour-cost differential persistently above the HICP differential, which triggers the C1-A2 check. Not crediting a positive differential is a conservative design choice that the DAP does not assess.

title: Fiscal Capacity
text: The parameter \(s̄\) represents fiscal capacity. It is the highest five-year average primary balance as a share of gross domestic product in the country’s own history. Data comes from the International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook and Fiscal Monitor. This figure shows the surplus the country has demonstrated it can sustain. The parameter \(s_t\) is the current-year projected primary balance. Soft information, such as institutional quality or restructuring history, may place \(s̄\) below this historical estimate. It never places it above the demonstrated maximum. Sensitivity grids typically show \(s̄\) to be the most consequential input.

title: Fiscal Capacity
text:
In the DAP
The discretionary adjustments process assesses fiscal capacity under task C3*. Teams look for three types of issues. C3-E applies when the estimator fails or rests on one episode. Red flags include never having a five-year surplus or relying on one exceptional pre-crisis window. Teams use realism benchmarks or the euro-area median as fallbacks. C3-T applies when history lags policy. Red flags include adopted consolidation or expansion plans and binding corrective paths under the EU fiscal framework. C3-A applies when default is chosen, not just suffered. Red flags include mainstream platforms normalizing restructuring, a collapse of the consolidation consensus, or sustained government instability at high debt.

title: Fiscal Capacity
text:
Methods by Document Type

Country Report

The European Commission assesses fiscal capacity based on the general government balance, primary balance, and structural adjustments. It references the Spring 2026 forecast for deficit projections. ⓘ
The document details general government balance, primary balance targets, tax revenue structures, and spending compositions to evaluate fiscal space and capacity. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses fiscal capacity based on the general government balance and debt sustainability. It notes whether a country has robust public finances and fiscal space to address challenges. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses fiscal capacity through the medium-term fiscal-structural plan. It targets a deficit below 3% of gross domestic product by 2028 and monitors compliance via the excessive deficit procedure. ⓘ
The document analyzes fiscal capacity through the lens of the medium-term fiscal structural plan, assessing the plausibility of the projected primary balance improvements. It notes that while the plan commits to consolidation, the actual implementation and effectiveness of measures remain to be seen. ⓘ
The document relies on the European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for projections of the general government deficit and debt. It assesses fiscal capacity through the lens of the new national fiscal framework (debt anchor of 40% of GDP) and the extended adjustment period under the EU fiscal rules. ⓘ
The Commission’s debt sustainability analysis indicates high fiscal sustainability risks in the medium term for France. The assessment relies on the government’s medium-term fiscal-structural plan and compliance with EU fiscal framework rules. ⓘ
Fiscal projections are based on the medium-term fiscal-structural plan (MTP) and the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast. The primary balance improvement is discussed in the context of the MTP’s commitment to limit net expenditure growth until 2029. ⓘ
The document reports the general government balance and primary surplus as percentages of gross domestic product. It highlights the primary surplus as a key indicator of fiscal capacity, noting it remains above 3.5% of gross domestic product. The impact of adopted consolidation measures (tax cuts, social spending) and defense expenditure increases on the fiscal balance is analyzed. ⓘ
The report relies on the European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for deficit and debt projections. It analyzes the primary balance and the impact of stock-flow adjustments. ⓘ
The document reports primary balance proxies via general government deficit and debt ratios. It details the impact of defence spending and tax reforms on fiscal sustainability. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses fiscal position using both standard GDP-based metrics and GNI*-adjusted metrics. It highlights the distortion caused by windfall corporate taxes in headline budget figures. The primary balance is implied by the general government surplus given the low debt stock. ⓘ
Fiscal projections incorporate the national escape clause for defence spending and tax reforms. The primary balance is implied by the general government balance and interest expenditure. ⓘ
The document relies on the European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast for general government balance, primary balance implications (via primary spending evolution), and debt sustainability analysis based on the country’s medium-term fiscal-structural plan endorsed by the Council. ⓘ
The report details general government deficit and debt projections, as well as primary balance components implied by deficit and interest expenditure. It discusses fiscal governance, including the role of independent fiscal institutions. ⓘ
The document provides data on general government balance, structural primary balance, and debt-to-GDP ratios, which are critical for assessing fiscal capacity and debt sustainability. ⓘ
Fiscal projections are based on the European Commission’s Spring 2026 economic forecast, incorporating the medium-term fiscal-structural plan and assumed policy measures. ⓘ
Fiscal projections are based on the medium-term fiscal-structural plan adopted by Slovenia, which includes measures to contain current expenditure and implement structural reforms. ⓘ
The analysis focuses on the best five-year average primary balance and current-year projected primary balance. The document highlights the need for significant fiscal consolidation to meet EU targets, noting the absence of a comprehensive long-term fiscal strategy. ⓘ
Fiscal assessments are based on the general government deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios, along with the medium-term fiscal structural plan (MTFSP). The primary balance target of 1.6% of GDP is derived from the MTFSP. ⓘ



Country-Specific Recommendations

The document references the “fiscal stance” as a measure of the annual change in the underlying budgetary position, defined as the difference between medium-term potential growth and the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures, including EU-funded expenditure. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission’s definition of fiscal stance, measured as the difference between medium-term potential growth and the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures, including expenditure financed by European Union funds. ⓘ
Fiscal assessments are based on the general government deficit, debt-to-GDP ratios, and net expenditure ceilings set by the Council of the EU. The document notes deviations from these ceilings but emphasizes the position in surplus. ⓘ
The document relies on the European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for projections of general government balance, primary surplus, and debt-to-GDP ratios. It uses Eurostat data for historical actuals. ⓘ
The European Commission assessed effective action under the excessive deficit procedure and evaluated compliance with net expenditure limits while implementing structural reforms. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for deficit and debt projections, incorporating known policy measures up to the cut-off date. ⓘ
The European Commission uses the concept of “net expenditure” and its growth rate to monitor compliance with the EU fiscal framework. The “fiscal stance” is defined as the annual change in the underlying budgetary position, measured as the difference between medium-term potential growth and the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
The document assesses fiscal capacity through the lens of the EU fiscal framework, using net expenditure growth rates, structural plans, and the definition of fiscal stance as the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to project general government balance and debt, based on policy measures known at the cut-off date. It assesses fiscal stance based on primary expenditure changes net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
The document assesses fiscal sustainability risks and the alignment of the budget with the corrective path under the excessive deficit procedure, focusing on net expenditure growth rates and the primary balance implied by the deficit and interest costs. ⓘ
The document defines the fiscal stance as a measure of the annual change in the underlying budgetary position, including nationally and EU-financed expenditure. It is measured as the difference between medium-term potential growth and the change in primary expenditure net of discretionary revenue measures. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses the fiscal stance and net expenditure growth against recommended maximum rates under the EU fiscal framework (Regulation (EU) 2024/1263). Deviations from these rates are calculated in percentage points of GDP. ⓘ
Net expenditure growth is assessed against recommended maximum growth rates established by the Council, accounting for flexibility under the national escape clause for defence spending. ⓘ
The document references Spain’s net expenditure growth exceeding recommended limits and deviation calculations under the national escape clause. ⓘ



Debt Sustainability Monitor

The document uses a no-fiscal-policy-change baseline from 2027 onwards, anchoring the structural primary balance to the 2026 forecast. This implies that any adjustment committed in medium-term plans beyond 2026 is not included in the baseline projection. ⓘ
The baseline assumes the structural primary balance remains constant at its 2026 forecast level until 2036, except for ageing costs. Alternative scenarios include a convergence to historical average SPB and a lower SPB scenario. ⓘ
The long-term fiscal sustainability indicators S1 and S2 measure the required fiscal effort. S2 is the immediate and permanent one-off change in the structural primary balance needed to stabilize public debt over an infinite horizon. S1 is the change needed to bring debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. Risk categories are assigned based on the size of these adjustments (low if <2% of GDP, medium if 2-6%, high if >6%). ⓘ
The document employs stochastic projections with 10,000 shocks to assess uncertainty, covering 80% of simulated debt paths. Deterministic stress tests include scenarios for adverse interest-growth differentials, lower SPB, historical SPB, and financial stress. ⓘ



Economic Forecast

The forecast highlights significant fiscal pressure due to defense investments and rising public debt for Finland. ⓘ
For Sweden, the general government deficit widens significantly due to tax cuts and increased defense spending. ⓘ



Economic Survey

Long-run fiscal projections assume current tax and spending policies unless specified otherwise. The “Consolidation scenario” assumes the primary budget surplus reaches 0.6% of GDP by 2030. ⓘ
The OECD assesses fiscal capacity using the structural primary balance, adjusted for the output gap and one-off measures. The analysis includes long-term projections of ageing-related expenditures. ⓘ
The OECD projects that without policy adjustments, the government debt ratio (Maastricht definition) would rise to 160% by 2060 due to current budget deficits and ageing pressures. A consolidation scenario assumes an improvement in the primary fiscal balance by 0.5% of GDP per year over 2027-2033. ⓘ
The OECD estimates the structural deficit and projects the general government fiscal balance based on policy assumptions, including the impact of recent tax changes and defense spending increases. The underlying government primary balance is used as a key indicator of fiscal effort. ⓘ
The OECD conducts simulations using the OECD Long-term Model to assess fiscal sustainability. Issuing public debt to finance additional defence and infrastructure spending, while using the structural deficit limit, would increase the debt-to-GDP ratio to about 81% by 2045. If rising spending pressures due to ageing are not addressed, debt would increase to about 128% of GDP in 2045. ⓘ
Fiscal sustainability is assessed using stylized debt scenarios. The “Current policies” scenario projects debt rising to 90% of GDP by 2040. The “Fiscal rules scenario” assumes a structural primary budget deficit of 0.4% is reached in 2028, stabilizing debt at around 55% of GDP. ⓘ
The analysis relies on OECD Long-Term Model simulations and European Commission ageing projections to assess debt sustainability and the impact of structural reforms on the primary balance. ⓘ
The document analyzes primary balance projections and debt sustainability scenarios, assuming primary surpluses of around 2% of GDP. ⓘ
The document analyzes primary budget balance figures, reporting positive balances projected for 2025-2027. ⓘ
Fiscal variables, such as public debt and budget balances, are assessed as a share of GNI* to provide a better assessment of the fiscal situation, removing globalization-related distortions. ⓘ
The document analyzes the underlying general government fiscal balance, noting a deterioration driven by pension benefit increases and public wage growth. ⓘ
The document analyzes the underlying government primary financial balance, projecting an increase in the structural fiscal deficit. ⓘ
The OECD analyzes primary balance trajectories implicitly through debt sustainability projections, highlighting the need for fiscal consolidation to offset aging costs. ⓘ
The OECD recommends adopting a national net spending rule to anchor fiscal policy, replacing the obsolete EU-mandated medium-term objective. ⓘ
The survey evaluates fiscal sustainability through stylised debt scenarios, projecting debt-to-GDP ratios under different policy assumptions, including pension reforms and defence spending increases. ⓘ
The analysis relies on Maastricht definition for debt and deficit, as well as OECD calculations for long-term fiscal sustainability. It incorporates scenarios based on AIReF’s projections for aging costs and pension sustainability. ⓘ
The OECD uses illustrative simulations to assess fiscal sustainability. It estimates that combining fiscal adjustment with structural reforms boosting employment could reduce the required primary balance improvement from 5.1% of GDP to 2.4% of GDP to bring debt to 40% of GDP within two decades. ⓘ



Post-Programme Surveillance Report

Fiscal assessments use the Commission’s Spring 2026 Economic Forecast and the Debt Sustainability Monitor 2025. ⓘ

Croatia
General government financial balance 2024: -1.9; 2025: -2.9; 2026: -2.9; 2027: -2.7 % of GDP
C3-T, history lags policy: The fiscal stance has been expansionary despite a positive output gap and elevated inflation. The general government deficit target for 2025 was revised up to 2.9% of GDP from 1.9% in 2024, driven by hikes in public sector compensations, social benefits, and cost-of-living support measures. A tighter fiscal policy stance is warranted. The medium-term fiscal-structural plan aims to reach a primary structural deficit of 0.4% of GDP by 2028, implying a consolidation need of around 1.8% of GDP between 2025-2028. Further measures to reach these targets have not been specified.
ⓘ


Bulgaria
Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: -1.7 % of GDP
C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to low risk, requiring only a 1.4% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator also points to low risk, requiring 0.7% of GDP effort to keep debt below 60% by 2070.
ⓘ

Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: -3.1 % of GDP
C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.9% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator also points to medium risk, requiring a 2.4% of GDP effort to prevent debt from exceeding 60% by 2070.
ⓘ

General government balance 2025: -3.4; 2026: -4.5; 2027: -4.6 % of GDP

Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: -2.1 % of GDP
C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 3.1% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator also points to medium risk, requiring a 3.9% of GDP effort to reduce debt to 60% by 2070.

Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: -2.1 % of GDP

Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: 1.8 % of GDP

Government primary budget balance 2023: -3.8; 2024: 0.3; 2025 (p): 0.6; 2026 (f): 0.9; 2027 (f): 1.1 % of GDP
C3-T, history lags policy: The Italy government has committed to a steady fiscal consolidation path under the Medium-Term Fiscal-Structural Plan (MTFSP) until 2031. This implies primary spending declining relative to GDP each year to reduce the debt ratio.

Underlying government primary financial balance 2024: -1.2; 2025: -1.7; 2026: -2.1; 2027: -2.8 % of GDP
C3-T, history lags policy: The fiscal stance was strongly expansionary in 2025 due to rising defense spending, which increased from 3.3% of GDP in 2024 to 3.7% in 2025 and is expected to reach 4.7% in 2026. The structural fiscal deficit is projected to increase to 2.5% of GDP in 2026.

Structural primary balance (before CoA) 2026–2036: 1.4 % of GDP

Underlying general government fiscal balance 2022: -1.7; 2023: -0.6; 2024: -2.2; 2025: -3.1; 2026: -2.9 % of potential GDP

The OECD projects the deficit to reach 3.3% of GDP in 2026, breaching the 3% Maastricht threshold.

title: Growth
text: The parameter Growth measures the economy’s expansion speed and its stability. It uses two symbols. The first is \(\mu_r\), the real log-growth drift. It is the average of the logarithm of real gross domestic product growth over the last 25 years. The data comes from the International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook. The second symbol is \(\sigma\), the volatility of nominal growth. It is the standard deviation of nominal growth. Nominal growth is real growth plus realized inflation. Default risk depends on nominal shortfalls, so nominal volatility matters. The model does not filter out crisis years. Crisis years are information, not outliers. The nominal drift is \(\mu\). It equals \(\mu_r\) plus expected euro-area inflation plus the inflation differential. Lower drift or higher volatility reduces the country’s borrowing capacity.

title: Growth
text:
In the DAP
Country teams assess Growth in task C1*. They look for four types of issues. First is C1-E, a broken or dominated sample. Red flags include a missing 25-year window, a regime change like euro accession, or a single year moving \(\sigma\) by more than a quarter. Second is C1-T, a structural break in trend. Red flags include a medium-term forecast more than one percentage point from the historical mean for two vintages, or evidence from demographics, energy prices, or sectoral shifts. Third is C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed or serially independent. Red flags include negative skewness, shortfalls in runs, or exposure to rare disasters like energy dependence. Fourth is C1-A2, an inherited competitiveness gap. Red flags include a cumulative real appreciation of unit labour costs against the euro area above 10 log points, or a medium-term forecast not below the historical trend despite such a gap. Type-A issues never justify a higher drift or a lower \(\sigma\).

title: Growth
text:
Methods by Document Type

Country Report

The European Commission uses historical gross domestic product data and medium-term forecasts to assess the Growth parameter. It notes that productivity growth can be uneven across sectors. ⓘ
The document reports real gross domestic product growth, nominal unit labour cost growth, and wage growth to assess economic momentum and competitiveness pressures. ⓘ
The European Commission estimates growth based on the Spring 2026 Forecast. The report highlights the importance of real gross domestic product growth in reducing the debt-to-gross domestic product ratio through the denominator effect. ⓘ
The European Commission estimates potential growth based on production function approaches. It notes stagnant labour supply due to population ageing and lagging total factor productivity. ⓘ
The report uses historical GDP growth data and medium-term forecasts to assess growth potential. It highlights structural factors such as labor market rigidity and low business dynamism as constraints on productivity and growth. ⓘ
The European Commission’s medium-term growth forecasts deviate from historical means, influenced by structural factors such as demographic trends, energy prices, and sectoral shifts in export markets. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to project potential growth (0.5% average 2026-2030) and real GDP growth (0.6% in 2026, 0.9% in 2027). ⓘ
The document uses historical gross domestic product growth data (2023-2025 average of 2.1%) and medium-term forecasts (2026: 1.8%, 2027: 1.6%) to assess the growth trend. It compares the medium-term forecast to the historical mean to identify structural breaks. ⓘ
The document uses historical GDP growth data to illustrate productivity stagnation and regional disparities. It references Eurostat and European Commission forecast data for medium-term trends. ⓘ
The document provides historical real GDP growth and medium-term forecasts from the Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast. It notes productivity levels relative to the EU average. ⓘ
The European Commission uses standard national accounts data for GDP. It also references Modified Gross National Income to better reflect the income standards of Irish residents, excluding globalization effects. The report notes that GDP figures are heavily influenced by multinational activity. ⓘ
The European Commission estimates real GDP growth based on contributions from private consumption, investment, and net exports. Potential growth is linked to productivity shifts towards higher value-added activities. ⓘ
The document provides estimates for real GDP growth, nominal growth components, and detailed analysis of productivity trends using unit labor costs and total factor productivity. It uses 25-year historical data windows for some comparisons but focuses heavily on recent structural breaks in the financial sector. ⓘ
The report provides historical real GDP growth and medium-term forecasts based on the European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast. It highlights structural factors affecting trend growth, such as demographic ageing and low investment. ⓘ
The document provides historical real GDP growth and medium-term forecasts, which are inputs for estimating the growth drift and volatility parameters. ⓘ
The European Commission estimates potential growth and historical trends using standard macroeconomic models, noting structural constraints such as labor productivity gaps and aging demographics. ⓘ
The European Commission uses macroeconomic forecasts based on demographic projections, energy-price regimes, and sectoral shifts to estimate medium-term growth. ⓘ
The document provides forecasts for real GDP growth, highlighting a slowdown in 2025-2026 driven by fiscal consolidation and external factors. The structural break in trend is evident in the deviation of the medium-term forecast from the historical mean. ⓘ



Country-Specific Recommendations

The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Austria of 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, following 0.6% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission notes that Spain’s GDP growth expanded by 2.8% in 2025 and is projected to remain robust in the near term (2.4% in 2026) before moderating to 1.9% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Belgium of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, following 1.0% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Croatia of 2.7% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, following actual growth of 3.4% in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Cyprus of 2.3% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027, following 3.8% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Bulgaria of 2.5% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027, following 3.1% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Estonia of 1.6% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027, following 0.6% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Germany of 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, following 0.2% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission projects real GDP growth for Finland of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, following 0.2% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Greece of 1.8% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027, following 2.1% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Ireland of -1.2% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, following 12.3% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission projects real GDP growth for France of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027, following 0.8% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission identifies weak productivity growth as a key macroeconomic imbalance. Productivity has declined recently and is forecast to stagnate, limiting potential GDP growth. This weakens the capacity to reduce the government debt ratio. ⓘ
The European Commission reports real gross domestic product growth of 2.9% in 2025. The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real gross domestic product growth of 3.0% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027 for Lithuania. ⓘ
Real GDP growth was 2.1% in 2025 for Latvia. The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027. ⓘ
The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth at 3.7% in 2026 and 3.6% in 2027 for Malta, following 4.0% growth in 2025. ⓘ
The European Commission reports that real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2025 was 0.6% for Luxembourg. The Spring 2026 Forecast projects growth of 1.6% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth of 1.7% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, following actual growth of 1.9% in 2025 for Portugal. ⓘ
Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was 0.8% in 2025 for Slovakia. The Commission projects growth of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. ⓘ
Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2025 for Netherlands was 1.8%. The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP to grow by 1.0% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027. Domestic demand has been the main contributor to recent real GDP growth. ⓘ
The Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth of 1.9% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, following 1.1% growth in 2025 for Slovenia. ⓘ
The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP growth for Spain of 2.4% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027, following 2.8% growth in 2025. ⓘ
Low private research and development (R&D) investment remains a major constraint, hampered by a fragmented business structure dominated by low-value micro-enterprises. Business R&D expenditure is insufficient across the whole country due to uneven territorial distribution of public spending. ⓘ
The International Monetary Fund points to insufficient market size and lack of access to equity financing as key factors underlying young firms’ inability to scale up rapidly. The OECD reports that lack of available financing is a considerable long-term barrier to investment for Spanish firms, notably small and medium-sized enterprises. ⓘ



Post-Programme Surveillance Report

Projections for the Growth parameter are based on the European Commission’s Spring 2026 Economic Forecast. ⓘ



Economic Survey

The OECD uses its Economic Outlook database for short-term projections and its Long-Term Model for long-term scenarios. Potential GDP is estimated using structural methods. ⓘ
The OECD uses historical gross domestic product (GDP) growth data and potential growth estimates based on production function approaches, accounting for capital stock, labour force, and total factor productivity. ⓘ
The OECD notes that potential gross domestic product per capita growth has weakened since the pandemic, driven by a shrinking working-age population, low productivity growth, and high energy costs. Trend labour productivity growth is low, held back by low capital intensity and rising part-time employment. The medium-term growth forecast deviates significantly from the pre-crisis trend, reflecting permanent output loss from the 2022–2024 recession. ⓘ
The economy experienced a prolonged recession, its longest since 1945, triggered by energy price shocks. Growth shortfalls came in runs, with real GDP declining between Q4 2022 and Q3 2024. The OECD highlights exposure to rare disasters, including energy dependence on imported fossil fuels and geopolitical risks affecting trade value chains. ⓘ
Unit labour costs rose significantly, eroding industrial competitiveness. Electricity prices for non-household consumers were substantially higher than in late 2021. ⓘ
Real gross domestic product growth is projected to moderate as the economy rebalances from consumption-led to investment-led growth. Labour productivity growth slowed since the pandemic. The manufacturing sector has seen negative average quarterly growth since 2023 due to higher energy prices and unit labour costs. ⓘ
The OECD notes that even at current growth rates, convergence to average OECD income levels would take decades. Structural reforms (investment, skills, productivity) are estimated to raise per capita gross domestic product. ⓘ
Unit labour costs have tripled since European Union accession, surpassing cost growth in other European Union competitor countries. This has eroded the country’s cost advantage, as manufacturing is positioned at low value-added segments of global value chains. ⓘ
Bulgaria joined the euro area in January 2026, replacing the longstanding currency board. This should reduce costs and strengthen integration, but a temporary increase in inflation from price resets is a risk. ⓘ
The OECD uses the OECD Economic Outlook projections for growth and unemployment. ⓘ
The OECD uses OECD Economic Outlook database projections for real GDP growth, unemployment, and inflation to assess growth momentum and potential output. ⓘ
The document uses the OECD Economic Outlook database for growth projections and historical data. Potential GDP growth is estimated to decline from over 4% in 2024 to 0.3% in 2070 due to demographic headwinds. ⓘ
The OECD uses its Economic Outlook Database for short-term projections (2025-2026) and the OECD Long-Term Model for medium- and long-term simulations (up to 2050). The long-term model incorporates scenarios for employment reforms, population growth, and fiscal consolidation. ⓘ
The OECD uses simulations to estimate that structural reforms could raise potential GDP per capita growth by about 0.8 percentage points per year until 2035. ⓘ
The OECD notes that labor productivity has stagnated at low levels over much of the past decade, partly reflecting a collapse in investment during the economic crisis. Real GDP growth has been weak during the last two decades, with negative contributions from labor productivity and employment. ⓘ
The OECD notes that Greece’s GDP-per-capita growth has outpaced the euro area since early 2021, marking a strong rebound from previous crises. ⓘ
Competitiveness gains have been achieved largely on the back of declining real wages. The OECD warns that these gains may be lost if wages grow in excess of productivity. Unit labor costs have been increasing, though less so than in other OECD countries. ⓘ
The OECD uses potential GDP growth estimates to assess structural growth trends. It projects potential growth at 2.2–2.3% for 2024–2026. ⓘ
The OECD notes that weak private investment, innovation, and a shrinking working-age population continue to weigh on potential economic growth. Implementing structural reforms could raise GDP per capita growth by about 1.1 percentage points per year until 2036. ⓘ
Rising wages have led to a strong increase in unit labor costs, weighing on the competitiveness of domestic firms. The working-age population is projected to further decline by 6% between 2024 and 2030. ⓘ
The OECD projects real GDP growth to remain modest at 0.4% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, weighed down by a surge in energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. This follows moderate growth of 0.5% in 2025. ⓘ
Labour productivity growth has lagged the euro-area average since the mid-1990s. The level of multi-factor productivity declined between 2000 and 2022. The large share of small, low-productivity firms weighs on aggregate performance. ⓘ
The OECD uses its Long-Term Model to project potential growth, accounting for policy reforms. It estimates that reforms in institutional quality, labor force participation, and R&D could raise GDP by 3.9% over 10 years and 11.9% over 25 years relative to baseline. ⓘ
The OECD projects robust real GDP growth of 3.7% in 2025 and 3.5% in 2026, driven by subsiding volatility from the multinational sector, improving financial conditions, and recovering exports ⓘ. Modified domestic demand, which excludes volatile multinational transactions, is projected to stabilize around 3.0% in 2025-26, below its long-term average of roughly 3.5% ⓘ.
Assessing Irish GDP performance is complicated by multinational firms whose large transactions heavily impact national accounts, such as the sharp contraction in real GDP in 2023 due to reduced contract manufacturing, contrasting with a 5% increase in Modified Gross National Income (GNI*) ⓘ.
Downside risks to growth have risen, including geopolitical fragmentation, weaker global demand, tighter capacity constraints, and renewed pressures on energy and food prices ⓘ. Potential shocks to systemically important large firms could adversely impact the domestic economy and tax revenues ⓘ.
The OECD uses Modified Domestic Demand (MDD) and Modified Gross National Income (GNI*) to capture underlying domestic dynamics, excluding volatile multinational transactions such as on-shored intellectual property and aircraft leasing ⓘ.
The OECD projects GDP growth to rebound to 3.1% in 2025 and 2.8% in 2026, significantly above the potential growth rates of 3.0% and 2.6% respectively, indicating a closing of the negative output gap from 2023 ⓘ.
Strong wage growth has eroded cost competitiveness. Relative unit labour costs in the tradable sector have increased significantly since 2019. While still lower than in Germany, the differential has narrowed from 40% pre-pandemic to 20% in mid-2024 ⓘ.
Exports of goods declined in 2023, partly due to deteriorating competitiveness, particularly in agricultural and chemical products ⓘ.
The OECD uses historical GDP growth data and projections for 2025–2026. It notes that potential GDP growth is expected to decline due to slower labour and productivity growth ⓘ.
The OECD uses macroeconomic projections to assess growth trends, noting the impact of fiscal expansion and external uncertainty on GDP growth rates. ⓘ
The document uses OECD Economic Outlook projections for real GDP growth, distinguishing between historical data and forecasts for 2025-2027. It also discusses potential GDP growth and the output gap, noting that the output gap is almost closed, supporting the case for fiscal consolidation ⓘ.
The OECD employs long-term modeling to estimate the impact of demographic changes and structural reforms on potential GDP growth. It projects that ageing could reduce the employment share of the population by 4 percentage points over 2025-2060 ⓘ.
