European Commission: Adopted the recommendation for a Council Recommendation. Published the 2026 country report for Bulgaria. Adopted a report under Article 126(3) TFEU assessing Bulgaria’s situation vis-à-vis the deficit criterion. Proposed opening an excessive deficit procedure. Published the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report, not identifying Bulgaria for in-depth review. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure for Bulgaria. Allowed Bulgaria to deviate from these rates under the national escape clause. Adopted a Decision on the existence of an excessive deficit in Bulgaria and a Recommendation to bring the situation to an end. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and defense expenditure. ⓘ
European Central Bank: Mentioned in the context of the European Semester and economic governance framework, but no specific actions or data attributed to the bank in this document. ⓘ
European Commission: Adopted the recommendation for a Council recommendation. Published the 2026 country report for Estonia. Adopted an opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan. Adopted the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report. Published the Competitiveness Compass. Adopted a report under Article 126(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union assessing Estonia’s compliance with the deficit criterion. Provided Spring 2026 Forecast projections. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and other indicators cited in the document. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area. Endorsed Estonia’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan. Activated the national escape clause for Estonia. The Council is the addressee of the Commission’s recommendation. ⓘ
European Investment Fund: Mentioned as a partner in new financing agreements that have expanded access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises. ⓘ
European Commission: Carried out the post-programme surveillance assessments. Provided the macroeconomic and budgetary projections (Spring 2026 Economic Forecast) and the Debt Sustainability Monitor 2025 assessments. ⓘ
European Central Bank: Staff from the ECB participated in the surveillance missions in liaison with the Commission. The ECB’s discontinuation of purchase programs is noted as a factor for Portugal. ⓘ
European Stability Mechanism: Staff from the ESM participated in meetings on aspects related to its Early Warning System. Outstanding ESM loans are cited for all four countries. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: Staff from the IMF participated in the meetings for Greece, Cyprus, and Portugal. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and defense expenditure used in the European Commission’s assessment. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The Council of the EU adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area, endorsed Germany’s medium-term fiscal-structural plan, and activated the national escape clause allowing Germany to deviate from net expenditure limits. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation for a Council Recommendation. Adopted the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast. Assessed the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the country-specific recommendations. Published the 2026 Country Report for Finland. Determined that Finland has complied with its commitments in a satisfactory manner regarding the extended adjustment period. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and expenditure used in the assessment. Specifically, data from Eurostat-Euro Indicators dated 22.04.2026 was cited for deficit and debt figures. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted a recommendation under Article 126(7) TFEU on 20 January 2026 to bring an end to the excessive deficit in Finland. Set maximum growth rates for net expenditure. Activated the national escape clause for defense spending on 8 July 2025. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation for the Council recommendation. Conducted the in-depth review under the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure. Concluded that Greece is no longer experiencing macroeconomic imbalances. Published the 2026 country report for Greece. Adopted an opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan. Projected economic and fiscal variables via the Spring 2026 Forecast. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government balance, debt, and employment indicators used in the assessment. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area. Endorsed Greece’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan. Allowed Greece to deviate from net expenditure growth rates under the national escape clause. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: Conducted surveys indicating that regulatory compliance is a major challenge for investment in Greece. ⓘ
OECD: Provided data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022, showing high underachievement rates among 15-year-old students in Greece. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation for a Council Recommendation. Adopted the 2026 country report for Ireland, the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report, and the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast. Published the Competitiveness Compass strategic framework. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area and the Joint Employment Report. Endorsed Ireland’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan on 10 March 2026. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government balance and debt for Ireland. ⓘ
European Commission: Adopted the recommendation for the Council recommendation on 3 June 2026. Published the 2026 country report for France. Adopted an opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan. Assessed effective action and held the excessive deficit procedure in abeyance. Produced the Spring 2026 Forecast used for projections. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation endorsing the national medium-term fiscal-structural plan of France on 21 January 2025. Recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure corresponding to the corrective path. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and other fiscal indicators used in the assessment. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: Referenced in footnotes regarding investment surveys and the scale-up gap for innovative firms. ⓘ
OECD: Referenced in the assessment of regulatory restrictions to cross-border trade in services and education data. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation. Conducted the in-depth review under Regulation (EU) No 1176/2011. Assessed effective action regarding the excessive deficit procedure. Provided the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast data. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The target of the recommendation. Previously endorsed Italy’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan on 21 January 2025. Recommended maximum growth rates for net expenditure. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and net expenditure growth. ⓘ
European Central Bank: Mentioned in the context of the address for the communication to the European Parliament, Council of the EU, and other bodies. No specific policy actions or data from the bank are detailed in the main text. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: Mentioned in the context of the address for the communication. No specific actions are detailed. ⓘ
European Commission: The European Commission authored the recommendation, published the 2026 country report for Lithuania, adopted the opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan, and produced the Spring 2026 Forecast. It also assessed compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact and the European Semester. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The Council of the European Union adopted the recommendation endorsing Lithuania’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan and allowed the activation of the national escape clause for defence spending. It also adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area. ⓘ
Eurostat: The European Commission relies on Eurostat data for general government deficit, debt, defence expenditure, and social spending figures. ⓘ
European Commission: Adopted the recommendation for a Council Recommendation on Latvia’s policies. Published the 2026 country report for Latvia, the Article 126(3) TFEU report, and the Spring 2026 Forecast. Concluded that Latvia fulfills the deficit criterion despite the planned deficit exceeding 3% of GDP. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted recommendations endorsing Latvia’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan (21 January 2025) and allowing deviation from net expenditure growth rates via the national escape clause (8 July 2025). ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and defense expenditure used in the Commission’s assessments. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: Not explicitly discussed in terms of specific actions, but EU funding instruments (including cohesion policy) supported by the Commission are referenced as essential for implementing reforms and investments. ⓘ
European Commission: Published the 2026 country report for Malta, adopted the opinion on the 2025 draft budgetary plan, adopted the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report, and produced the Spring 2026 Forecast used for macroeconomic projections. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government deficit, debt, and defence expenditure used in the assessment. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation endorsing the national medium-term fiscal-structural plan, set maximum growth rates for net expenditure, and abrogated the excessive deficit decision for Malta. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation and the Spring 2026 Forecast. Assessed Luxembourg’s draft budgetary plan and adherence to expenditure ceilings. Identified structural challenges in pensions, housing, and competitiveness. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Endorsed the national medium-term fiscal-structural plan of Luxembourg in January 2025, setting binding net expenditure growth ceilings for 2025–2029. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government balance, debt, defence expenditure, and labour market statistics cited in the document. ⓘ
OECD: Provided assessments on regulatory barriers in professional services and data on pension replacement rates. ⓘ
European Commission: Issuer of the document. It published the 2026 country report for Portugal, adopted an opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan, and provided the Spring 2026 Forecast projections used in the assessment. It also adopted the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report, which did not identify Portugal for an in-depth review. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The recipient of the recommendation. It previously endorsed Portugal’s fiscal plan and allowed the activation of the national escape clause for defense spending. The document calls for the Council to adopt the recommendation. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on general government surplus, debt, and defense expenditure cited in the document. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation, conducted the in-depth review under Regulation (EU) No 1176/2011, and produced the Spring 2026 Forecast and 2026 Country Report for Slovakia. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted recommendations on net expenditure growth rates, endorsed the fiscal-structural plan, and allowed deviation from expenditure limits via the national escape clause. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on government deficit, debt, and defense expenditure used in the assessment. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: Mentioned in the context of financing options for transport infrastructure development. ⓘ
European Commission: Published the 2026 country report for the Netherlands, concluded that the Netherlands is no longer experiencing macroeconomic imbalances, and adopted the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast. The European Commission also adopted an opinion on the 2026 draft budgetary plan. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Endorsed the national medium-term fiscal-structural plan of the Netherlands and set maximum growth rates for net expenditure. The Council of the EU is the addressee of the European Commission’s recommendation. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on the general government deficit, debt, and net expenditure. ⓘ
European Central Bank: Not directly discussed in the text, but the context of the economic and monetary union and the euro-area recommendations implies the broader institutional framework. ⓘ
European Commission: Issued the recommendation for the Council Recommendation. Published the 2026 country report for Slovenia. Adopted the Alert Mechanism Report (not identifying Slovenia for in-depth review). Adopted an opinion on Slovenia’s 2026 draft budgetary plan. Published the Competitiveness Compass. Produced the Spring 2026 Forecast. Adopted a report under Article 126(3) TFEU. Estimated the budgetary cost of additional measures. Calculated net expenditure growth and deviations. Recommended opening of the excessive deficit procedure is deferred. ⓘ
Council of the EU: Adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area. Adopted the Recommendation on human capital. Endorsed Slovenia’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan with recommended maximum growth rates of net expenditure. Activated the national escape clause for Slovenia allowing deviation from expenditure limits. Adopted the Recommendation allowing Slovenia to deviate from expenditure limits. ⓘ
Eurostat: Provided data on Slovenia’s general government deficit, debt, and defence expenditure. ⓘ
European Commission: The Commission adopted the recommendation for the Council Recommendation. It assessed Spain’s progress on previous country-specific recommendations and implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Facility. It projected gross domestic product growth, inflation, deficit, and debt figures in its Spring 2026 Forecast. It identified Spain as not requiring an in-depth review in the 2026 Alert Mechanism Report. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The Council adopted the Recommendation on the economic policy of the euro area and the Joint Employment Report. It endorsed Spain’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan in January 2025. It allowed Spain to deviate from recommended net expenditure growth rates via the national escape clause. ⓘ
Eurostat: Eurostat provided data on general government deficit and debt for 2024 and 2025. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund highlighted insufficient market size and lack of access to equity financing as key factors limiting the scaling up of young firms in Spain. ⓘ
OECD: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development reported that a large share of Spanish firms, notably small and medium-sized enterprises, cite lack of available financing as a considerable long-term barrier to investment. ⓘ
European Commission: The European Commission opened an excessive deficit procedure for Austria in July 2025. It recommended limiting net expenditure growth and setting a consolidation path to return the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2028. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank’s monetary policy normalization has led banks to shift portfolios away from central bank reserves towards government bonds, increasing exposure to sovereign risk. ⓘ
Eurostat: Data on GDP, inflation, and government debt are sourced from Eurostat and national accounts, with revisions noted for 2021–2024. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: The European Investment Fund is mentioned as a potential partner in supporting Austria’s venture capital market through public financial institutions. ⓘ
European Commission: The European Commission assessed in June 2025 that Bulgaria fulfills the conditions for euro adoption. The Commission’s 2024 assessments estimated Bulgaria’s VAT gap at 6.3% of VAT Total Tax Liability. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank provided positive assessments for Bulgaria’s euro adoption. Four Bulgarian banks are classified as significant institutions and have been subject to direct supervision by the ECB since 2020. ⓘ
OECD: The OECD Economic Outlook 118 database is the primary source for macroeconomic projections. The OECD estimates that structural reforms could raise GDP per capita by 9% by 2060. ⓘ
European Commission: The OECD references the European Commission’s Ageing Working Group projections for public health expenditure and long-term care costs. ⓘ
Eurostat: The OECD uses Eurostat data for employment, unemployment, and inflation statistics. ⓘ
Bank for International Settlements: Not explicitly mentioned as a source, but the OECD references the IMF Financial Soundness Indicators for banking data. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: The OECD references the IMF Financial Soundness Indicators for banking data. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The OECD references ECB data for household and business leverage. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: Stress tests conducted under the International Monetary Fund’s 2025 Financial Sector Assessment Program indicate that French banks and insurance companies would remain resilient under severe adverse scenarios. ⓘ
European Commission: European Commission projections are used to estimate the evolution of ageing-related costs in debt sustainability scenarios. Simulations by the European Commission suggest that linking retirement age to life expectancy could reduce public pension expenditure by 1.0 percentage point of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
European Commission: The European Commission is referenced regarding the EU fiscal framework, providing “technical information” for Croatia’s fiscal plan. It is also cited for the 2024 Ageing Report, which projects aging-related expenditure, and for assessments of rule of law and corruption. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank is referenced in the context of climate risk stress tests for commercial banks, which complement domestic supervisory expectations. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank cut policy rates since June 2024, which has supported private consumption and investment in Finland by lowering borrowing costs. ⓘ
OECD: The OECD provides macroeconomic forecasts, debt sustainability simulations, and policy recommendations. It estimates the fiscal impact of reforms and projects long-term debt trajectories using its Long-Term Model. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: The European Investment Bank’s Investment Survey indicates that almost half of Finnish firms view the green transition as an opportunity, the highest share among the 23 surveyed countries. ⓘ
European Commission: The document references European Commission data and policies, such as the European Union fiscal framework and the European Union’s Restoration Regulation, which impact Finnish fiscal and environmental policy. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank started to ease monetary policy in 2024, reducing policy rates from 4% in June 2024 to 2.25% in April 2025. Market inflation expectations over the next 12 months are well-anchored at the ECB’s target of 2%. ⓘ
European Commission: The OECD cites the European Commission’s Ageing Report, which projects a decline in ageing-related expenditures in Greece compared to the European average. It also references the European Commission’s Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI), noting Greece’s rapid progress in digitalising public services. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The OECD notes that Greece’s return to investment grade made its bonds eligible for the European Central Bank’s standard collateral framework for monetary policy operations. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: The document references International Monetary Fund analyses, which broadly align with the OECD’s debt sustainability simulations. It also notes that Greece repaid its International Monetary Fund loans in April 2022. ⓘ
Eurostat: The OECD uses data from Eurostat for employment rates, unemployment, and other macroeconomic indicators. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: The OECD cites European Investment Bank surveys on regulatory burdens and investment obstacles, noting that perceived burdens in Greece remain high. ⓘ
European Stability Mechanism: The document mentions that improvements in the banking sector’s resilience, noted by the European Stability Mechanism, contributed to Greece’s sovereign credit rating upgrade. ⓘ
Council of the EU: The OECD references the newly adopted EU fiscal rules by the Council of the EU, noting that Greece’s projected debt decline ensures compliance with these rules. ⓘ
European Commission: The document references the European Commission’s assessment of Latvia’s National Energy and Climate Plan and its data on cohesion policy funding absorption. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank is mentioned regarding the monitoring of macroprudential stance and banking sector profitability. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: The European Investment Bank is cited in the context of surveying business constraints. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund is referenced regarding financial soundness indicators and stress tests. ⓘ
Eurostat: Eurostat data is used for life expectancy, healthy life years, and unit labor cost comparisons. ⓘ
European Commission: The OECD notes that Italy’s MTFSP aligns with commitments under the revised EU fiscal rules approved by the European Commission. Revisions to the NRRP milestones were agreed with the Commission in late 2025. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: Data from the International Monetary Fund is cited for Financial Soundness Indicators regarding banking system vulnerabilities. ⓘ
World Bank: Corruption perceptions and governance indicators are sourced from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators. ⓘ
European Investment Bank: The European Investment Bank is mentioned in the context of public guarantee schemes and investment surveys. ⓘ
European Commission: The survey references the European Commission’s Ageing Report for economic and budgetary projections for EU Member States from 2022 to 2070 ⓘ. It also cites the European Commission’s assessment of the draft Updated National Energy and Climate Plan of Ireland ⓘ.
International Monetary Fund: The survey cites International Monetary Fund Article IV consultations and selected issues reports regarding Ireland, particularly concerning financial stability risks and non-bank financial institutions ⓘ.
European Commission: The OECD cites the European Commission’s 2024 Ageing Report for projections of ageing-related expenditure, which indicate a significant increase between 2022 and 2070 ⓘ.
European Commission: The European Commission assessed Slovenia’s 2026 Draft Budgetary Plan as at risk of non-compliance with the EU fiscal framework but noted that deviations were within allowed flexibility margins. The Commission also confirmed the implementation status of the Slovenian Recovery and Resilience Plan. ⓘ
European Central Bank: The European Central Bank implemented a policy rate cut in June 2025, leading to decreasing interest rates on loans and deposits in Slovenia. The Bank of Slovenia (national central bank) adjusted macroprudential tools, such as increasing the countercyclical capital buffer. ⓘ
International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund is cited regarding the assessment of active labour market policies and the fiscal impact of pension reforms. ⓘ
European Commission: The document references the EU Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) funds, which have supported investment and growth. The European Commission has endorsed Spain’s medium-term fiscal plan. The document also notes the alignment of national fiscal rules with the new EU fiscal framework overseen by the Commission ⓘ.
European Central Bank: The Bank of Spain has introduced a countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) of 0.5%, increasing to 1%, aligning with European Central Bank guidance on climate risk and financial stability. The ECB’s projections on the impact of RRP funds on potential growth are cited ⓘ.
International Monetary Fund: The document cites IMF stress tests indicating the banking sector is well-positioned to withstand shocks. It also references IMF Article IV consultations regarding fiscal policy and environmental taxation ⓘ.
European Investment Bank: The document mentions the European Investment Bank’s role in supporting infrastructure and green transition projects, although specific financial flows are not detailed in the extracted figures ⓘ.
World Bank: The World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators are cited in the context of corruption and public procurement challenges in Spain ⓘ.
European Commission: The European Commission notified a reversal of a milestone in April 2024 regarding the approval of national expenditure ceilings under the EU Recovery and Resilience Plan. The Commission also issued Country-Specific Recommendations in 2025, highlighting weaknesses in investment planning and transparency ⓘ.
European Investment Bank: The European Investment Bank (EIB) Investment Survey data are cited to show that lack of skilled staff is a pressing obstacle for investment in Slovakia. The EIB also notes that few companies report financing constraints as a major obstacle to investment ⓘ.
International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) conducted stress tests in 2024, concluding that the Slovak banking sector possesses strong capacity to absorb shocks. The IMF’s Article IV Consultation Staff Report is also cited regarding pension reforms ⓘ.
Eurostat: Eurostat data are used to track AI adoption among enterprises, showing that 18% of Slovak enterprises used AI in 2025. Eurostat also provides data on energy prices and electricity trading ⓘ.

title: Growth
text:
Country Overview




Country
Latest figures
Red flags with reported evidence
Source




Austria
Real GDP growth 2023: -0.7%; 2024: -0.8%; 2025: 0.6%; 2026f: 1.1%; 2027f: 1.3%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Potential GDP per capita growth weakened since the pandemic, driven by shrinking working-age population and low productivity. Medium-term forecast deviates significantly from pre-crisis trend. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Prolonged recession (2023–2024) with growth shortfalls in runs. Exposure to rare disasters including energy dependence and geopolitical risks. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Unit labour costs rose by 24% since 2021. Industrial competitiveness eroded by high energy prices and rapid wage growth.
ⓘ


Belgium
Real GDP growth 2025: 1.0%; 2026f: 0.7%; 2027f: 0.9%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth decelerates to 0.7% driven by weaker demand. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Energy supply disruptions and price volatility. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Low business dynamism and high labour costs.
ⓘ


Croatia
Real GDP growth 2024: 3.8%; 2025: 3.2%; 2026f: 2.7%; 2027f: 2.4%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth moderates to 2.4% in 2027 due to slower real disposable income growth and end of EU funding. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Wage growth exceeded productivity growth. Unit labour costs rose rapidly, eroding cost-competitiveness.
ⓘ


Cyprus
Real GDP growth 2025: 3.8%; 2026f: 2.3%; 2027f: 2.7%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Infrastructure projects face delays. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: High energy import dependency and fossil fuel reliance. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Low R&D investment and weak knowledge valorisation.
ⓘ


Spain
Real GDP growth 2024: 3.5%; 2025: 2.9%; 2026: 2.2%; 2027: 1.8%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth projected to moderate to 2.2% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027 due to weakening external demand. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Risks tilted to the downside due to escalating global trade measures and climate-related shocks. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Labor productivity growth remains sluggish compared to peer countries. GDP per capita has not converged to peer levels.
ⓘ


Bulgaria
Real GDP growth 2023: 1.7%; 2024: 3.4%; 2025: 3.0%; 2026f: 2.6%; 2027f: 2.4%
C1-E Broken or dominated sample: Euro adoption in January 2026. C1-T Structural break in trend: Even at current growth rates, convergence to average OECD income levels takes decades. Structural reforms needed to raise per capita GDP. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Unit labour costs tripled since EU accession, eroding cost advantage. Manufacturing positioned at low value-added segments.
ⓘ


Estonia
Real GDP growth 2023: -2.8%; 2024: -0.1%; 2025: 0.5%; 2026f: 1.8%; 2027f: 2.7%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth recovers to 1.8% in 2026 supported by fiscal stimulus. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Unit labour costs in manufacturing rose significantly, leading to a 15% fall in export market share volume between 2022 and 2024.
ⓘ


Finland
Real GDP growth 2023: -0.9%; 2024: -0.1%; 2025f: 0.7%; 2026f: 1.1%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth recovers modestly but lags behind Nordic peers. Productivity growth weakened significantly. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Fragile recovery with downside risks skewed by geopolitical tensions, cyber-attacks, and trade policy uncertainty.
ⓘ


France
Real GDP growth 2022: 1.9%; 2023: 1.4%; 2024: 0.9%; 2025f: 0.7%; 2026f: 0.8%
C1* Context: Growth remains subdued. GDP per capita growth lagged behind top-performing OECD economies. Political uncertainty reduced GDP growth by an estimated 0.2–0.4 percentage points. Labour productivity remains limited by weak technology adoption.
ⓘ


Germany
Real GDP growth 2023: -0.1%; 2024: -0.2%; 2025f: 0.4%; 2026f: 1.2%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Stagnation driven by structural challenges including high administrative burdens and weak business dynamism. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Rising trade policy tensions and supply chain disruptions weighed on investor confidence. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Export competitiveness deteriorated due to rising unit labour costs.
ⓘ


Greece
Real GDP growth 2021: 5.7; 2022: 2.3; 2023: 2.3; 2024f: 2.3; 2025f: 2.2; 2026f: 2.5
C1-T Structural break in trend: Labour productivity has stagnated at low levels over much of the past decade. Real GDP growth has been weak during the last two decades. C1-E Broken or dominated sample: GDP-per-capita growth has outpaced the euro area since early 2021, marking a strong rebound from previous crises. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Competitiveness gains achieved on back of declining real wages. Unit labor costs increasing.
ⓘ


Italy
Real GDP growth 2023: 0.9; 2024: 0.8; 2025 (p): 0.5; 2026 (f): 0.4; 2027 (f): 0.6
C1-T Structural break in trend: Real GDP growth projected to remain modest at 0.4% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, weighed down by energy price surges. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Labour productivity growth has lagged the euro-area average since the mid-1990s. Multi-factor productivity declined between 2000 and 2022.
ⓘ


Latvia
Real GDP growth 2024: 0.0; 2025: 2.1; 2026: 1.9; 2027: 2.2
C1-T Structural break: Weak private investment, innovation, and a shrinking working-age population continue to weigh on potential economic growth. C1-A2 Competitiveness gap: Rising wages have led to a strong increase in unit labor costs, weighing on competitiveness. Working-age population projected to decline by 6% between 2024 and 2030.
ⓘ


Ireland
Real GDP growth 2023: -5.7; 2024: 0.3; 2025: 3.7; 2026: 3.5
C1-T Structural break in trend: Robust real GDP growth projected for 2025-2026 driven by subsiding volatility from multinational sector. Modified domestic demand projected to stabilize around 3.0% in 2025-26, below long-term average of roughly 3.5%. C1-E Broken or dominated sample: GDP performance complicated by multinational firms whose large transactions heavily impact national accounts. C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed: Downside risks include geopolitical fragmentation and potential shocks to systemically important large firms.
ⓘ


Lithuania
Real GDP growth 2021: 6.4; 2022: 2.5; 2023: 0.3; 2024: 2.7; 2025: 3.1; 2026: 2.8
C1-T Structural break in trend: GDP growth rebound to 3.1% in 2025 and 2.8% in 2026, significantly above potential growth rates, indicating closing of negative output gap. Potential GDP growth expected to decline due to slower labour and productivity growth. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Strong wage growth has eroded cost competitiveness. Relative unit labour costs in tradable sector increased significantly since 2019.
ⓘ


Luxembourg
Real GDP growth 2025: 0.6%; 2026e: 1.6%; 2027f: 2.0%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Real GDP growth slowed to 1.1% in 2020–2025, significantly below historical mean. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Labor productivity has stagnated since the early 2010s.
ⓘ


Netherlands
Real GDP growth 2025: 1.8%; 2026f: 1.0%; 2027f: 1.1%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Medium-term forecast deviates from historical mean; structural bottlenecks constrain productivity. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: High labour costs and energy prices undermine competitiveness.
ⓘ


Malta
Real GDP growth 2025: 4.0%; 2026f: 3.7%; 2027f: 3.6%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Nominal wage growth projected to ease. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Labour shortages persist despite strong employment growth.
ⓘ


Portugal
Real GDP growth 2025: 1.9%; 2026f: 1.7%; 2027f: 1.8%
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth moderated to 1.9% in 2025. Long-term outlook constrained by aging population. C1-A1 Growth volatility: Exposure to external risks and climate events. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Labor productivity remains well below euro-area average.
ⓘ


Slovenia
Real GDP growth 2023: 2.4; 2024: 1.7; 2025: 1.1; 2026e: 1.9; 2027e: 2.2
C1-T Structural break in trend: Growth projected to strengthen from 1.1% in 2025 to 1.9% in 2026, driven by domestic demand and fiscal expansion. This contrasts with recent slowdown. C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Strong nominal wage growth, particularly in the public sector, is driving inflation and potentially eroding external competitiveness. C1-E Broken or dominated sample: Labour market remains tight with unemployment at a historical low.
ⓘ

Real GDP growth 2023: 2.1; 2024: 1.9; 2025: 0.8; 2026: 0.7; 2027: 1.6

title: Greece
text: This dossier draws on the Economic Survey issued by the OECD on 2024-12-05, the Debt Sustainability Monitor issued by the European Commission on 2026-02-12, the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast issued by the European Commission on 2026-05-21, and the Country Report and the Post-Programme Surveillance Report issued by the European Commission on 2026-06-03 and 2026-06-02, respectively. The reports assess Greece’s solid post-pandemic growth, which is projected to moderate as the Recovery and Resilience Facility implementation concludes and due to new global energy shocks. They highlight significant structural vulnerabilities, including low productivity, high public and external debt, and a high current account deficit. Fiscal policy remains solid with a projected surplus, though the National Escape Clause is activated for higher defense spending. The documents also address institutional challenges, such as judicial inefficiencies and the slow resolution of non-performing loans, which continue to burden the banking sector and private balance sheets. The post-programme surveillance assessment confirms that Greece retains the capacity to service its debt, supported by substantial cash reserves and a long debt maturity profile, despite downside risks from geopolitical shocks.

Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample

C1-E, broken or dominated sample: The document highlights that Greece’s GDP-per-capita growth has outpaced the euro area since early 2021, marking a strong rebound from previous crises. ⓘ



C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break in trend: The OECD notes that labor productivity has stagnated at low levels over much of the past decade, partly reflecting a collapse in investment during the economic crisis. Real GDP growth has been weak during the last two decades, with negative contributions from labor productivity and employment. ⓘ
C1-T, Structural break in trend: The European Commission estimates long-term real growth at around 1.5%, slightly exceeding the European Union average, implying slow economic convergence. Real gross domestic product was still almost 14% below its 2008 peak level in 2025. The medium-term growth forecast of 1.8% for 2026 and 1.6% for 2027 deviates from the historical mean of 2.1% (2023-2025), driven by the end of the Recovery and Resilience Facility implementation and the energy crisis weighing on activity ⓘ.
C1-T, context: Real GDP grew by 2.1% in 2025. Growth is projected to moderate to 1.8% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027 as implementation of the recovery and resilience plan ends. Risks are tilted to the downside due to potential escalation of the Middle East conflict ⓘ.
**C1*, context**: Real GDP growth is projected at 2.1% in 2025, 2.2% in 2026, and averaging 0.7% from 2028 to 2036. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: GDP growth is forecast to decelerate to 1.8% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027. Investment remains robust due to Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) absorption. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent: Exposure to rare disasters is highlighted as a significant risk. Climate change increases economic costs, with extreme weather events causing EUR 18.3 billion in economic losses between 1980 and 2024, of which only 5% was covered by insurance. Greece is one of the five most water-stressed Member States in the European Union. The economy is also vulnerable to geopolitical shocks affecting tourism and transport services, which account for around 20% of gross domestic product ⓘ.



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Competitiveness gains have been achieved largely on the back of declining real wages. The OECD warns that these gains may be lost if wages grow in excess of productivity. Unit labor costs have been increasing, though less so than in other OECD countries. ⓘ
C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap: Low non-cost competitiveness is reflected by a persistently high current account deficit of 5.7% of gross domestic product in 2025. Labour productivity is only 54.6% of the European Union average, compensated by long working hours. The economy relies on low value-added sectors like tourism and agriculture. Import dependence remains high, with an import ratio of direct material inputs at 49% compared to the European Union average of 22.4% ⓘ.

C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, history lags policy: The OECD recommends maintaining primary fiscal surpluses of 2% of GDP in 2024–25 as planned. It also suggests phasing out VAT reductions and exemptions and strengthening tax compliance to broaden tax bases. ⓘ
C3-T, History lags policy: Adopted consolidation measures include permanent tax cuts and targeted social measures aimed at supporting households’ disposable incomes. The Council endorsed Greece’s medium-term fiscal structural plan for 2025-2028. The country is required to limit the growth in net expenditure consistent with putting public debt on a plausibly downward trajectory while utilizing the allowance for higher defense expenditure under the National Escape Clause ⓘ.
C3-T, context: Greece registered a general government surplus of 1.7% of GDP in 2025. The primary surplus is projected at 4.0% in 2026 and 3.7% in 2027. The projection incorporates temporary and permanent measures to contain energy price rises and support low-income households, costing around 0.3% of GDP ⓘ.
**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance is projected at 1.8% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 33% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The SPB before cost of ageing is assumed at 1.8% of GDP from 2026 onwards. This is ambitious compared with past performance. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government surplus is set to moderate to 0.8% of GDP in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, despite expansionary fiscal measures. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

C3-A, context: Fiscal risks remain related to ongoing legal cases and rising spending pressures including defence, energy, and ageing ⓘ.



Other fiscal context

C3*, context: The OECD states that significant primary surpluses over many years are needed to reduce public debt, which amounted to 163.9% of GDP in 2023. The government plans primary surpluses of 2.4% of GDP in 2024, 2.5% in 2025, and 2.4% in 2026. ⓘ
C3*, context: Greece recorded a general government budget surplus above 1% of gross domestic product in both 2024 and 2025 (1.7% in 2025). This is projected to narrow to 0.8% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. The primary surplus is expected to remain above 3.5% of gross domestic product. The shrinking surplus reflects the implementation of permanent tax cuts, targeted social measures, and higher defense expenditure (2.6% of gross domestic product in 2026). Total government expenditure on defense increased from 2.2% of gross domestic product in 2024 to 2.4% in 2025. The National Escape Clause is activated to accommodate higher defense spending ⓘ.
C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to low risk, as no improvement relative to the baseline is needed to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator points to low risk, requiring only a 1.5% of GDP effort to reduce debt to 60% by 2070. ⓘ

Institutions

R6* Backstop eligibility (Backstop Eligibility)

Bright-line inputs

R6*, context: Greece’s credit rating returned to investment grade in late 2023, making Greek sovereign bonds eligible for the European Central Bank’s monetary policy operations in the standard collateral framework. This upgrade reflects sustained structural reforms and enhanced banking-sector resilience. ⓘ
R6*, context: Greece is subject to the reformed Stability and Growth Pact. The Council activated the National Escape Clause for Greece to facilitate the transition to higher levels of defense spending. The European Commission undertook an in-depth review of the Greek economy as part of the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure in 2026. Greece is not under an Excessive Deficit Procedure but is monitored for compliance with the fiscal rules. The European Commission assesses Greece’s compliance with maximum growth rates of net expenditure ⓘ.
**R6*, context**: The document notes the activation of the national escape clause (NEC) for Greece. ⓘ



R6-A Bright lines versus real eligibility
No evidence in the sources yet.



Bank–sovereign nexus and captive creditors

Outlook Factors, Bank–sovereign nexus: Legacy non-performing loans continue to weigh on the economy and private sector balance sheets. The stock of non-performing loans managed by credit servicers remains high. The resolution of these loans is delayed by judicial inefficiencies. The banking sector remains resilient with a common equity tier 1 ratio of 15.9% in the third quarter of 2025. However, the concentration of capital in ‘zombie’ companies hinders investment by healthy companies. The banking sector is largely state-backed through initiatives like EquiFund, indicating limited private market maturity ⓘ.
Banking stability: Non-performing loan ratio stood at 3.3% in December 2025, the lowest since joining the euro area. However, the workout of legacy debt managed by servicers is slow ⓘ.
Contingent Liabilities: State guarantees, non-performing loans in the banking sector (above EU average), negative net international investment position, and contingent liabilities from pending legal cases are risk-increasing factors. ⓘ
Debt Structure: Major share of debt held by official lenders at low interest rates and high cash buffers are risk-mitigating factors. ⓘ



Willingness to pay and political stability

Outlook Factors, political stability: The OECD notes that the balance of risks to the economic outlook is tilted to the downside, citing potential geopolitical tensions, slower growth among main trading partners, and delays in the implementation of the Recovery and Resilience Plan. ⓘ

text:
Market Signals

Factor decoupling: Markets have priced down Greek sovereign bond risks significantly following the return to investment grade. The OECD notes that spreads on Greek government debt have declined, reflecting improved investor confidence. ⓘ
Factor decoupling, rollover pessimism: The document does not provide specific bond spread or yield data to assess decoupling from global risk appetite or rollover pessimism directly. However, it notes that Greek firms report more barriers to investment than their European Union peers, and access to finance remains constrained, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. The European Investment Bank reports that 89% of Greek firms perceive business regulation as an investment barrier, compared to 69% in the European Union average ⓘ.
Factor decoupling, context: The Greek sovereign spread over the 10-year German Bund averaged 78 basis points in April 2026, reflecting some widening due to the international environment ⓘ.

title: Greece
text:
Outlook Material

Topic: Judicial efficiency: The justice system faces significant operational challenges, including lengthy civil and commercial proceedings (737 days in first-instance courts in 2023) and insufficient digitalization. Delays in auctioning properties and post-auction disputes hinder the resolution of non-performing loans. Recent reforms aim to streamline proceedings and adopt alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, but impact assessment is pending ⓘ.
Topic: Housing market: Housing affordability has deteriorated sharply. The standardised house price-to-income ratio grew by 13% in the last decade. House prices increased by 7.8% in 2025. Housing construction remains limited, with dwelling investment at 3.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, well below the European Union average. A significant portion of the housing stock is vacant or uninhabitable, tied up in legal processes. Short-term rentals reduce long-term rental availability ⓘ.
Topic: Energy transition and security: Greece relies heavily on fossil fuels, with natural gas accounting for a significant share of electricity production. The country is exposed to high energy prices and volatility. Progress is being made in renewable energy capacity and grid interconnection (e.g., Crete to mainland). However, the phasing out of fossil-fuel subsidies has not been initiated. Energy storage capacity is limited, leading to curtailments of renewable energy ⓘ.
Topic: Climate change: The document highlights that Greece is particularly vulnerable to a warming climate, with high risks from forest fires and floods. Extreme weather events, such as the 2023 floods in Thessaly, have caused large economic damages and may become more frequent and severe. ⓘ
Geopolitical shocks: Risks remain tilted to the downside as a potential further escalation of the Middle East conflict could have a material impact on tourism and domestic demand ⓘ.
Climate Risk: Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 6 pps. of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ

title: Italy
text: This dossier draws on the OECD’s Economic Survey for Italy, published on 2026-04-23, the European Commission’s 2026 Country Report for Italy, published on 2026-06-03, the European Commission’s 2026 Spring 2026 Economic Forecast, published on 2026-05-21, and the European Commission’s 2025 Debt Sustainability Monitor, published on 2026-02-12. The OECD survey assesses the economy as resilient but facing medium-term headwinds from high public debt, population ageing, and weak productivity growth. The European Commission reports highlight a deceleration in real GDP growth, persistent labor productivity stagnation, and a rise in the debt-to-GDP ratio. The Spring 2026 Economic Forecast projects a slowdown in growth in 2026 due to a global energy shock. The Debt Sustainability Monitor classifies medium-term risks as high, noting large gross financing needs and projected debt increases. Key themes include fiscal sustainability risks under the Medium-Term Fiscal-Structural Plan, regional disparities, demographic challenges, and exposure to global energy price volatility.

title: Italy
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

[C1-T, structural break in trend]: The OECD projects real GDP growth to remain modest at 0.4% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, weighed down by a surge in energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. This follows moderate growth of 0.5% in 2025. ⓘ
[C1-T, structural break in trend]: Real GDP growth decelerated to 0.5% in 2025 due to geopolitical uncertainty and trade barriers. Investment rebounded after a decline in 2024. Exports grew, reversing two years of decline, though imports grew faster. ⓘ
[C1-T, structural break]: Real GDP is expected to grow by 0.5% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. Domestic demand is dampened by loss of purchasing power and geopolitical tensions. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

[C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap]: Labour productivity growth has lagged the euro-area average since the mid-1990s. The level of multi-factor productivity declined between 2000 and 2022. The large share of small, low-productivity firms weighs on aggregate performance. ⓘ
[C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap]: Labor productivity stagnation persists. Italy’s GDP growth has consistently lagged behind employment growth over the past two decades. Unit labor costs rose, contributing to inflation, but the protracted slump in labor productivity weakens competitiveness. ⓘ
[C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap]: Significant regional gaps persist. Southern regions’ GDP per head is 65% of the EU average, compared to above EU average for the rest of the country. Productivity in the South is ~80% of EU levels versus 99% for the rest of Italy. R&D investment in the South is 1% of GDP versus 1.5% in the rest of the country. ⓘ



Other growth context
No evidence in the sources yet.

C2-E Projections unavailable or implausible
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-T Projections stale

[C2-T, projections stale]: Headline inflation is projected to rise to 2.4% in 2026 due to disruptions in global energy supplies from the Middle East conflict, before falling to 1.8% in 2027. Core inflation remains higher than pre-pandemic levels. ⓘ



C2-A Imperfect indexation
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-M Labour-cost versus consumer-price differential

[C2-M, labour-cost versus consumer-price differential]: Nominal wage growth is around 3% annually, recovering from pre-pandemic levels of 1%, but real contractual wages were still 8.8% below their January 2021 level in 2025. ⓘ

title: Italy
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

[C3-T, history lags policy]: The Italy government has committed to a steady fiscal consolidation path under the Medium-Term Fiscal-Structural Plan (MTFSP) until 2031. This implies primary spending declining relative to GDP each year to reduce the debt ratio. ⓘ
[C3-T, history lags policy]: Primary surpluses are expected to remain insufficient to offset the debt-increasing effects of the interest-growth differential and stock-flow adjustments. As a result, the debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to increase from 137.1% in 2025 to 139.2% in 2027. ⓘ
[C3-T, history lags policy]: The government deficit is projected to fall to 2.9% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

[C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered]: Public debt exceeds 137% of GDP (Maastricht) and is projected to rise further under current tax and spending settings. Ageing costs are projected to rise by at least 1% of GDP by the mid-2030s, primarily due to pensions. ⓘ
[C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered]: The European Commission notes high fiscal sustainability risks in the medium term. Sizeable debt servicing costs and skewed public expenditure towards pensions limit budgetary flexibility. The automatic link between retirement conditions and life expectancy is set to resume but will be phased in gradually. ⓘ



Other fiscal context

[C3*, context]: The general government deficit fell to 3.1% of GDP in 2025, supported by stronger revenue from higher employment and wages. It is projected to decline to 2.9% in 2026 and 2027. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The structural primary balance is projected at 1.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 43% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The European Commission projects a structural primary surplus of 1.1% of GDP as of 2026. This is broadly in line with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to increase. ⓘ
[C3*, context]: The S2 indicator points to low risk, as no improvement is needed to stabilize debt due to projected decreases in ageing costs. The S1 indicator points to low risk, requiring a 1.6% of GDP effort. ⓘ

title: Italy
text:
Debt

R1* Refinancing need (Refinancing Need)

R1-E Components missing or distorted

[R1-E, components missing or distorted]: Gross refinancing needs are currently near 25% of GDP. The term structure of outstanding debt is near the euro-area average at close to 8 years. ⓘ
[R1-E, components missing or distorted]: Stock-flow adjustments related to the delayed cash effect of housing renovation tax credits contribute to the rise in debt. ⓘ
[R1-E, components missing]: The debt-to-GDP ratio is set to rise to 139.2% by 2027, driven by a debt-increasing interest-growth-rate differential. ⓘ
[R1*, context]: Gross financing needs were 23.3% of GDP in 2025. Debt is projected to increase to 149.1% of GDP by 2036. ⓘ
[R1*, context]: Gross financing needs are expected to remain large, reaching around 27% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ



R1-T Financing behavior shifts
No evidence in the sources yet.


R1-A Part of the debt not exposed to the market

[R1-A, part of the debt not exposed to the market]: Insurers and pension funds hold significant amounts of government debt. Italian insurers hold roughly 10% of the outstanding stock of Italian government bonds. Pension fund assets were EUR 243 billion at end-2024. ⓘ
[R1-A, context]: Risk-increasing factors relate to the share of short-term government debt. Risk-mitigating factors include the major share of debt held by domestic lenders and euro denomination. The favourable net international investment position mitigates fiscal risks. ⓘ



Other refinancing context

[R1*, context]: The debt-to-GDP ratio reversed its downward trajectory in 2024 and started rising again, driven mainly by the lagged impact of tax credits for housing renovations. ⓘ




C5* Haircut (Haircut)

C5-A Politically feasible haircut differs from 30%

[C5-A, politically feasible haircut differs from 30%]: Domestic banks hold a relatively large share of government bonds (approx. 25% of bank assets). The average residual duration of these holdings has risen to near 4.8 years, exposing banks to deterioration in the government bond market. ⓘ

title: Italy
text:
Market Signals

[Factor decoupling]: Interest spreads have narrowed and agencies have upgraded credit ratings. The spread with the 10-year German government bond yield has decreased significantly in recent years. ⓘ
[Factor decoupling]: The report notes that global trade uncertainty poses a major challenge for export-driven economies like Italy. ⓘ
[Rollover pessimism]: The 10-year sovereign yield spread vs. German Bund is 74 basis points as of 31 December 2025. ⓘ

title: Italy
text:
Outlook Material

[Energy security]: The 2026 Middle East conflict has renewed volatility in global energy markets. Italy remains exposed due to high reliance on imported fossil fuels (74% of net total energy consumed). ⓘ
[Trade policy]: Global trade policy restrictions and competition from emerging economies (e.g., China) weigh on Italian exports and industrial production. ⓘ
[Demographic Challenges]: Italy faces long-standing demographic challenges. By 2050, the total population is expected to decline by more than 4 million. The fertility rate was 1.18 in 2024, well below the EU average of 1.34. The share of the population under 15 decreased to 11.9% in 2025. ⓘ
[Brain Drain]: A significant outflow of young, highly qualified Italians seeking opportunities abroad persists. In 2024, around 188,000 people left the country, while 450,000 migrated to Italy. ⓘ
[Labor Market Segmentation]: Atypical work remains common. 11.3% of workers had involuntary temporary contracts and 8.5% were in involuntary part-time roles. Undeclared work concerned about 3.13 million full-time equivalent jobs in 2023. ⓘ

title: Slovakia
text: This dossier draws on the Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations for Slovakia, both issued by the European Commission on June 3, 2026. It also integrates data from the Debt Sustainability Monitor published by the European Commission on February 12, 2026, and the Economic Forecast from May 21, 2026. Additionally, the dossier incorporates findings from the Economic Survey issued by the OECD on June 25, 2026. The reports highlight weak economic growth driven by fiscal consolidation and an unfavorable external environment, with significant fiscal pressures as the general government deficit rises and public debt increases. Structural weaknesses include regional disparities, low innovation, high unit labor costs, and a severe housing shortage. The analysis notes vulnerabilities in the judicial and anti-corruption framework, continued energy dependency on Russia, and high long-term fiscal sustainability risks based on debt-to-GDP projections. The OECD survey further emphasizes the long-term risks posed by demographic aging and the need for structural reforms to improve the business environment and competitiveness.

title: Slovakia
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample

C1-E, Broken or dominated sample: Demographic shifts pose a significant long-term headwind. The population aged 15-64 is set to shrink by nearly 30% over 2025-2065, while the number of people above 64 will increase by 52%. This demographic change is expected to have a large downward impact on GDP per capita, potentially reducing it by up to 17.5% relative to a scenario with constant employment ratios. ⓘ



C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T Structural break in trend: Economic growth slowed significantly to 0.8% in 2025 due to fiscal consolidation and global uncertainty. Growth is forecast to remain subdued at 0.8% in 2026. The medium-term growth forecast (1.5% in 2027) deviates from the historical mean, reflecting structural challenges in productivity and innovation. ⓘ
C1*, context: Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was 0.8% in 2025. The European Commission projects growth of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: Real GDP growth is expected to remain modest at 0.8% in 2026, picking up to 1.5% in 2027. Domestic demand is subdued due to fiscal consolidation. ⓘ
C1-T, Structural break in trend: The OECD notes that convergence in living standards has stalled. Real GDP per capita growth has fallen behind regional peers since the Global Financial Crisis. The gap in GDP per capita with Germany is primarily due to lower total factor productivity (TFP), which accounts for 64% of the gap. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap: Slovakia’s competitiveness is weakening, reflected by sluggish productivity growth and decreased foreign direct investment (FDI). Real convergence has stalled, with GDP per capita at 56.8% of the EU average in 2024. High unit labor costs undermine cost competitiveness. ⓘ
C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Fast-rising unit labor costs have further weakened competitiveness and are still expected to grow relatively fast in 2026. ⓘ
C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap: The automotive sector, a key driver of the economy, faces acute challenges from structural changes and high trade barriers. US effective tariff rates on Slovak exports have increased substantially, affecting the automotive sector disproportionately compared to other Visegrad countries. ⓘ



Other growth context
No evidence in the sources yet.



C2* Inflation differential (Inflation Differential)

C2-E Projections unavailable or implausible
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-T Projections stale
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-A Imperfect indexation
No evidence in the sources yet.


C2-M Labour-cost versus consumer-price differential

C2-M Labour-cost versus consumer-price differential: Inflation remains elevated at 4.2% in 2025, driven by tax increases and services prices. It is expected to remain high at 4.3% in 2026 due to rising energy prices. The cumulated inflation differential to the euro area is widening, weighing on competitiveness. ⓘ



Other inflation context

C2*, context: HICP inflation was well above the euro area in 2025, partly due to value-added tax (VAT) rate increases. Core inflation is forecast to stay among the highest in the euro area in 2026. ⓘ

title: Slovakia
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

C3-T History lags policy: Slovakia is struggling to correct its excessive budget deficit. The deadline for bringing the deficit below 3% of GDP has been postponed to 2028. The adjustment requires an improvement in the structural primary balance of around 5.2 percentage points of GDP between 2024 and 2028. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The Council of the EU endorsed Slovakia’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan in January 2025, setting maximum net expenditure growth rates. Slovakia activated the national escape clause for defense spending (2025–2028). ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The public deficit is projected to rise to 4.6% in 2026 and 5.4% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, History lags policy: The government adopted a fiscal consolidation plan for 2025 and 2026, aiming to reduce the deficit. The 2026 plan includes revenue measures totaling 1.0% of GDP (taxes on high earners, VAT increases, health insurance contributions) and spending reductions of 0.9% of GDP. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered: The Slovak Council for Budgetary Responsibility warns that, without additional measures, the deficit could reach 6% of GDP and public debt could rise to 75% of GDP by 2029. Consolidation measures have focused primarily on tax increases, which reduce competitiveness, while discretionary spending (e.g., 13th pension, energy support) reduces net fiscal consolidation. ⓘ
C3-A, Default is chosen, not only suffered: The OECD critiques the composition of consolidation, noting that heavy reliance on taxes (especially labor and corporate) and across-the-board spending cuts is detrimental to growth. It recommends prioritizing spending cuts (energy subsidies, pensions) and less distortionary taxes. ⓘ



Other fiscal context

**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance is projected at -2.6% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 44% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The SPB is assumed to be a deficit of 2.6% of GDP as of 2026, excluding changes in the cost of ageing. This level is broadly in line with past fiscal performance. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: Long-term fiscal sustainability risks are high. The S2 indicator signals that Slovakia would need to improve its structural primary balance by 7.2 percentage points to ensure debt stabilizes over the long term. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The S1 indicator shows that a fiscal effort of 6.2 percentage points would be needed to limit debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
C3*, context: The general government deficit decreased to 4.5% of GDP in 2025 but is projected to rise to 5.4% in 2027 due to military equipment deliveries. ⓘ
C3*, context: Net expenditure grew by 1.7% in 2025, below the recommended maximum. It is projected to grow by 2.9% in 2026, exceeding the recommended maximum growth rate by 0.8% of GDP in annual terms, though cumulative growth remains below the limit. ⓘ
C3*, context: Insufficient implementation of existing spending reviews limits their potential for savings. ⓘ
C3*, context: The tax wedge on labor earnings remains above the European Union (EU) average. Revenues from recurrent property and environmental taxation are below the EU average. ⓘ
C3*, context: Public expenditure to GDP was 47% in 2024, well above the OECD average. Energy subsidies remain large, with nearly 90% of households eligible for targeted subsidies in 2026. The OECD recommends phasing out these subsidies. ⓘ
C3*, context: The debt brake, a constitutional rule, has historically been suspended for two years after parliamentary approval of government programs, limiting its effectiveness. The OECD recommends reforming the debt brake to increase credibility by removing exemption periods. ⓘ

title: Slovakia
text:
Debt

R1* Refinancing need (Refinancing Need)

R1-E Components missing or distorted

R1-E, components missing: Public debt is set to rise to 66.9% by 2027. ⓘ
R1-E, Components missing or distorted: The introduction of a financial transactions tax (FTT) in April 2025 is highlighted as a risk. The FTT imposes a 0.4% tax on corporate bank transactions and 0.8% on cash withdrawals. The OECD argues this is highly distortionary, reduces economic activity, and may increase informality, warranting its abolition. ⓘ



R1-T Financing behavior shifts
No evidence in the sources yet.


R1-A Part of the debt not exposed to the market

R1-A, investor base: Risk-increasing factors include the share of government debt held by non-residents. Mitigating factors include a low share of short-term government debt and most debt being denominated in euro. ⓘ



Other refinancing context

**R1*, context**: Gross financing needs were 10.1% of GDP in 2025. Debt is projected to increase to 101.2% of GDP by 2036, crossing the 90% threshold. ⓘ
R1* Refinancing need: The current account has marginally improved, but risks for external sustainability remain due to the worsened trade balance and persistently high government deficit. Housing supply remains limited, pushing up prices and household debt. ⓘ
R1*, context: General government debt increased to 61.4% of GDP at the end of 2025 and is projected to reach 66.9% by the end of 2027. The increase reflects persistent deficits and interest expenditures growing faster than the economy. ⓘ
**R1*, context**: Government gross financing needs are expected to remain around 10.5% of GDP over 2026-2027, reaching around 14% of GDP in 2036. ⓘ
R1*, context: Public debt (Maastricht definition) rose to 61.4% of GDP in 2024. Without further adjustment, debt-to-GDP could exceed 100% over the next 15 years due to ageing pressures. ⓘ

title: Slovakia
text:
Institutions

R6* Backstop eligibility (Backstop Eligibility)

Bright-line inputs

Council of the EU: The Council adopted a recommendation endorsing Slovakia’s medium-term fiscal-structural plan and activated the National Escape Clause for higher defence spending. The Council also held the Excessive Deficit Procedure in abeyance. ⓘ
R6*, context: The excessive deficit procedure for Slovakia is held in abeyance following the endorsement of its fiscal-structural plan. ⓘ



R6-A Bright lines versus real eligibility

R6-A, Bright lines versus real eligibility: The OECD notes that the debt brake’s track record is poor. An empirical investigation found no significant stabilising response to debt levels around the introduction of the debt brake in 2012, but a stabilising response did emerge after EU accession preparations began in 2001-2003. ⓘ




Bank–sovereign nexus and captive creditors

Outlook Factors, Bank-sovereign nexus: The banking sector appears robust with strong capital buffers. However, the FTT poses a risk to bank resources by incentivizing deposit outflows into cash. Commercial real estate shows some vulnerability, with nearly three out of four CRE loans served by firms with negative equity. ⓘ



Willingness to pay and political stability

Outlook Factors, political stability: Concerns persist regarding the judicial system and anti-corruption framework. The dismantling of specialized anti-corruption agencies and reforms shortening limitation periods have reduced the detection and prosecution of high-level corruption cases. ⓘ
Political stability: A recent downgrade reflects broad institutional challenges and political tensions. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, Political stability: The OECD highlights issues with the rule of law and judicial independence. Perceptions of corruption are high, with 85% of companies perceiving corruption as widespread. Recent reforms, including the dissolution of the Special Prosecutor’s Office, have raised concerns about the effectiveness of anti-corruption efforts. ⓘ



National institutions
No evidence in the sources yet.

title: Slovakia
text:
Market Signals

Factor decoupling: The economy is heavily reliant on low-value-added automotive production, which accounts for around half of industrial revenues. This sector faces pressures from global trade tensions and the transition to electric vehicles. ⓘ
Context: Financial markets’ perceptions of sovereign risk are investment grade, but a recent downgrade reflects broad institutional challenges and political tensions. The 10-year sovereign yield spread is 65 basis points versus the German Bund as of December 31, 2025. ⓘ
Factor decoupling: The OECD does not provide specific bond spread data but notes that high effective tariff rates on exports to the US and weak foreign demand are weighing on the economy. The current account deficit remains substantial, though expected to narrow slightly due to fiscal consolidation. ⓘ

title: Slovakia
text:
Outlook Material

Regional Disparities: Significant regional disparities persist, with GDP per capita ranging from 151% of the EU average in Bratislava to 55% in eastern Slovakia. Eastern Slovakia faces higher unemployment and poverty rates, and significant outward migration of skilled workers. ⓘ
Energy Security: Slovakia remains heavily reliant on Russian energy imports. Dependence on Russian gas and crude oil poses risks to economic security amid geopolitical tensions. ⓘ
Housing market: Slovakia faces a severe housing shortage with the lowest housing stock per capita in the EU. House prices surged in 2025 amid lower mortgage rates and are likely to keep rising due to constrained supply. ⓘ
Energy dependence: Over 50% of natural gas and over 80% of oil were of Russian origin in 2025. The share of renewables in the electricity mix was among the lowest in the EU. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, rule of law: Safeguards for the independence of the judiciary remain insufficient, posing risks to the business and regulatory environment. ⓘ
Topic: AI Adoption: AI adoption in Slovakia is lagging behind EU peers. Only 18% of enterprises reported using AI in 2025, up from 7% in 2023. The OECD recommends streamlining regulation to ease access to data and helping firms comply with the EU AI Act to accelerate adoption. ⓘ
Topic: Climate Change and Net-Zero Transition: Slovakia is well-positioned for the net-zero transition due to its low-carbon electricity mix (nuclear and hydro). However, administrative procedures for low-carbon power projects are cumbersome. The OECD recommends streamlining permitting and moving to market-based electricity pricing while supporting low-income households with targeted transfers. ⓘ
Topic: Skills Shortages: Severe skills shortages, particularly in the automotive and industrial sectors, hinder growth. The OECD recommends improving the education system, facilitating lifelong learning, and increasing the use of active labor market policies focused on retraining and upskilling. ⓘ

title: Finland
text: This dossier draws on the OECD Economic Survey (published May 2025), the European Commission Debt Sustainability Monitor (published February 2026), the European Commission Economic Forecast (Spring 2026, published May 2026), and the European Commission Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations (published June 2026). The evidence highlights a fragile economic recovery with modest growth projections for 2026 and 2027. Fiscal sustainability remains a core challenge, with public debt projected to rise significantly to over 90% of gross domestic product by 2027, driven by increased defence spending, aging demographics, and structural deficits. The European Commission has opened an excessive deficit procedure (EDP), which is held in abeyance. Long-term fiscal sustainability risks are assessed as medium, requiring a structural primary balance improvement of 4.1 percentage points of gross domestic product to stabilize debt.

title: Finland
text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break in trend: The real gross domestic product contracted by 0.1% in 2024 after a sharper decline in late 2023. Growth is projected to recover modestly to 0.7% in 2025 and 1.1% in 2026, supported by declining interest rates and easing inflation, but this recovery lags behind Nordic peers and the OECD average ⓘ.
C1-T, Structural break in trend: The European Commission states that Finland’s economy is emerging from stagnation and is expected to transit to broad-based growth in 2026. After a decline in 2023 and a small rebound in 2024, real GDP grew only marginally in 2025. Subdued performance is attributed to declining private and public consumption and low consumer confidence ⓘ.
C1*, context: Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was 0.2% in 2025. The European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP to grow by 0.8% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027 ⓘ.
C1-T, structural break: Real GDP growth is projected at 0.8% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027 ⓘ.
C1*, context: Real GDP growth is projected to accelerate to 0.8% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, driven by domestic demand. In 2025, growth was modest at 0.2%. Private consumption is expected to increase by 0.6% in 2026, supported by rising disposable income from significant wage increases (8% total for 2025-27). However, the household savings rate remains high (12.4% in 2026) due to weak consumer confidence and high unemployment. Investment is set to rise in 2026, driven by machinery and equipment spending, including the delivery of F-35 fighter jets and data centre construction. Net exports are forecast to turn negative in 2026 due to import growth outpacing exports ⓘ.

title: Finland
text:
Outlook Material

Outlook Factors, geopolitical shocks: Finland faces significant security risks from Russia, including cyber-attacks and infrastructure sabotage. The country closed its border with Russia indefinitely in April 2024 and joined the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in April 2023. These factors contribute to economic uncertainty and defense spending increases ⓘ.
Outlook Factors, demographic trends: The working-age population is projected to shrink in the 2030s under baseline migration assumptions, although recent high migration levels have led to upward revisions in population projections. Net inward migration of 40,000 annually from 2026 is assumed in the high population scenario, which would stabilize public debt at around 110% of gross domestic product from 2035 onwards ⓘ.
Geopolitics and Defence: Finland is increasing defence expenditure to 3% of gross domestic product by 2029, up from 2.4% in 2024. The 2026 budget includes EUR 6 billion in new procurement for defence materiel. The Council of the EU has made financial assistance of up to EUR 1 billion available through the Security Action for Europe instrument ⓘ.
Social Stability: High unemployment (10.3% in late 2025) and reforms to the social security system are raising concerns about poverty risks among vulnerable groups. The social security reforms, effective in 2026, tighten conditions and may increase labour market participation but could also disproportionately affect low-income families and young people ⓘ.
Innovation and Productivity: Commercialisation of innovation remains problematic, with declining cooperation between academia and businesses. Scaling-up innovative firms is hampered by a lack of large-scale domestic venture capital funding for later-stage rounds ⓘ.

title: Malta
text: This dossier draws on the 2025 Debt Sustainability Monitor and the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast, both issued by the European Commission in early and mid-2026, alongside the 2026 Country Report issued on 2026-06-03. The evidence characterizes the Malta economy as robust, with real gross domestic product growth projected at 3.7% for 2026, driven by tourism and domestic consumption. Fiscal indicators show a general government deficit stabilizing around 2.2% of GDP and public debt remaining below 47% of GDP, with a projected decline to 40.8% by 2036 under a no-policy-change baseline. Key themes include persistent labor shortages, pressure on housing and infrastructure, and institutional challenges related to the justice system and transparency. Long-term fiscal sustainability assessments indicate high risk for debt stabilization due to ageing costs, requiring significant structural primary balance improvements.

title: Malta
text:
Outlook Material

Outlook Factors, rule of law: Concerns persist over the efficiency of the justice system. The time to resolve civil and commercial cases increased from 432 to 491 days between 2016 and 2024. Resources for the judiciary are limited, with a low number of judges per capita. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, rule of law: Transparency issues exist in public procurement and lobbying. Ministers stopped publicly declaring family income after 2023. No comprehensive rules on lobbying or robust asset declaration requirements are in place. ⓘ
Housing and Infrastructure: Rapid population growth (34% increase between 2015 and 2025) has put strain on infrastructure, land use, and public services. Housing costs are a significant driver of poverty, with 7.7% of those at risk of poverty having mortgage or rent arrears in 2025. ⓘ
Energy Security and Climate: Malta is highly vulnerable to climate risks. The energy mix is skewed towards imported fossil fuels. Renewable energy share in electricity mix was 16.7% in 2025, below the EU average of 45%. Fossil fuel subsidies accounted for 1% of GDP in 2024. ⓘ
Labor Market and Skills: Severe skills shortages exist, particularly in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) and green transition sectors. Participation in STEM post-secondary education is significantly below the EU average (13.8% vs 25.2%). ⓘ
Social Protection: Social transfers reduced the monetary poverty rate by only 24.9% in 2025, below the EU average of 33.2%. Vulnerable groups, including third-country nationals and persons with disabilities, face higher risks of poverty and exclusion. ⓘ
