title: Germany
text: This dossier draws on the European Commission Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations published on 2026-06-03, the OECD Economic Survey published on 2025-06-12, the European Commission Debt Sustainability Monitor published on 2026-02-12, and the European Commission Economic Forecast published on 2026-05-21. The evidence highlights prolonged economic stagnation with real gross domestic product (GDP) growth near zero since 2019, alongside a modest projected recovery hindered by a new global energy shock triggered by conflict in the Middle East. Fiscal policy has turned expansionary following a 2025 reform of the national debt brake, creating space for defense spending and a special infrastructure fund. Structural challenges include high insolvency rates, low public investment quality, demographic pressures, and weak business dynamism. The European Commission projects debt to rise to 91% of GDP by 2036, though the European Commission assessed that fiscal sustainability is preserved over the medium term despite the activation of the national escape clause.

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample

C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, Structural break in trend: The OECD notes that economic growth has slowed down after a decade of strong export-led growth. Structural challenges, including high administrative burden and barriers to entry, have hampered business dynamism and productivity growth even before the pandemic ⓘ.
C1-T, structural break in trend: The European Commission projects real GDP growth of 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027, following actual growth of 0.2% in 2025. The document notes that economic transformation is intensifying, with insolvencies at a 20-year high and structural challenges in industrial regions. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break in trend: The report states that real GDP growth has been almost non-existent since 2019. Potential growth is projected to average just 0.5% annually from 2026 to 2030, placing it at the low end among European Union (EU) economies. This low potential is attributed to demographic aging, a shrinking labor force, low average hours worked, weak education outcomes, and a lack of disruptive innovation. Long-term growth remains among the lowest in the EU. ⓘ
**C1*, context**: Real GDP growth is projected at 0.2% in 2025, 1.2% in 2026, and averaging 0.9% from 2028 to 2036. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: Real GDP growth is forecast at 0.6% in 2026 and 0.9% in 2027. The energy price shock weighs on real incomes and investment. Public spending ramp-up following the debt brake reform supports growth. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent: Rising trade policy tensions and supply chain disruptions have weighed on investor confidence, particularly in export-oriented manufacturing sectors. High uncertainty regarding fiscal policy and green transition measures has also affected investment ⓘ.
C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed: The document cites risks from energy supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions, noting that broad measures to mitigate energy price impacts have large fiscal costs. It highlights exposure to rare disasters via energy dependence. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, Inherited competitiveness gap: Export competitiveness has deteriorated. Rising unit labour costs in manufacturing have contributed to weaker export performance. The OECD emphasizes the need to foster business dynamism and productivity growth to improve international competitiveness ⓘ.
C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Germany has recorded one of the weakest recoveries and lowest long-term growth rates in the EU since the pandemic. Global export market shares have declined sharply due to waning competitiveness, fading technological leadership, skills shortages, and high wage and energy costs. Private investment fell below its 2015 level by 2025. ⓘ

C3-T, History lags policy: A recent reform of national fiscal rules approved in March 2025 allows additional borrowing for defence and public investment. Spending exceeding 1% of GDP in defence and specific areas is exempted from fiscal rules. A special infrastructure fund of up to EUR 500 billion is established for the next 12 years ⓘ.
C3-T, History lags policy: The OECD projects that the fiscal stance will tighten in 2025 by 0.3% of GDP and expand by 0.9% of GDP in 2026. The tightening in 2025 is due to the fall of the previous coalition government and a provisional budget ⓘ.
C3-T, History lags policy: Rapid population ageing will increase yearly public spending on pension benefits by around 2 percentage points of GDP until 2045. Without reforms, spending on pensions, health, and long-term care is projected to rise by about 3.5% of GDP by 2045 ⓘ.
C3-T, history lags policy: The Council of the EU activated the national escape clause for Germany, allowing deviation from maximum growth rates of net expenditure to support defense spending. The European Commission projects a general government deficit of 3.7% of GDP in 2026 and 4.1% of GDP in 2027, exceeding the 3% reference value. However, no excessive deficit procedure is proposed because the deviation is explained by defense expenditure under the escape clause. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The fiscal framework changed significantly in 2025 with the reform of the national debt brake (Schuldenbremse). This reform created additional fiscal space by exempting defense spending above 1% of GDP from the debt brake and allowing federal states (Länder) to issue debt of 0.35% of GDP annually in structural terms. A Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality worth EUR 500 billion was legislated. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance is projected at -2.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 90% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ

C3-T, history lags policy: The European Commission assessed the fiscal sustainability condition for activating the NEC. It concluded that sustainability is preserved over the medium term. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government deficit is projected to increase to 3.7% of GDP in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, driven by higher defense spending, public investment, and tax relief. ⓘ

title: Germany
text:
Outlook Material

Elections: The fall of the coalition government in November 2024 and the formation of a new government in early 2025 reduced domestic policy uncertainty. A provisional budget was approved for 2025 ⓘ.
Geopolitical shocks: Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and rising trade tensions have hit the German economy. Supply chain bottlenecks and higher energy prices have affected the globally integrated German economy more than others ⓘ.
Economic Security: The war in Iran has reduced growth prospects and driven inflation up. Uncertainty due to the situation in the Middle East and US tariffs detracts from private consumption, investment, and exports. Germany faces economic security challenges linked to its export-oriented economy, including reliance on raw material imports and vulnerabilities in supply chains. ⓘ
Structural Reforms: The document recommends reforms to pension sustainability, tax structure to incentivize labor supply, and improvement of innovation ecosystems. It notes challenges in digitalization of public administration, housing affordability, and energy transition. ⓘ
Structural Reforms: The report highlights limited progress on structural reforms. Key challenges include accelerating the green transition, improving education outcomes, expanding housing supply, and modernizing public administration. Cyberattacks are estimated to have caused losses of almost EUR 200 billion (5% of GDP) in 2025. ⓘ
Contingent Liabilities: Potential additional debt uptake allowed by the reform of the debt brake and the creation of the special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality are risk-increasing factors. ⓘ
Climate Risk: Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 3 pps. of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ

title: France
text: This dossier draws on the European Commission’s 2025 Debt Sustainability Monitor, published on 2026-02-12; the European Commission’s Spring 2026 Economic Forecast, published on 2026-05-21; the European Commission’s 2026 Country Report, published on 2026-06-03; and the OECD’s 2026 Economic Survey, published on 2026-06-30. The evidence highlights persistent economic stagnation, with real GDP growth projected between 0.7% and 0.8% for 2026 and 2027. Fiscal challenges are significant, as the general government deficit remains above 5% of GDP and debt is projected to rise above 144% of GDP by 2036 under a no-policy-change baseline. Structural issues include weak labor productivity, high public spending, slow progress in renewable energy deployment, and political uncertainty stemming from recent government changes and a hung parliament.

C3-T, history lags policy: France committed to placing debt on a downward trajectory under its medium-term fiscal-structural plan for 2025–2029, aiming to reduce the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2029. However, the general government deficit is projected to remain at 5.1% of GDP in 2026. Political gridlock in 2026 budget adoption weakened deficit reduction plans, and the suspension of the 2023 pension reform until January 2028 is expected to worsen the budget balance and increase public debt in the medium term ⓘ.

C3*, context: The tax burden is significantly higher than the EU average, with tax revenues at 44.3% of GDP in 2025. High taxes on production (4.4% of GDP) and labor (implicit tax rate of 38.8% in 2024) weigh on growth. Fiscal and social tax expenditures amount to nearly 6% of GDP, complicating the tax system and posing a heavy budgetary burden ⓘ.

title: Spain
text: This dossier draws on the Debt Sustainability Monitor issued by the European Commission on 2026-02-12, the Economic Forecast issued by the European Commission on 2026-05-21, the Country Report and Country-Specific Recommendations issued by the European Commission on 2026-06-03, and the Economic Survey issued by the OECD on 2025-11-26. The reports assess Spain’s economic, social, and structural performance in 2025–2026. They highlight robust but moderating GDP growth driven by domestic demand, stable fiscal deficits, and declining debt-to-GDP ratios in the near term, though long-term projections indicate a rise in debt due to aging-related costs. Key themes include weak productivity growth, political fragmentation hindering budget approval, and structural challenges such as regional disparities, housing affordability, and climate vulnerability. The recommendations emphasize reinforcing fiscal sustainability, improving spending efficiency, addressing climate resilience, and enhancing SME productivity.

Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break in trend: Real GDP growth was 3.5% in 2024, surpassing European peers. Growth is projected to moderate to 2.9% in 2025, 2.2% in 2026, and 1.8% in 2027, driven by domestic demand and weakening external demand due to global trade uncertainty ⓘ.
C1-T, structural break: The European Commission forecasts that real GDP is set to grow at 2.4% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027. Growth is driven by domestic demand, supported by a robust labor market and investment. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: The European Commission notes that Spain’s GDP growth expanded by 2.8% in 2025 and is projected to remain robust in the near term (2.4% in 2026) before moderating to 1.9% in 2027. Growth is supported by domestic demand and private consumption, but external demand is expected to weigh on growth due to a more fragile external environment. ⓘ
C1*, context: Real GDP growth was 2.8% in 2025. The European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projects real GDP to grow by 2.4% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027. ⓘ
**C1*, context**: Real GDP growth is projected at 2.9% in 2025, 2.3% in 2026, and averaging 1.3% from 2028 to 2036. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent

C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed or serially independent: The external sector is resilient with a current account surplus of 3.2% of GDP in 2024. However, risks are tilted to the downside due to escalating global trade measures, potential tariffs, and climate-related shocks that could disrupt agriculture and infrastructure ⓘ.
C1-A1, growth not thin-tailed or serially independent: Productivity growth remains weak, with labour productivity reaching 96.4% of the EU average in 2024 but projected to decline to 94.8% in 2027. This stagnation is linked to weak business innovation, a fragmented business structure dominated by micro-enterprises, and skills mismatches. ⓘ



C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Labor productivity growth remains sluggish compared to peer countries. While total factor productivity has improved recently, Spain’s GDP per capita has not converged to peer levels, reflecting weak productivity and capital stock per worker ⓘ.
C1-A2, inherited competitiveness gap: Spain faces chronically low R&D investment (1.50% of GDP in 2024, well below the EU average of 2.24%) and weak science-business linkages. Private R&D expenditure is stagnant, and the country has a large VAT policy gap, indicating tax inefficiencies. ⓘ
C1-A2, context: Low private research and development (R&D) investment remains a major constraint, hampered by a fragmented business structure dominated by low-value micro-enterprises. Business R&D expenditure is insufficient across the whole country due to uneven territorial distribution of public spending. ⓘ
C1-A2, context: The International Monetary Fund points to insufficient market size and lack of access to equity financing as key factors underlying young firms’ inability to scale up rapidly. The OECD reports that lack of available financing is a considerable long-term barrier to investment for Spain firms, notably small and medium-sized enterprises. ⓘ

title: Spain
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode

C3-E, history lags policy: The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 5.3% of GDP improvement in 2027 to stabilize debt. The S1 indicator also points to medium risk, requiring a 4.8% of GDP effort to reduce debt to 60% by 2070. ⓘ



C3-T History lags policy

C3-T, history lags policy: The general government fiscal deficit declined to 3.2% of GDP in 2024. The government’s medium-term fiscal plan aims to reduce the deficit to 0.8% by 2031 and debt to 90.6% by 2031. However, the plan lacks detailed policy measures, and the underlying structural deficit remains near 3% of GDP ⓘ.
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government deficit is set to stabilize at 2.4% in 2026 and fall to 2.0% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government deficit is projected to stabilize at 2.4% of GDP in 2026 and fall to 2.0% in 2027. The debt-to-GDP ratio fell to 100.7% in 2025 and is expected to drop below 100% in 2026, driven by strong nominal GDP growth and improved fiscal outcomes. However, fiscal space is limited by rising expenditure pressures from ageing and defence. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: Spain requested the activation of the National Escape Clause (NEC) in April 2026 for defence expenditure. Cumulated deviation in 2025 was 0.1% of GDP (fully explained by NEC flexibility), and in 2026 is projected at 0.7% of GDP (partially explained). ⓘ
C3*, context: The general government deficit decreased from 3.2% of GDP in 2024 to 2.4% of GDP in 2025. The European Commission projects a deficit of 2.4% of GDP in 2026 and 2.0% of GDP in 2027. The stabilisation in 2026 reflects positive revenue developments compensating for measures to ease the consequences of floods and the Middle East crisis. ⓘ
C3*, context: Net expenditure grew by 4.8% in 2025, exceeding the recommended maximum growth rate with an annual deviation of 0.4% of GDP. Cumulative growth over 2024 and 2025 was 9.3%, exceeding the recommended maximum by 0.1% of GDP. This deviation is within the flexibility of the national escape clause based on defense spending estimates. ⓘ
C3*, context: Net expenditure is projected to grow by 5.1% in 2026, exceeding the recommended maximum rate with an annual deviation of 0.6% of GDP. Cumulative growth over 2024, 2025, and 2026 is projected at 14.9%, with a cumulative deviation of 0.7% of GDP (or 0.4% taking into account defense spending flexibility). ⓘ
C3-T, context: The Council of the EU endorsed Spain’s national medium-term fiscal-structural plan covering 2025–2028, recommending maximum net expenditure growth rates of 3.7% in 2025, 3.5% in 2026, 3.2% in 2027, and 3.0% in 2028. ⓘ
C3-T, context: Spain activated the national escape clause of the Stability and Growth Pact for the period 2025–2028 to allow for deviation from recommended net expenditure growth rates to support increased defense spending. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The structural primary balance is projected at -0.3% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 47% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
**C3*, context**: The SPB before cost of ageing is assumed at -0.3% of GDP from 2026 onwards. This is in line with past fiscal performance. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered

C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered: Long-term fiscal pressures are rising due to aging, with pension spending projected to increase by 3.2 percentage points of GDP from 2023 to 2050. The gap between pension expenditure and social security contributions is widening, creating implicit liabilities. Reforms such as a life expectancy adjustment are recommended to ensure sustainability ⓘ.
C3-A, default is chosen, not only suffered: Political fragmentation has prevented the approval of a budget by parliament since 2023. This has impeded the implementation of necessary tax reforms, such as simplifying the tax system and shifting the tax burden from labour to consumption and environmental taxes. The European Commission notes that no substantial reforms of the tax mix have been delivered due to parliamentary difficulties. ⓘ
C3-A, context: The average share of labor taxes in total tax revenue increased from 48.7% in 2015–2019 to 51.8% in 2020–2024. Non-indexation of personal income tax brackets and rises in social security rates have accelerated the shift towards labor taxation. Spain has the largest value-added tax (VAT) policy gaps in the European Union. ⓘ

title: Spain
text:
Outlook Material

Topic: Productivity and SMEs: SMEs face barriers including limited access to finance, high administrative burdens, and low adoption of advanced digital technologies. Only 26% of SMEs adopted cloud services in 2023, below the EU average. Productivity gaps persist between micro/small firms and large firms ⓘ.
Topic: Labor Market and Demographics: Population aging is advancing faster than in most OECD countries. The old-age dependency ratio is projected to increase by 41 percentage points by 2054. Employment rates for older workers remain low, and non-contributory unemployment assistance for those over 52 discourages job search ⓘ.
Topic: Climate Resilience: Spain is highly exposed to climate risks, with economic losses from disasters among the highest in Europe. Floods, droughts, and heatwaves threaten growth and public finances. Water pricing does not reflect scarcity, undermining efficient use ⓘ.
Outlook Factors, investor base: Slightly increasing share of government debt held by non-residents is a risk-increasing factor. ⓘ
Climate Risk: Under the “Fragmented Action” climate scenario, debt could be around 6 pps. of GDP higher in 2050. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, defense: Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine constitutes an existential challenge. Spain is utilizing the national escape clause to increase defense spending, which is permitted under the EU fiscal framework provided it does not endanger fiscal sustainability in the medium term. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, energy: Geopolitical tensions and the war in the Middle East have led to risks of energy supply disruptions. Spain adopted temporary, targeted fiscal measures to mitigate high energy prices. The European Commission warns that broad and untargeted measures entail large fiscal costs and are inefficient. ⓘ
Outlook Factors, climate: Climate-related hazards pose significant risks. Extreme weather events resulted in economic losses of EUR 119.6 billion between 1980 and 2024. Climate insurance coverage remains low. ⓘ
Regional disparities: Long-standing structural challenges persist, with only four regions (Madrid, Basque Country, Navarra, Catalonia) having GDP per capita above the EU average. Depopulation in rural areas and concentration of growth in coastal and capital areas exacerbate territorial imbalances in labour supply, public services, and development capabilities. ⓘ
Housing and social inclusion: Spain faces severe housing affordability issues, particularly in urban centers and tourist areas. Child poverty remains high (33.8% at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025), and the effectiveness of social transfers in reducing poverty is among the lowest in the EU. ⓘ
Energy and climate: Spain is expanding renewable energy capacity but faces grid constraints and permitting bottlenecks. The country is vulnerable to climate change impacts, including heatwaves, droughts, and wildfires, which pose significant economic and environmental costs. ⓘ

Key themes include the slowdown in GDP growth due to a global energy shock, rising inflation, and a widening general government deficit driven by increased defence spending and labour tax reforms. Structural challenges regarding productivity, a shrinking working-age population, and regional disparities are highlighted. Long-term debt sustainability assessments indicate medium-term risks, with debt projected to rise significantly over the next decade.

text:
Economic

C1* Growth (Growth)

C1-E Broken or dominated sample
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-T Structural break in trend

C1-T, structural break: The European Commission forecasts that EU GDP growth will slow to 1.1% in 2026 and the Euro area to 0.9%, due to an energy price shock from the Middle East conflict. Growth is projected to recover to 1.4% (EU) and 1.2% (Euro area) in 2027. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: GDP growth is forecast to slow to 1.4% in 2026 and pick up to 1.6% in 2027 due to the Middle East conflict. ⓘ
C1-T, context: Labour productivity reached 62.2% of the EU average (GDP per hour worked) in 2025. Productivity growth has lagged behind wage growth, reducing cost competitiveness. ⓘ
C1-T, structural break: The OECD notes that weak private investment, innovation, and a shrinking working-age population continue to weigh on potential economic growth. Implementing structural reforms could raise GDP per capita growth by about 1.1 percentage points per year until 2036. ⓘ



C1-A1 Growth not thin-tailed or serially independent
No evidence in the sources yet.


C1-A2 Inherited competitiveness gap

C1-A2, competitiveness gap: Rising wages have led to a strong increase in unit labor costs, weighing on the competitiveness of domestic firms. The working-age population is projected to further decline by 6% between 2024 and 2030. ⓘ



Other growth context

C1*, context: The economy recovered with real GDP growth of 2.1% in 2025, driven by private consumption and investment. Growth is forecast to slow to 1.4% in 2026 and pick up slightly to 1.6% in 2027. ⓘ
C1*, context: Nominal compensation per employee increased by 8.4% in 2025. Wage growth is predicted to slow to 7.0% in 2026 and 5.8% in 2027. ⓘ

title: Latvia
text:
Fiscal

C3* Fiscal capacity and plan (Fiscal Capacity)

C3-E Estimator fails or rests on one episode
No evidence in the sources yet.


C3-T History lags policy

C3*, context: The European Commission projects a structural primary deficit of 2.1% of GDP as of 2026. This is low compared with past fiscal performance. Ageing-related expenditure is projected to remain stable. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The general government deficit is forecast to increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, context: The Council of the EU activated the national escape clause for Latvia in July 2025 to facilitate the transition to higher levels of defence spending. Total government expenditure on defence amounted to 3.2% of GDP in 2025 and is forecast to increase to 4.1% in 2026 and 5.5% in 2027. ⓘ
C3-T, history lags policy: The fiscal stance was strongly expansionary in 2025 due to rising defense spending, which increased from 3.3% of GDP in 2024 to 3.7% in 2025 and is expected to reach 4.7% in 2026. The structural fiscal deficit is projected to increase to 2.5% of GDP in 2026. ⓘ



C3-A Default is chosen, not only suffered
No evidence in the sources yet.


Other fiscal context

C3*, context: The structural primary balance is projected at -2.1% of GDP on average for 2026-2035. The fiscal consolidation space is 75% in the baseline scenario. ⓘ
C3*, context: The government deficit increased to 2.5% of GDP in 2025. The Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast projects the deficit will increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. This widening is driven by increasing defence expenditure and the impact of labour tax reforms on revenue. ⓘ
C3*, context: Latvia’s tax revenue was 34.9% of GDP in 2024, remaining below the EU average of 39.4%. A 2025 labour tax reform lowered the tax burden for low- and middle-income earners but created a significant revenue gap. ⓘ
C3-T, consolidation needs: To stabilize public debt, a fiscal adjustment of 2.3% of GDP is needed by 2032, requiring a shift from a structural primary deficit of 1.2% of GDP in 2026 to a surplus of 0.8% of GDP. ⓘ
C3*, context: The OECD recommends raising tax revenue by shifting the burden from labor to corporate income, property, and environmental taxes, and strengthening tax enforcement to reduce informality. ⓘ
C3*, context: The S2 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.2 percentage point improvement. The S1 indicator points to medium risk, requiring a 2.4 percentage point effort. ⓘ

title: Latvia
text:
Outlook Material

Competitiveness: Latvia’s GDP per capita was 71% of the EU average in 2025, significantly below its Baltic peers. Convergence is slowing due to lagging productivity and skills shortages. ⓘ
Security: Latvia successfully disconnected from the Russian-operated electricity system in February 2025, synchronizing with the Continental European Synchronous Area. This increases energy independence. However, the country faces hybrid threats and cyberattacks, particularly in border regions. ⓘ
Regional Disparities: Significant disparities exist between Riga and other regions. Non-Riga regions have GDP per capita below 50% of the EU average and suffer from depopulation and low productivity. ⓘ
Political/Geopolitical Risks: Downside risks include escalation of geopolitical tensions, particularly the war in Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East, which could affect risk premiums and energy prices. ⓘ
Labor Market: Labor shortages are exacerbated by a declining working-age population and emigration, contributing to inflationary pressures and rising unit labor costs. ⓘ

title: Economic Forecast
text:
Methods

The forecast uses technical assumptions derived from futures markets for energy prices, exchange rates, and interest rates. The baseline assumes a relatively swift, albeit partial, normalization of global energy supply conditions. ⓘ
Inflation projections incorporate the pass-through of higher energy prices to consumer prices, with a focus on the divergence between energy-sensitive and wage-sensitive components. ⓘ
The forecast is made under a ‘no-policy-change’ assumption, incorporating adopted or credibly announced fiscal measures by the cut-off date. ⓘ
Debt projections are based on the general government balance, interest expenditures, and stock-flow adjustments. ⓘ

title: Debt Sustainability Monitor
text:
Methods

The document uses a “no-fiscal-policy-change” baseline from 2027 onwards, anchoring the structural primary balance (excluding cost of ageing) at the level projected for 2026. ⓘ
The baseline assumes the structural primary balance remains constant at its 2026 forecast level until 2036, except for ageing costs. ⓘ
Gross financing needs consist of the general government deficit, debt redemptions, and stock-flow adjustments. ⓘ
Long-term fiscal sustainability indicators S1 and S2 measure the required fiscal effort. S2 is the change needed to stabilize debt over an infinite horizon. S1 is the change needed to bring debt to 60% of GDP by 2070. ⓘ
Risk categories for S1 and S2 are assigned based on the size of the adjustment: low if less than 2% of GDP, medium if 2-6%, and high if greater than 6%. ⓘ
Medium-term growth projections beyond the forecast horizon use the Economic Policy Committee and Price and Inflation Projections Working Group (EPC/POWG) T+10 methodology. ⓘ
Real GDP growth is adjusted for fiscal multiplier effects in the year T+2 using a multiplier of 0.6. ⓘ
Stochastic projections employ 10,000 shocks to assess uncertainty, covering 80% of simulated debt paths. ⓘ
Stock-flow adjustments are explicitly modeled for 2025 and 2026 in some cases but set to zero thereafter in the baseline. ⓘ
Interest rates on new and rolled-over debt converge linearly to market-based forward nominal rates by 2035. ⓘ
Inflation is assumed to converge linearly towards the inflation expectations 10 years ahead. ⓘ

title: Country Report
text:
Methods

The European Commission uses historical data and medium-term forecasts (e.g., Spring 2026 Forecast) to assess Growth, noting productivity trends and GDP drivers. ⓘ
Fiscal Fiscal Capacity is assessed based on the general government balance, primary balance, and structural adjustments, referencing specific forecast years. ⓘ
Refinancing Need and debt sustainability are evaluated using debt-to-GDP ratios and public investment levels, within the European Commission’s debt sustainability analysis framework. ⓘ
The document reports real GDP growth, nominal unit labour cost growth, and wage growth to assess economic momentum and competitiveness pressures. ⓘ
Inflation Differential is assessed using Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) data to evaluate price stability and differentials. ⓘ
Fiscal capacity evaluations include tax revenue structures and spending compositions. ⓘ
Refinancing risks are analyzed via tax arrears and shadow economy estimates. ⓘ
Backstop Eligibility context is derived from compliance with EU fiscal frameworks and the use of flexibility clauses. ⓘ
Outlook Factors are assessed through structural issues like public procurement inefficiencies and institutional quality. ⓘ
The European Commission estimates potential growth using production function approaches, accounting for labour supply and total factor productivity. ⓘ
Fiscal capacity is monitored via the medium-term fiscal-structural plan and excessive deficit procedures. ⓘ
The report uses historical GDP growth data and medium-term forecasts to assess growth potential, highlighting structural factors such as labor market rigidity and low business dynamism as constraints on productivity and growth. ⓘ
The document analyzes fiscal capacity through the lens of the medium-term fiscal structural plan, assessing the plausibility of the projected primary balance improvements. ⓘ
The report details the composition of public debt and financing needs, including the impact of high interest payments and the use of EU loans for defence. ⓘ
The assessment of backstop eligibility is informed by Belgium’s status under the Excessive Deficit Procedure and its compliance record. ⓘ
The document relies on the European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for projections of the general government deficit and debt, assessing fiscal capacity through the new national fiscal framework. ⓘ
The assessment of backstop eligibility is informed by the status of the excessive deficit procedure, noting it is held in abeyance due to the national escape clause. ⓘ
The European Commission’s medium-term growth forecasts deviate from historical means, influenced by structural factors such as demographic trends, energy prices, and sectoral shifts. ⓘ
The Commission’s debt sustainability analysis indicates high fiscal sustainability risks in the medium term for France. ⓘ
The MRP inputs for refinancing need are derived from the projected general government debt stock, interest expenditure, and primary balance. ⓘ
The assessment considers France’s status under the EU fiscal framework (EDP) and compliance with recommendations. ⓘ
The document uses the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast to project potential growth and real GDP growth. ⓘ
Fiscal projections are based on the medium-term fiscal-structural plan and the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast. ⓘ
Debt and deficit figures are sourced from the Commission Spring 2026 Forecast and national accounts. ⓘ
The document uses historical gross domestic product growth data and medium-term forecasts to assess the growth trend. ⓘ
The document reports the general government balance and primary surplus as percentages of gross domestic product. ⓘ
The document provides general government gross debt as a percentage of gross domestic product, with projections for 2026 and 2027. ⓘ
The document references Greece’s status under the Stability and Growth Pact, including the activation of the National Escape Clause. ⓘ
The document uses historical GDP growth data to illustrate productivity stagnation and regional disparities. It references Eurostat and European Commission forecast data for medium-term trends. ⓘ
The report relies on the European Commission Spring 2026 Forecast for deficit and debt projections. It analyzes the primary balance and the impact of stock-flow adjustments. ⓘ
The document details the debt stock, including holdings by insurers and pension funds, and discusses the cost of servicing public debt. ⓘ
The document references the European Commission’s assessment under the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure and the status of the excessive deficit procedure. ⓘ
The document provides historical real GDP growth and medium-term forecasts from the Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast. It notes productivity levels relative to the EU average. ⓘ
The document reports HICP inflation forecasts for 2026 and 2027. It does not provide a specific euro-area average inflation projection for direct differential calculation, but implies convergence toward the ECB target via the 2027 forecast of 2.2%. ⓘ
The document reports primary balance proxies via general government deficit and debt ratios. It details the impact of defence spending and tax reforms on fiscal sustainability. ⓘ
The document reports general government debt-to-GDP ratios and gross financing needs are implicit in the deficit and debt figures. It notes the activation of the national escape clause. ⓘ
The European Commission uses standard national accounts data for GDP. It also references Modified Gross National Income (GNI*) to better reflect the income standards of Irish residents, excluding globalization effects. The report notes that GDP figures are heavily influenced by multinational activity. ⓘ
The European Commission assesses fiscal position using both standard GDP-based metrics and GNI*-adjusted metrics. It highlights the distortion caused by windfall corporate taxes in headline budget figures. The primary balance is implied by the general government surplus given the low debt stock. ⓘ

The document relies on the European Commission’s Spring 2026 Forecast for general government balance, primary balance implications (via primary spending evolution), and debt sustainability analysis based on the country’s medium-term fiscal-structural plan endorsed by the Council. ⓘ

The document provides historical real GDP growth and medium-term forecasts, which are inputs for estimating the growth drift and volatility parameters. ⓘ
The document reports headline HICP inflation for Malta and compares it with EU trends, providing inputs for the inflation differential parameter. ⓘ

Structural factors such as regional disparities, low innovation, energy dependency, and weaknesses in the justice and anti-corruption systems are highlighted as key outlook factors. ⓘ

title: Post-Programme Surveillance Report
text: The European Commission issues these reports for euro-area member states that received financial assistance, until most of the loans are repaid. They assess the countries’ capacity to repay the loans of the European Stability Mechanism and its predecessor institutions. The document type covers economic, fiscal, and financial developments and is published every spring and autumn. This card currently draws on one source document.
